answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. A determination as to whether an applicant satisfies the statutory criteria for naturalisation can only be made after an application has been received. Last week, Minister O'Callaghan and I secured Government approval for the priority drafting of legislation to strengthen Ireland's naturalisation framework. The proposed legislation is intended to both strengthen the integrity of the naturalisation system and align Ireland more closely with the processes in several other EU Member States. The number and nationalities of those applying for naturalisation are provided in the document at the link below. My Department continues to register applications received in 2025, and the information provided is current up to 30 September 2025. In the document at the link, countries of origin with fewer than 10 applicants have been grouped under "Rest of the World" to avoid the possibility of identifying any individual. The processing times for applications are outlined in the table below. Decisions issued in any given year may relate to applications received in previous years, due to the time required to process applications. It is not possible to provide a maximum or minimum processing time. Table 1. Citizenship application processing times Year Median Processing time in months 2021 24 2022 19 2023 15 2024 8 2025 8 *Figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing Finally, the grounds for the revocation of citizenship are as set out in section 19 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 (as amended). Changes to this process were made by the Court, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024; these changes were required to address issues identified in a Supreme Court judgment that had found the then revocation process to be unconstitutional. Amendments to the process of revocation of citizenship came into effect from 7 April 2025 and the revised provisions can be found at: revisedacts.lawreform.ie/eli/1956/act/26/section/19/revised/en/html Under the new procedure, where the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration decides to revoke citizenship, they may do so under the five grounds set out in the 1956 Act. A notification of this intention is issued to the individual, who will be provided with the opportunity to make representations, and has 28 days to so, before a decision is made to revoke their certificate of naturalisation. Following receipt of those representations, or on expiry of the 28 days, if it is decided to proceed to revoke the certificate of naturalisation, then the individual has 14 days in which to request a Committee of Inquiry. Upon receipt of this request, the Minister will appoint a Committee of Inquiry, which will be composed of a chairperson who will be a retired Judge of the Circuit Court, the High Court, the Court of Appeal, or the Supreme Court, and two ordinary members with appropriate experience and qualifications. The Committee of Inquiry will be independent in its function of inquiry into the Minister's decision and can either affirm the decision or set it aside. In the last 10 years, 8 people have had their citizenship revoked, this includes two revocations since 7 April 2025. Naturalisation Applications Data

question: 278. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for naturalisation which satisfied the statutory conditions in section 15(1) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended, but which were nonetheless refused in the exercise of the Minister's discretion, in each of the past five years; the nature and extent of any data or evidence held by his Department on deficiencies in English, Irish or Irish Sign Language proficiency among applicants for naturalisation; and whether any such data informed the proposal to introduce mandatory language testing. [66112/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. I can inform the Deputy that my Department does not collate statistics on the number of applications refused under Section 15. Proficiency in either English or Irish does not form part of the current statutory criteria for naturalisation. Accordingly, my Department does not collect or record information on applicants' proficiency in either language for naturalisation purposes. Government recently approved the priority drafting of legislation to amend aspects of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. The General Scheme of the Bill, which will be published shortly, includes proposals to create a power to introduce language tests in either English, Irish or Irish Sign Language, together with an Irish civics, society and politics test. The policy objective underpinning these reforms is to strengthen the integrity, durability and public confidence in the naturalisation system and to support the integration of those who seek to become Irish citizens.

question: 279. Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there is any flexibility to the moving date for families (details supplied). [66031/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On 26 May 2026, the Government agreed to commence a phased withdrawal of state-contracted commercial accommodation for people fleeing the war in Ukraine with Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland prior to 14 March 2024. This forms part of a wider transition programme to support people towards greater independence, while ensuring continued support for those who remain in need of state accommodation. The phased withdrawal of some commercial accommodation is being implemented on a region-by-region basis. All affected residents have received advance notice of the changes, as well as information and support from my department, the Irish Red Cross and the International Organisation for Migration regarding available accommodation and transition options. Ongoing supports are being provided for people with particular circumstances that would make it difficult for them to manage in independent accommodation. People in those circumstances were asked to self-declare their need for continued accommodation and provide evidence to support their application. The application form for continued state-supported commercial accommodation was available online from 04 August to 11 September 2026. Applicants who have been approved will be accommodated in a Designated Accommodation Centre in various locations around the country. There is no guarantee continued accommodation will be in the same area in which a person currently lives. Every effort will be made to continue to accommodate those with established HSE care plans to remain in the relevant Community Health Organisation area for continuity of care. Families with children attending school who move area can contact their local Regional Education and Language Team (REALT) if they need help finding a school place. Relevant information is provided by the Department of Education at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-education/publications/information-for-schools-ukraine/ Schools are required to admit all applicants unless the school is full or in very limited, defined circumstances. Families are encouraged to enrol their children as soon as they know the location of their new accommodation. Residents who have not submitted an application for ongoing accommodation within the application period will not receive a further offer of state-contracted commercial accommodation as part of this process. They will be required to vacate the premises by the date specified in the notification they have received, which for residents of the property referred to is 31 October 2026. It is not possible to remain at the accommodation after this date. Persons availing of temporary protection are also free to make their own private arrangements for accommodation through their own means, or by using supports provided by the Department of Social Protection.

question: 280. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of declarations of intention to retain Irish citizenship received from naturalised Irish citizens residing outside the State in each year since 2015, in tabular form. [66030/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 274, 275 and 280 together. As the Deputy is aware, any person granted Irish citizenship through naturalisation must intend in good faith to continue to reside in the State after their naturalisation. Since 2011, approximately 236,000 people have been granted Irish citizenship through naturalisation. My Department does not collect or maintain data on the residence status of persons after they have attended a citizenship ceremony and received a certificate of naturalisation. Accordingly, my Department does not hold data on the number or proportion of naturalised citizens who remain resident in the State for five, ten or fifteen years following naturalisation. Similarly, my Department does not maintain datasets relating to the long-term residence, emigration or retention rates of naturalised Irish citizens. Where a naturalised citizen resides outside the State, for whatever reason, the person concerned should complete a “Declaration of Intention to Retain Irish Citizenship” (Form 5). This form should be submitted annually for so long as the person remains ordinarily resident outside Ireland. Further information is available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/intention-to-retain-irish-citizenship/ It has not been possible to compile the figures of Form 5 declarations received from 2015 as the Deputy has requested. I will write to the Deputy directly once this information is to hand. The below table outlines the number of Form 5 declarations received by my Department in each year since 2021. Year Form 5 2021 632 2022 688 2023 753 2024 768 2025 785 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing.

question: 281. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to advise if there are protocols for prisoners during their time in prison for a crime (details supplied) regarding access to the public, being in public-facing environments and being in less secure areas with prison officers, such as staff canteens. [66065/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by the Irish Prison Service (IPS) that, as part of the initial committal process, every person committed to custody is referred to the Chief Officer responsible for Work and Training for an assessment of their suitability to engage in work, training and other constructive activities within the prison. This assessment takes account of all known risk and suitability information. Decisions are supported by the Governors Committal Interview, Incentivised Regimes Policy, the Approved Working Gratuity policy and Integrated Sentence Management Policy. As people in custody progress through their sentences, their suitability to undertake roles involving greater responsibility is kept under review as part of their sentence management and preparation for reintegration into the community. People in custody work in internal staff canteens in most closed prisons as part of their work and training. They may also work in selected staff areas, subject to security and risk assessment and appropriate sentence management. In these circumstances, the Governor must be satisfied that appropriate security, risk assessment and supervision arrangements are in place. I am advised that where a work, training or rehabilitative activity requires a person to work outside the prison grounds, the Governor may recommend that the person be granted temporary release, subject to specific conditions. Each application is considered on its individual merits and must be approved by the Operations Directorate. I am further advised that within the open-centre estate, members of the public may enter an open centre to avail of a service, such as the car-wash service and coffee shop at Loughan House. In these circumstances, the Governor must be satisfied that appropriate security, risk assessment and supervision arrangements are in place. People accommodated in open centres may also be approved for temporary release to avail of work and training opportunities in the community as part of their sentence-management plans. Before a final determination is made, a number of factors are considered, including: • the nature and gravity of the offence to which the sentence being served by the person relates • the sentence concerned and any recommendation made by the Court in relation to the sentence imposed • the person’s previous criminal record • the potential threat to the safety and security of the public should the person be released • the risk that the person might commit an offence during any period of temporary release • the risk of the person failing to comply with any of the conditions of temporary release • any report or recommendation made by the Governor, the Garda Síochána or the Probation Service. The legislative basis for temporary release is set out in the Criminal Justice Act 1960, as amended by the Criminal Justice (Temporary Release of Prisoners) Act 2003. All applications for temporary release are assessed on a case-by-case basis, having regard to all relevant information available and public safety is paramount when these decisions are made.

question: 282. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has conducted any workforce planning exercise, manpower assessment, service-capacity review or similar exercise relating to the future provision of criminal legal aid services since 1 January 2020; the dates on which such reviews were completed; if he will provide details of the principal findings; if his Department has undertaken any assessment of recruitment and retention trends among solicitors undertaking criminal legal aid work for the same period; and if he will provide details of any such assessment. [66123/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 282 to 285, inclusive, together. I fully recognise the crucial role played by the legal professions in the effective administration of criminal justice, and equally that the Criminal Legal Aid scheme is fundamental to upholding the constitutional and human right to a legal defence. I am committed to improving efficiencies for court users, legal practitioners and the Irish taxpayer. The new District Court Criminal Legal Aid Scheme will allow for those efficiencies. I published the Review and Reform Proposal of the Criminal Legal Aid fee structure for the District Court on 2 July 2026, which provides detail on the analysis conducted on these reforms. My department has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas, at oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. More than 600 solicitors remain on the Criminal Legal Aid panel as criminal cases continue to be dealt with in the courts. 24 have recently reapplied to join the panel. Since the commencement of the new system over 1,430 new certificates for legal aid have issued. Of the cases concluded under the new system since 1st July 2026, 75% concluded with one court appearance only and 99% of concluded cases were finalised within five appearances. Since October 2025, there has been ongoing engagement between myself and my officials with the Law Society and Bar Council in relation to the changes to the criminal legal aid fee structure. My department continues to keep the operation of the new criminal legal aid arrangements in the District Court under review.

question: 286. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeline for the processing of a peace commissioner application for a person (details supplied). [66196/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Peace Commissioners are appointed by the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in accordance with section 88 of the Courts of Justice Act 1924. The appointment of a Peace Commissioner is entirely at the discretion of the Minister. The fact that an applicant or nominee may be suitable for appointment does not, in itself, provide any entitlement to appointment as a Peace Commissioner and other factors, such as the need for appointments in particular areas at a specific point in time, may be taken into account. I can confirm to the Deputy that the matter raised is currently under consideration and the person concerned will be contacted in the coming weeks.

question: 287. Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide details of the costs incurred to date, together with the total estimated expenditure for phases 1 and 2, of the development at Castlerea Prison, including the provision of four modular six-bedroom houses, an additional ancillary services building and the construction of 21 lower-security units at The Grove, including all associated planning, construction and related project expenses, in tabular form. [66291/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by the Irish Prison Service that Phase 1 of the development at The Grove, Castlerea Prison has been completed and is fully operational. Phase 1 provided a single terrace of four modular houses, each with six bedrooms (24 spaces in total), together with a new support and ancillary services building, expanding the footprint of The Grove. The total final cost, including all associated planning, construction and consultancy, will be confirmed once the final account process is completed, which is expected by the end of October 2026. I am further advised that Phase 2 will see the construction of 21 modular houses, each with 6 bedrooms within The Grove area of Castlerea Prison, creating an additional 126 prison spaces. Four of the units will provide access for a wheelchair user resident at ground floor level. As this phase of the project remains in progress, in line with public procurement and contract management procedures, cost information cannot be provided at this point as the final account has not yet been settled and remains commercially sensitive. Phase 2 is due to be completed and operational by the end Q2 2028.

question: 288. Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the budgeted cost of demolishing the old Cork Prison buildings, including all associated preparatory and clearance works. [66288/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised that the Irish Prison Service (IPS) has recently conducted a Part 9 planning process for certain demolitions on the old Cork Prison site in line with the Planning and Development Regulations 2001 (as amended, which corresponds to provisions under Section 181 of the Planning and Development Act). The IPS has engaged the services of consultants and contractors to carry out various investigative works/surveys in the old Cork Prison, the outcome of which will inform the potential tender process for demolition. As the tendering process is commercially sensitive it is not proposed to outline potential costs at this juncture.

answer: Minister for Health Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices; therefore, the matter has been referred to the HSE for attention and direct reply to the Deputy.

question: 7. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Taoiseach when the Cabinet Committee on justice, migration and social affairs will meet next. [64288/26]
answer: An Cathaoirleach Gníomhach (Deputy Marie Sherlock) With the agreement of the House, I propose that each Member be allocated two minutes each. Is that agreed? Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett Can I get in as well? An Cathaoirleach Gníomhach (Deputy Marie Sherlock) Yes. We can have 1 minute, 45 seconds each. The Taoiseach We are very tolerant people here. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett I am a regular. The Taoiseach We are very generous. I propose to take Questions Nos. 7 to 13, inclusive, together. The Cabinet committee on justice, migration and social affairs oversees the implementation of programme for Government commitments that are in relation to matters under those areas. It covers a range of policy areas, including domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, policing and justice reform, migration and initiatives tackling local-area disadvantage. Getting more gardaí on our streets to prevent and detect crime is the Government's first priority, and the Government has allocated over €2.74 billion to the Garda Vote this year, the largest allocation ever. The Government welcomes the progress made by An Garda Síochána with respect to recruitment in recent years. It is expected that the number of gardaí will soon exceed the previous record high of 14,758 in March 2020 and the number of gardai will reach 15,000 in the near future. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is continuing apace. Groups of around 200 new gardai are now regularly entering and attesting from the Garda College approximately every three months. Five hundred and sixty-six probationer gardaí have been assigned to stations around the country already in 2026, with two more attestations due to take place before the end of the year. The 2025 programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer migration system that, among other things, protects the integrity of our immigration framework. Last November, the Government approved a package of policy and legislative reforms to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system, ensuring it is rules-based, efficient and more closely aligned with those of other EU member states. The Cabinet committee was established in February 2025 following the appointment of the new Government in January. Its first meeting was on 10 April 2025 and it met most recently on Monday, 14 September. The next meeting will be scheduled in due course. In addition to meetings of the Cabinet committee, I have regular engagements with Ministers at Cabinet and individually to discuss issues relating to their Departments. Deputy Albert Dolan A huge amount of work has been done by An Garda Síochána to recruit new members. Understandably, after each attestation, the gardaí are allocated to different stations right across the country. My huge problem with that is that in the last three attestations, Galway received, in total across the over 700 gardaí that were allocated, only four gardaí. That is not four gardaí for one town in Galway or one small village; that is for the entirety of County Galway, the city and Connemara. It is a huge area that received only four gardaí. I wrote to the Commissioner on 24 July to highlight this matter because I was really frustrated by it. What it worked out at was that in Galway, we were receiving one garda per 64,000 of population. That was our allocation. I welcome the recent reallocation of 28 additional gardaí to the high-visibility policing efforts now taking place in Galway city. From speaking to the community gardaí in Galway city centre, they are seeing hugely positive results from this high-visibility policing. It is working in Galway city. Galway needs to be focused on and given a greater allocation moving forward. That means that stations in Athenry, Gort, Loughrea, Headford, Portumna and Tuam would see an increased allocation, that we would start to see that flow not just into Galway city but throughout the county, and that people would see higher visibility from the gardaí in the county because there would be the resources to do so. What consideration will be given to the fact that Galway has had such an underallocation of gardaí from recent attestations? Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan I raise an issue in relation to migration, our deportation process and how it works. I have been in here six and a half years. I have never once objected to an international protection accommodation service, IPAS, centre. I have never once come in here and spoken about migration, if the truth be told. I feel obliged to say that before I make my suggestion or criticism. At present, when somebody is given a deportation order to leave the country - 4,700 were given in 2025 and approximately 434 of those were enforced - the vast majority of those people in this country who are issued such a notice are expected to voluntarily return themselves. To be fair, I would say that happens in the majority of the cases I have come across and it is what gardaí and people involved with migration are telling me. However, there is a third cohort of people who are termed "otherwise confirmed". Essentially, those people volunteer the information to the authorities before they leave. However, from speaking with gardaí, a number of people go unaccounted for and a vast amount of the State's time is spent looking for those people. We do not know if they have actually left. My observation is that the Garda's powers and resources are better utilised enforcing the deportation orders and the laws we have, rather than finding out whether somebody has left the country. Gardaí find themselves seeking out people who might have left six months previously as they have no way of tracing that. Next week, at our policy meeting with the Minister for Justice, who has done a good job since taking over, I will raise with him the issue of traceability and what we are going to do to ensure the people who are served with notices are actually leaving. I would love to say they will leave of their own volition, but in cases where they are not how are we going to trace that in future? Deputy Tom Brabazon Yesterday, the Garda Representative Association told the justice committee that gardaí need greater clarity on the pursuit policy, proper pursuit training, stronger legal protections and adequate roads policing resources. My constituents certainly want to see our gardaí supported in order that they can carry out their duty. I have previously raised the introduction of a separate driving licence for gardaí and a statutory indemnity for gardaí carrying out their role reasonably. What measures will the Government introduce to address these concerns and ensure gardaí are properly equipped and protected when carrying out their duties? Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere Everyone has the right to be safe and to feel safe in their homes and communities. Across the country, communities are dealing with the scourge of crime and antisocial behaviour. The Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities and significant funding has been put into resourcing An Garda Síochána. There has been an additional €500 million over the last five years. As the Taoiseach said, by the end of this year, for the first time ever, we will have about 15,000 gardaí serving the State. It will be the highest figure since the foundation of the State. I want to see a greater geographical spread of the new resources that are coming on board. Two attestations will take place towards the end of the year. While I welcome the additional gardaí who have been stationed in Cork, Dublin and Limerick, I would like to see a greater geographical spread around the country, in particular, in my constituency. People who live in rural Ireland want to feel safe every bit as much as people living in the cities. I look at stations in places like Graiguenamanagh, Goresbridge, Thomastown, across to Bennetsbridge, down to Callan and Mooncoin and over to Borris and Bagenalstown. We need additional gardaí in all these places because people are telling me they want to see gardaí with their boots on, on the street, on the beat and engaging with the community. We have put fantastic resources into the Garda but we just need a greater geographical spread. I implore the Taoiseach to use his influence to try to get a greater rural spread with the additional gardaí. Deputy Louis O'Hara I too raise Garda numbers. Only four of 566 new Garda recruits this year have been allocated to Galway and all four went to Galway city. In recent weeks, there was an announcement of 28 new gardaí for Galway city and Salthill but none for stations in county towns like Athenry, Loughrea, Gort and Tuam. These are stations that have not seen any meaningful increase in Garda numbers in years. Assurances have been given that rural towns and villages will see an increased allocation but it has not happened. Across County Galway, there are ongoing issues with rural crime and antisocial and criminal behaviour in towns and villages. This is causing an awful lot of misery for people and I am being contacted regularly by residents about serious issues and by people who do not feel safe because of the lack of a Garda presence in our areas. Athenry, which is a growing town of 5,000 people, does not even have a full-time Garda station or Garda presence. It is totally unacceptable. When are stations in rural east Galway going to see increased allocations to ensure we have an adequate Garda presence in our communities? Deputy Mark Ward Yesterday at the justice committee, we heard that not one garda in the State is trained in pursuit driving. We heard this from the AGSI, the GRA and Garda management. In 2026, I find this absolutely shocking. From speaking to members of the public after yesterday’s meeting, they also find it absolutely shocking. During the meeting, one of the Garda representatives pulled out a policy document from 1988 which stated Garda members were to get pursuit training. Since Ray Houghton put the ball in the England net that year, we have not seen one garda trained in pursuit in this country. The Government said it was going to prioritise pursuit training after the M9 tragedy but we heard yesterday that by the end of this year, only six gardaí in the State will have completed pursuit training. How did we get to a situation where, in 2026, not one garda in the State is trained to pursue a vehicle that is fleeing or refusing to stop for gardaí? It is a simple question and the public want to know the answer to it. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett Last year, 122 students from Palestine, many of them coming from the horror of Gaza, were accepted into universities and colleges here to study and were given the visas to do that. Only 22 of those visa applications were refused. This year, 39 were granted and 103 refused. It is clear from the testimony of the colleges, universities, student unions and so on that something has changed, which is quite incredible, in the refusal of visas to people fleeing the most horrific conditions in Gaza. These students have been accepted by the third level institutions and in most cases the fees are not an issue, meaning there is no real cost for the State at all. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett I am a regular. The Taoiseach We are very generous. I propose to take Questions Nos. 7 to 13, inclusive, together. Getting more gardaí on our streets to prevent and detect crime is the Government's first priority, and the Government has allocated over €2.74 billion to the Garda Vote this year, the largest allocation ever. The Government welcomes the progress made by An Garda Síochána with respect to recruitment in recent years. It is expected that the number of gardaí will soon exceed the previous record high of 14,758 in March 2020 and the number of gardai will reach 15,000 in the near future. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is continuing apace. Groups of around 200 new gardai are now regularly entering and attesting from the Garda College approximately every three months. Five hundred and sixty-six probationer gardaí have been assigned to stations around the country already in 2026, with two more attestations due to take place before the end of the year. The 2025 programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer migration system that, among other things, protects the integrity of our immigration framework. Last November, the Government approved a package of policy and legislative reforms to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system, ensuring it is rules-based, efficient and more closely aligned with those of other EU member states. The Cabinet committee was established in February 2025 following the appointment of the new Government in January. Its first meeting was on 10 April 2025 and it met most recently on Monday, 14 September. The next meeting will be scheduled in due course. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan I raise an issue in relation to migration, our deportation process and how it works. I have been in here six and a half years. I have previously raised the introduction of a separate driving licence for gardaí and a statutory indemnity for gardaí carrying out their role reasonably. What measures will the Government introduce to address these concerns and ensure gardaí are properly equipped and protected when carrying out their duties? Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere Everyone has the right to be safe and to feel safe in their homes and communities. Across the country, communities are dealing with the scourge of crime and antisocial behaviour. The Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities and significant funding has been put into resourcing An Garda Síochána. There has been an additional €500 million over the last five years. As the Taoiseach said, by the end of this year, for the first time ever, we will have about 15,000 gardaí serving the State. It will be the highest figure since the foundation of the State. I want to see a greater geographical spread of the new resources that are coming on board. Two attestations will take place towards the end of the year. While I welcome the additional gardaí who have been stationed in Cork, Dublin and Limerick, I would like to see a greater geographical spread around the country, in particular, in my constituency. People who live in rural Ireland want to feel safe every bit as much as people living in the cities. I look at stations in places like Graiguenamanagh, Goresbridge, Thomastown, across to Bennetsbridge, down to Callan and Mooncoin and over to Borris and Bagenalstown. We need additional gardaí in all these places because people are telling me they want to see gardaí with their boots on, on the street, on the beat and engaging with the community. We have put fantastic resources into the Garda but we just need a greater geographical spread. I implore the Taoiseach to use his influence to try to get a greater rural spread with the additional gardaí. Deputy Louis O'Hara I too raise Garda numbers. Only four of 566 new Garda recruits this year have been allocated to Galway and all four went to Galway city. In recent weeks, there was an announcement of 28 new gardaí for Galway city and Salthill but none for stations in county towns like Athenry, Loughrea, Gort and Tuam. These are stations that have not seen any meaningful increase in Garda numbers in years. Assurances have been given that rural towns and villages will see an increased allocation but it has not happened. Across County Galway, there are ongoing issues with rural crime and antisocial and criminal behaviour in towns and villages. This is causing an awful lot of misery for people and I am being contacted regularly by residents about serious issues and by people who do not feel safe because of the lack of a Garda presence in our areas. Athenry, which is a growing town of 5,000 people, does not even have a full-time Garda station or Garda presence. It is totally unacceptable. When are stations in rural east Galway going to see increased allocations to ensure we have an adequate Garda presence in our communities? Deputy Mark Ward Yesterday at the justice committee, we heard that not one garda in the State is trained in pursuit driving. We heard this from the AGSI, the GRA and Garda management. In 2026, I find this absolutely shocking. From speaking to members of the public after yesterday’s meeting, they also find it absolutely shocking. During the meeting, one of the Garda representatives pulled out a policy document from 1988 which stated Garda members were to get pursuit training. Since Ray Houghton put the ball in the England net that year, we have not seen one garda trained in pursuit in this country. The Government said it was going to prioritise pursuit training after the M9 tragedy but we heard yesterday that by the end of this year, only six gardaí in the State will have completed pursuit training. How did we get to a situation where, in 2026, not one garda in the State is trained to pursue a vehicle that is fleeing or refusing to stop for gardaí? It is a simple question and the public want to know the answer to it. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett Last year, 122 students from Palestine, many of them coming from the horror of Gaza, were accepted into universities and colleges here to study and were given the visas to do that. Only 22 of those visa applications were refused. This year, 39 were granted and 103 refused. It is clear from the testimony of the colleges, universities, student unions and so on that something has changed, which is quite incredible, in the refusal of visas to people fleeing the most horrific conditions in Gaza. These students have been accepted by the third level institutions and in most cases the fees are not an issue, meaning there is no real cost for the State at all. They come through either sanctuary programmes or sponsors. I was talking to a young Palestinian woman whose two siblings were refused. They have an American sponsor paying the fees, so there is no cost but they are still being refused. This looks like a sort of performative cruelty by the Department of justice. It is asking questions like whether the students can provide bank statements from the last couple of years from Gaza. Gaza has been bombed to bits and subjected to a genocide. The Department has asked the students whether they can prove they are going to return to Gaza. The people of Palestine and Gaza want to go home. Their problem is they are being bombed to bits by Israel and the world allows it to happen. When they are coming here to study, having been accepted by third level institutions, and given their numbers are tiny, could we show a bit of humanity and decency by allowing them to come here to study and giving them visas? Deputy Louis O'Hara Hear, hear. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett Will the Taoiseach ask the Minister, Deputy O'Callaghan, to do that? Deputy Michael Cahill I also raise Garda numbers in towns and villages, this time in Kerry. I am referring not just to Killarney and Tralee but to Castleisland, Dingle, Kenmare, Killorglin and Cahersiveen. In one particular area, Portmagee, there was always a garda until a few years ago. I have made representations on that. The other issue I wish to raise is drink spiking. It is becoming very common across the world, but also here, including in the Taoiseach's county. I am aware of cases there. I was approached recently by a prominent businessman in Killarney whose daughter had her drink spiked. He said only for the fact that he was working in the town, he would not have got to her in time. These incidents are leading to sexual assaults in most cases. Deputy Séamus McGrath and I will sit down shortly with the Minister for justice in regard to a Private Members' Bill. I hope the Taoiseach, the Government and our colleagues will support it. The Taoiseach I thank the Deputies for the range of questions that has been asked. We began with Deputy Dolan and there was another question later about Galway. Deputy Dolan made a very strong case for Galway county, particularly east Galway. As I said, Garda numbers have increased dramatically since Covid. There are 200 gardaí being attested every three months now. It seems the Commissioner has concentrated on getting big cities done first, and Dublin was the first of these. It got a very significant tranche for the high-visibility policing initiative. There was also Cork and Limerick. I will speak to the Minister and Commissioner in respect of Galway. It is an operational issue for the Garda, first and foremost. He understands the desire of the Government for wide coverage and so forth. That seems a low number. In reference to the figure of 28 mentioned by the Deputy, did that relate to Galway? Deputy Albert Dolan They were repatriated outside Galway. The Taoiseach That is an extra 28 for Galway. Deputy Albert Dolan For the city. The Taoiseach It was four for the county and 28 for the city. That is good. I take the Deputy's point. The towns he mentioned are large, including Athenry, Gort and so on. Deputy Cleere gave us a strong sense of the towns in Kilkenny. I take the point. Rural Ireland has its unique crime issues and people feel vulnerable if there is a sense that there is not a sufficient Garda presence. It is a budget priority to continue the momentum in terms of Garda recruitment for 2027. Deputy O'Sullivan made an interesting point on the migration question. He essentially said there should be better follow-up in terms of deportations. In 2025, about 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. Up to 24 July, 2,650 deportation orders had been signed this year. The number of deportation orders signed to 4 September 2026 has increased by 12% on 2025. In 2025, 2,111 people departed from the State under various mechanisms. I will speak to the Minister in respect of the voluntary return issue. It is a more effective and efficient way of doing it because deportations are significant in themselves. There has been an increase of about 80% in the number of deportations that have occurred compared to 2024. The Deputy's fundamental point is that we know the figures. People have nothing to live on if they hang around, and therefore there is an incentive to move on. I will speak to the Minister about tightening up the number of voluntary deportations. There has been a sea-change in the number of deportation orders that have been signed and planes have taken off with people on them. We have to have a firm and fair migration system and people have to know that the rules are enforced. There is a faster application process. We are speeding up the appeals process. The asylum pact is working. Migration numbers generally are down about 40% this year across Europe. A lot of Deputies opposite voted against the European Union asylum and migration pact. It is working and is effective, in particular in terms of returns. In response to Deputy Brabazon, the Minister indicated a commitment to changing legislation in respect of gardaí so that they would not lose their driving licence in the course of doing their duties or have their lives undermined by being dragged before the courts in the line of duty. That is a significant issue that the Minister is pursuing. Pursuit is dangerous and that is why gardaí need training. I acknowledge we need far more training than is in place. It is not today or yesterday that gardaí have been aware of these issues in terms of pursuing people. It is very dangerous because it can lead to further accidents and deaths. The training will happen. Further protocols are required. Deputy Shane Moynihan referred on Leaders' Questions to technology being deployed effectively. That is also very important. The Minister is considering a change in the law in respect of what Deputy Brabazon said in respect of protecting gardaí. I dealt with Deputy Cleere's issue in terms of better geographic spread around the country. Kilkenny is keen----- Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere And Carlow. The Taoiseach Tuigim, tuigim, tuigim. I have dealt with the issues in respect of Galway city. Deputy Mark Ward referred to pursuit training. It was a very good goal by Houghton in 1988. I take the Deputy's point. We must also be mindful of the fact that a lot has happened in the past four or five years in An Garda Síochána, in terms of recruitment activities and so on. There needs to be more focused training and so on, and there will be. Work is already under way with senior gardaí in colleges in the UK who are endeavouring to share expertise with UK police in terms of training and pursuit operations. Deputy Cahill provided a long list of Kerry towns that could do with gardaí. I will take on board what he said about Portmagee. The spiking of drinks is a horrendous and heinous crime and the Deputy is correct that there can be horrific consequences in terms of sexual assault. We would be supportive of a Private Members' Bill in that respect. The Deputy is pursuing that with Deputy McGrath. I will engage with the Minister.

question: 96. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if a further funding call is expected under the Community Climate Action Fund; and when he envisages this call to be made. [64183/26]
answer: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment The Community Climate Action Programme (CCAP) is funded by my Department through the Climate Action Fund. Across two strands, it supports and empowers communities to shape and build low carbon, sustainable communities and contribute to our national climate and energy targets. Strand 1 of CCAP is providing €56.1 million in funding across two phases to Local Authorities to enable community groups to run projects across five themes: Community Energy; Travel; Food and Waste; Shopping & Recycling; and Local Climate and Environmental Action. The initial phase, funding 650 projects, is due to complete before the end of 2026. In May this year, I announced the second phase of Strand 1 of CCAP valued at €29.5 million. In addition to this funding, I subsequently provided an additional €2.6 million which will enable local authorities fund projects from their reserve lists. This combined funding will see a further 820 community projects deliver between now and the end of 2027. In addition, €5m was provided under Strand 2 of CCAP between 2022 and 2025 to 19 community projects that focused on Climate education and capacity building. The potential for further rounds of funding under this programme are kept under active review. No further announcements are planned at this time and any future calls will be signalled well in advance.

question: 473. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Education and Youth the latest update on an application for additional school accommodation for a school (details supplied). [64167/26]
answer: Minister for Education and Youth I can confirm to the Deputy, that my department is in receipt of an application for capital funding under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme from the school in question. A total capital allocation of €7.55 billion for the Department of Education and Youth has been confirmed for the period 2026-2030 under the National Development Plan. As part of this NDP allocation my department will place a strong emphasis on provision for children with special educational needs, with a particular focus on meeting annual school place needs. In relation to project rollout for Large-Scale projects and Additional School Accommodation scheme projects, the approach will be to continue to maximise the capacity of the existing school estate as much as possible in the first instance and provide necessary additional capacity through targeted and prioritised project rollout over the course of 2026 to 2030 period to meet the most urgent and prioritised needs. As part of the NDP Implementation Plan for the education and youth sector, a first tranche of projects to progress to tender and/or construction during 2026 and 2027 was published in January 2026. Prioritisation will continue to identify further tranches of projects to proceed to tender and construction over the NDP period, with stakeholder consultation ongoing. Our NDP Implementation Plan will optimise outputs from the NDP allocations, with a strong focus on maximising existing school capacity, progressing priority projects where local capacity across schools in the area is insufficient, and ensuring delivery that is affordable, offers value for money, and meets functional needs. It is in this context that the application from the school in question will be considered and the school authorities will be notified of a decision in due course.

question: 729. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the way in which he envisages the secretarial scheme for councillors will look like as laid out in the local government taskforce implementation plan. [65072/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage I propose to take Questions Nos. 729, 730, 735, 754 and 755 together. The establishment of the Local Democracy Taskforce was a key priority in the Programme for Government. Government committed to strengthening local democracy and examining opportunities to increase the powers of elected Councillors, devolve functions to local government and improve local decision-making. The Taskforce, chaired by Jim Breslin, former Secretary General, undertook its work between June 2025 and February 2026. In relation to engagement with Chief Executives, the membership of the Taskforce comprised of Local Authority elected member representative bodies, Local Authority executive representatives, including from the County and City Management Association and Local Government Management Agency, the National Oversight and Audit Commission, the Local Government Audit Service, Department of Housing Local Government and Heritage and independent and other experts. The Local Democracy Taskforce Report was considered by Government and published on 22 July 2026, alongside the launch of the Government's Implementation Plan for Local Democracy Reform 2026-2029. This marks the beginning of the next phase of local government reform. The reforms set out in the Implementation Plan are designed to ensure that local government has the powers, structures, resources, and accountability mechanisms necessary to fulfil its role effectively. The reforms span a broad range of areas, including strengthening the role of councillors, enhancing public participation in local decision-making, improving transparency and accountability arrangements, strengthening the financial foundations of local government, and creating more structured engagement between central and local government. Action 9 of the Local Democracy Taskforce Implementation Plan deals with secretarial supports for councillors: “ Ensure appropriate and consistent administrative, secretarial and meeting supports for Councillors to enable a more effective balance between the statutory obligations and representative role.” The implementation plan sets out a phased programme of action running through to 2029. A number of reforms will commence in the coming months through administrative and policy measures. Other recommendations will require legislative change and will be progressed over the lifetime of the Implementation Plan. Implementation will involve a process of detailed policy development in consultation with key local government sector stakeholders, including in relation to Action 9 referred to above. As implementation progresses, my Department will work closely with local authorities, elected members, and all stakeholders to deliver this ambitious programme of reform. As a phased body of work, with implementation of the structural changes not taking effect until after the next local elections in 2029, my Department will engage with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation through the normal Estimates processes regarding any agreed funding needs arising from the reform programme.

question: 800. Deputy Ged Nash asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department can review a case (details supplied) where it appears that a systems error in INIS resulted in a case being prematurely closed, despite the applicant’s best efforts to supply the required information. [64173/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 800 to 804, inclusive, together. In relation to the case referred to by the Deputy, I am advised that the naturalisation application in question was deemed ineligible on 11 March 2026, as it was incomplete because a certified copy of the parent's passport had not been provided. The application was returned to the applicant on 28 April 2025, seeking the missing documentation. The requirement to provide a certified copy of the passport was clearly communicated to the applicant. A subsequent reminder also issued, which again outlined the documentation required. The requested document was not received within the timeframe provided. Although no appeal mechanism is provided for under the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, it remains open to any person to submit a new application at any time. There is no time limit within which a new application may be made. Applicants are advised, when making a new application, to have regard to the reasons their previous application was deemed ineligible. My Department has recently launched a new webpage to help people better understand the naturalisation application process, including the key documents required to establish identity and residency. The page also provides guidance on how documents may be certified; it can be accessed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/ I can advise the Deputy that there are currently no plans to establish a separate review or oversight mechanism in relation to the administration of naturalisation applications. As an Oireachtas Member, the Deputy may also request the status of individual immigration cases by email through the Oireachtas Mail facility at IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been established specifically for this purpose. This service enables up-to-date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information through the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 805. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will supply a breakdown of the funding the various front-line organisations that support gender-based violence victims and survivors receive from his Department; and if he will consider a significant increase of the funding in view of the vital service they provide. [64182/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. Cuan's annual reports contain a breakdown of funding for Cuan funded services. This can be found on Cuan's publications page on gov.ie, along with the organisation's financial statements: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/cuan-publications/#cuan-annual-report-2025 Future budgetary allocations to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV will be considered by Government as part of the annual Estimates process.

question: 806. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in circumstances where the Irish Prison Service has not been established on a statutory basis, the person or body that constituted the 'relevant authority' under the Department of Finance Circular 22/2007 for determining an application by a prison officer for retirement on grounds of ill health since 2019; the authority to make the final decision vested or delegated; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64177/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by my officials in the Irish Prison Service that the criteria and procedures required for an employee to retire on grounds of ill health are set out in Circular 22/2007: Ill-Health Retirement from the Civil Service. I am further advised that where a civil servant applies to retire early on the grounds of ill-health he or she must provide the Chief Medical Officer (CMO) with a completed Ill-Health Retirement form along with a medical report detailing his/her diagnosis, treatment and prognosis. The CMO will arrange for the civil servant to be medically examined and may also arrange for an outside specialist opinion if the CMO feels that this would be of benefit. If the CMO is of the opinion that the civil servant is incapable on medical grounds of regular and effective service and that the situation is likely to be permanent, then the CMO will sign the relevant part of the Ill-Health Retirement form and return the form to the civil servant's Department/Office. In all cases, the final decision on whether or not a civil servant is granted ill-health retirement, lies with the relevant appropriate authority having received the advice of the CMO. The appropriate authority for the Irish Prison Service (IPS) is vested with the Personnel Officer assigned to the IPS HR Directorate.

question: 811. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has examined the establishment of a publicly accessible, State-operated register of persons convicted of serious sexual offences not covered under the Domestic Violence Register; the principal constitutional, data-protection and human-rights issues identified; and whether he will publish any policy analysis undertaken. [64226/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government's priority is to ensure the effective management, monitoring and risk assessment of convicted sex offenders, while balancing the need to protect the public with constitutional, data protection and human rights obligations. There is a robust legislative framework in place to monitor and manage the risk posed by convicted sex offenders. Under Part 2 of the Sex Offenders Act 2001, certain convicted sex offenders are required to notify An Garda Síochána of their personal details and any changes to those details for specified periods, up to and including life in the most serious cases. The Garda National Protective Services Bureau, through its Sex Offender Management and Intelligence Unit (SOMIU), oversees the management and monitoring of these offenders nationwide. The Sex Offenders (Amendment) Act 2023 strengthened monitoring arrangements by reducing notification periods from seven to three days and introducing additional requirements regarding travel, temporary addresses and annual notifications. It also provides for electronic monitoring, powers to verify identity through fingerprints and photographs, and enables courts to prohibit offenders from working with children or vulnerable persons. The Act also placed the Sex Offenders Risk Assessment and Management (SORAM) process on a statutory footing. SORAM is a multi-agency framework involving An Garda Síochána, the Probation Service, local authorities and Tusla to support information sharing and the effective management of offenders in the community. Eligibility for SORAM was expanded to include a greater number of higher-risk offenders, who may remain subject to multi-agency oversight for as long as they are subject to notification requirements. It is important that offenders in these very serious crimes are properly supervised after release and encouraged to engage with rehabilitative services in order to prevent reoffending behaviour. The main objective is to keep sex-offenders engaged with supports and interventions to better manage them and reduce the risk of reoffending. There is also a need for caution in relation to disclosure measures. Wide disclosure of information such as the name and location of sex offenders may lead to offenders withdrawing from engagement with post-release services. However, in limited circumstances disclosure is necessary to protect the safety of the public or a member of the public. The 2023 Act allows An Garda Síochána to disclose information relating to persons on the sex offender register in extenuating circumstances (for example, where there is a risk of harm to a member of the public). An Garda Síochána can disclose the offender’s name and photograph, their address, the nature of the sexual offence, the level of risk posed by the offender and any other information deemed necessary by An Garda Síochána. The disclosure can only be made to those persons to whom such disclosure is necessary to prevent harm. Where An Garda Síochána believe a convicted offender poses a serious and imminent risk to the public, an application may be made to the courts for a Sex Offender Order under section 16 of the 2001 Act. Such an order can prohibit an offender from engaging in specified activities where necessary to protect the public from serious harm. My Department keeps this legislation under review to ensure it continues to achieve its intended purpose.

question: 813. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of appeals submitted for penalty points fines issued at two locations (details supplied); and the number of appeals that were successful. [64140/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, the use of technology is a vital component of reducing speeding on our roads. Road safety cameras are intended to be, first and foremost, a tool to support safety, prevention and behavioural change across the road network. The aim of an enhanced use of cameras across Ireland is to encourage safer driving practices, reduce collisions and protect road users by promoting compliance with speed limits. Nine static speed safety cameras are in operation across the country. The locations of these cameras were selected based on fatal and serious injury collision data and speed data, as well as feedback from stakeholders. Fixed Charged Penalty Notices provide a system to avoid court proceedings for specific motoring offences by allowing offenders to pay a set fine and accept penalty points. If an individual does not pay a fixed charge amount on receipt of a Fixed Charge Notice within 56 days, he or she will be summonsed to appear in court. I am advised by the Garda authorities that the Fixed Charge Processing Office does not possess a system which captures data in the detail requested. However Garda authorities have advised that since the introduction of the static speed camera on the N25 at Ballinamona, Glenmore, South Kilkenny, there have been 45,862 non-intercept speed FCNs at this location and 2,358 of these were subsequently terminated. Since the introduction of the static camera on the N80 at Graiguenaspiddoge, Carlow in May 2025, there have been 28,680 non-intercept speed FCNs at this location and 964 of these were subsequently terminated. Figures are based on incidents which occurred from 01/05/2025 to 31/08/2026, inclusive. All information contained in this report is based upon operational data from the FCPS system as was available on 10/09/2026 and is liable to change.

question: 814. Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of interventions made in Dublin, by area within Dublin, and by age in each of the years from 2015 to 2025, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64132/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Anti-social behaviour is a broad term often used to describe a range of actions and behaviours that violate social norms in specific contexts. Along with increased Garda recruitment and resources, the Government is taking a range of targeted and integrated measures to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour generally. These include: • Introducing Community Safety Partnerships around the country, to develop Community Safety Plans for every area. • Continued expansion of youth justice and youth diversion measures to reduce youth offending and improve safety for everyone in the community. The budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has increased by 144% from 2020 to 2026 with a significant allocation of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding for Youth Justice measures announced as part of Budget 2026. • Strengthening the laws around Anti-Social Behaviour Orders (ASBOs) to enable swifter action by Gardaí in such cases. • The implementation and expansion of the High Visibility Policing Plan by An Garda Síochána. Anti-Social Behaviour Warnings and Anti-Social Behaviour Orders provide a response, through a civil process, to the behaviour of an individual. Gardaí can give a Behaviour Warning verbally or in writing. If they give it verbally, the Garda must put it in writing as soon as reasonably possible and then serve it on the individual in person or by post. Gardaí apply to the court to make an Anti-Social Behaviour Order. I am informed by the Garda Authorities that the following table is the annual count of the relevant PULSE Incident Types recorded since 2015 and for H1 2026. In accordance with standard practice An Garda Síochána do not provide specific figures relating to incidents of fewer than ten for data protection reasons. As such a breakdown by Garda Division and by age cannot be disclosed as volumes are too low so may result in the identification of individuals. I am also advised by the Garda authorities that due to the way PULSE is configured there is no option to record Behaviour Orders for adults. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded by An Garda Síochána on the PULSE system and publishes regular releases on recorded crime, by offence type, including public order and related offences. The most recent release includes recorded crime up to the end of 2025 and are available at the following link: data.cso.ie/table/CJA01

question: 815. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the extent to which he has implemented the recommendations of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2024 report on IPAS contracting, particularly regarding proof of ownership, fire certification, insurance documentation, and planning compliance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64240/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 815, 816, 817, 818, 819 and 831 together. Providing reception conditions, including accommodation and other basic supports, to international protection applicants is a requirement of Irish and EU law. There are nearly 297 IPAS Accommodation Centres located around the country, with over 31,000 residents.? My Department worked closely with the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) in carrying out an extensive review of costs and processes within the international protection accommodation system published in 2025. I can confirm that all recommendations in the C&AG report have been implemented by the Department. The Department receives offers of international protection accommodation on an ongoing basis from external commercial providers. All offers are reviewed by the Department under a standardised appraisal procedure. A dedicated team appraises each offer to accommodate people seeking international protection, and the Department carries out due diligence on the provider who is offering the accommodation service. This includes checks on the provider offering the service to the Department via the Companies Registration Office (CRO) to ensure compliance with CRO requirements. Providers must be registered in Ireland. All payments made in respect of International Protection accommodation are to an Irish entity, to an Irish bank account, with tax clearance in Ireland. Providers may be part of wider commercial groups. The Department carries out its appraisals on the providers making the submission and does not appraise wider commercial entities which may be associated with providers. Each new or renewing provider of accommodation services must provide a declaration of their personal circumstances. This declaration, which must be notarised, confirms that they are tax compliant, free of any convictions for corruption, fraud or being a member of a criminal organisation. It also confirms that they are solvent and have no history of failing to meet terms of public service contracts, among other requirements. All provider payments are published on a quarterly basis by the Department, and a provider's tax compliance is verified at each payment by way of a Tax Clearance Certificate. Planning regulation and compliance is a matter between the relevant Local Authority and the property or provider. However, for IPAS accommodation centres, since 2025, all contracts that are being renewed, and any new contract entered into since that time, must be accompanied by the appropriate documentation from the Local Authority to verify their compliance with the relevant planning regulations. This is reviewed by the Department at appraisal or contract renewal stage. The Department is also taking action across all aspects of the international protection accommodation system to improve value for money, strengthen governance and compliance, and renegotiate contracts with providers. Through increased inspections and application of a new rate-card to contracts, costs have been reduced on renewed and new contracts, and 36 contracts have terminated since 2025. Details of individual contractual arrangements and processes are treated as confidential, but reasons for not renewing or ending a contract may include compliance concerns, including failure to meet contractual requirements, health and safety concerns, fire safety issues, planning issues, or other regulatory non-compliance, or non-agreement of commercial terms. Contracts may also be terminated at the request of the provider within the terms of the contract. In line with the Programme for Government 2025 the State is working to develop more State-owned international protection accommodation and reduce reliance on commercially contracted accommodation. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and has passed into law. The new rules came into effect on 12 June. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation.

question: 820. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of garda interviews of persons in custody that have taken place in Garda stations since 1 July 2026 without the accused having consultation or representation by defence solicitors. [64128/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 820 and 902 together. I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that information on whether individuals were interviewed with or without legal representation is not recorded on a centralised system. I am also advised that, while requests for legal representation are recorded in hard-copy custody records maintained at individual Garda stations, the attendance of solicitors at interviews is not recorded. As such it is not possible to accurately establish the information sought as to do so would require a manual check of records that would require a disproportionate use of time and resources to compile. I am advised by Garda authorities that during the investigative process, every individual is afforded the opportunity to avail of legal representation. While it is a matter for each individual to decide whether they wish to avail of legal representation every effort is made to assist an individual who requests representation, and every individual is entitled to representation.

question: 821. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when a service provider will receive payment due (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64351/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The State provides accommodation for nearly 32,000 international protection applicants at 297 accommodation centres nationwide. The Department has robust verification and payment control processes in place to oversee payments for international protection accommodation services. These are in place to ensure that payments are made only where the charges claimed are in accordance with the terms of the relevant contract and the services provided within the relevant period. These processes also ensure that of the volume of invoices and payments made each month, the vast majority of these are completed without delay. As part of the invoice verification process, the Department may seek additional information or clarification from a provider where necessary. Where such queries arise, payment may be withheld pending receipt of appropriate information or additional documentation. While the Department can't publish information on individual contractual processes, I am informed that the matters raised by the Deputy have been resolved.

answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I have requested the information sought by the Deputy from the Garda authorities. Regrettably, this was not available in time and I will write to the Deputy once the information is to hand.

question: 824. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí transferred out of the Galway division in 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025; the districts and stations these Gardaí were removed from as part of these transfers; and the division they were transferred to, in tabular form. [64295/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the allocation, deployment and transfer of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. I am informed by the Garda authorities that the attached table provides the number of Gardaí transferred out of the Galway division from 2022 to 2025, the stations these Gardaí were removed from as part of these transfers, and the division they were transferred to. I am advised that the transfer of Garda members is considered on an ongoing basis in the context of the policing needs of the Garda organisation and of Garda Divisions nationwide. The significant number of new Gardaí now regularly attesting from the Garda College and the allocation of probationer Garda intakes has facilitated the approval of a significant number of existing member's transfers. The situation regarding individual transfer applications is kept under ongoing review. With this in mind each transfer application is considered on its own merit and is fully considered within the overall context of the needs of the applicant’s own Division in conjunction with the needs of the Divisions applied for.
