question: 2181. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to urgently intervene and assist in a case (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60571/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy may be aware, my Department is unable to publish any information that would identify any person as being an international protection applicant. This is a separate matter to the law dealing with data protection matters more generally. My officials and I are legally obliged, under Section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015, to ensure that the identity of any person who applies for international protection is kept confidential. Section 26(1) sets out that: “ the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential ”. As I am sure you will appreciate, these confidentiality requirements are especially important for an asylum-seeker, whose claim inherently supposes a fear of persecution by the authorities of their home country and whose situation, or that of their family or friends still living in the country from which they have sought protection, can be jeopardised if the protection of their personal information is not ensured. An applicant for such protection status, or their legal representative, should contact either the International Protection Office (IPO) or the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) directly, as appropriate if they wish to receive an update on the status of their case. Contact information for The International Protection Office can be found at: https://ipo.irishimmigration.ie/contact-us/. Contact information for The International Protection Appeals Tribunal can be found at: www.protectionappeals.ie/contact-us/. Both the International Protection Office (IPO) and the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) are fully independent in deciding whether or not to grant international protection. Each application is examined individually on its own merits, in line with national and international asylum law. They are also bound by confidentiality provisions in respect of applicants as set out in the International Protection 2015 Act. Alongside this, should an international protection applicant have queries on the labour market access permission works, they can direct any queries in relation to Labour Market Access eligibility to the Labour Market Access Unit of this Department at Lmauqueries@justice.ie. Labour market access permission for international protection applicants gives eligible applicants the opportunity to work and helps them to integrate into Irish society while providing for themselves and their families outside of the State’s directly provided services and supports. It also helps people to plan and prepare for their future in Ireland if they receive a positive decision on their application for international protection. Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018), people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if: • They are an international protection applicant; and • They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and • They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a recommendation must not be attributable to the applicant. Following that, a person may be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application. Lastly, should an international protection applicant have any queries in relation to their state provided accommodation, they can contact the International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) at ipasinbox@justice.ie.

question: 2182. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status and occupancy of the rapid-build modular housing sites at Ballinure Way, Mahon, Cork city, and at Charleville, County Cork; the number of units at each site; the number currently occupied; and the number of residents accommodated at each site as of the most recent date available. [60594/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2182, 2183, 2184 and 2648 together. The rapid build programme has delivered 654 homes at 11 sites nationwide which are providing temporary accommodation for just over 2,600 people fleeing the war in Ukraine. Together, the two sites in Co Cork, referred to by the Deputy, comprise a total of 130 units designed for families of four, with 64 units at Ballinure Way in Mahon and 66 units at Charleville. These rapid build sites have a combined maximum occupancy of 520 people and there are currently no vacant units. A licence agreement is signed by each adult occupant allowing them to remain in their allocated unit while the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) is in force. Residents must adhere to the conditions of the agreement and fulfil satisfactory annual unit inspections undertaken by the Approved Housing Body, Tuath Housing, who manage all rapid builds across the 11 sites. At present, the licence agreements are dated to 4th March 2027. Now that the TPD has been extended to 4th March 2028, these licenses can be extended on expiry of the current license period. Contributions are payable at a rate of 16% of income plus a flat fee of €40 per household per week towards utility costs. The same contribution is payable at all rapid build sites and there has been no change in the contribution percentage or utility amount since the sites were initially occupied. These contributions are offset against the management costs of the sites. The rapid build sites fall outside of the scope of the commercial accommodation wind down and, subject to meeting license conditions, current rapid build residents will not be required to vacate this accommodation until the end of the TPD. Rapid build residents will be able to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process becomes available. question: 2183. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2182, 2183, 2184 and 2648 together. question: 2185. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will approve visas for students from Gaza who have been granted scholarships to Irish universities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60604/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. question: 2188. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures his Department is taking to address the use of fireworks in the leadup to Halloween 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60818/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am aware of the distress the use of illegal fireworks can cause around Halloween. The use of illegal fireworks is of serious concern in terms of anti-social behaviour and they pose a real risk to the health and safety children, teenagers and older or more vulnerable people. They also cause distress to family pets, service dogs and other animals. All pyrotechnics in Europe, including fireworks, fall under the EU Pyrotechnic Directive 2013/29/EU. Under Article 4, Member States are permitted to restrict the availability of hazardous fireworks to the general public. In Ireland, the only fireworks available to the general public are Category F1 fireworks which present a 'very low hazard' and negligible noise level. Only professional pyrotechnic operators are permitted to use more hazardous Category F2, F3 and F4 fireworks for public displays at festivals and weddings, following the successful conclusion of a risk assessment and consultation with relevant local authorities including the Fire Service and An Garda Síochána. Anyone importing or selling fireworks of any kind must have a licence, and licences are only issued for hazardous fireworks if they are to be used in organised displays conducted by professional and competent operators. The penalties for importing, selling or using unlicensed fireworks are significant. The Criminal Justice Act 2006, specifically Part 6, grants members of An Garda Síochána the power to arrest individuals found with unlicensed fireworks and impose significant penalties, including fines up to €10,000 or up to five years' imprisonment for possession with intent to sell or supply, or for igniting them. These penalties, which can also apply to those convicted or throwing an ignited firework at a person or property, demonstrate the seriousness attached to breaches of the legislation governing the importation and use of fireworks. My Department runs an annual Fireworks Awareness Raising Campaign that informs the public about the serious dangers associated with fireworks and the penalties that people can face for selling or using illegal fireworks. An Garda Síochána, through Operation Tombola, runs a nationwide policing plan focused on the prevention and detection of the sale of fireworks and associated public order and anti-social behaviour issues during the Halloween period. Operation Tombola combats the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks, through intelligence-led operations, visits to local car boot sales, searches and seizures of fireworks, as well as focusing on preventing associated public disorder and anti-social behaviour through the incremental deployment of resources. Since 2016, An Garda Síochána have carried out 1,883 fireworks seizures, with a value of €347,516. These seizures have undoubtedly contributed to reducing harm associated with the illegal use of fireworks. A key component of Operation Tombola is active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each Garda division, and gardaí collaborate closely with these stakeholders to ensure a unified approach to preventing anti-social behaviour during the Halloween period. In addition, very good work is undertaken by local authorities and community groups to organise safe fun events for children and young people in our communities around Halloween and these often include firework displays by professional pyrotechnic operators.

question: 2194. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the recommendation in the first annual report of the Special Rapporteur on Racial Equality and Racism for an urgent update to incitement to hatred legislation is under consideration by his Department, given the removal of the incitement to violence or hatred provisions from the legislation enacted as the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60944/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Any discrimination or criminal action taken against a person because of their race, religion, gender or sexual orientation is unacceptable and will not be tolerated. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 was commenced at the end of 2024 and placed specific hate offence provisions in Irish law for the first time, in line with EU obligations. This provided for increased prison sentences for certain offences, where proven to be motivated by hatred, or where hatred is demonstrated, based on personal identity characteristics like race, colour, nationality, religion, national or ethnic origin, descent, disability, gender, sex characteristics or sexual orientation. Ireland has had incitement to hatred legislation in place for 37 years, which remains in force. It is an offence under the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 to incite hatred based on a person’s race, colour, nationality, religion, ethnic or national origins, membership of the travelling community or sexual orientation. The protections against incitement to hatred are in line with Ireland’s constitutional obligation and democratic tradition of protecting freedom of speech. This means that people are free to express opinions that we may find deeply offensive as long as there is no intention to incite others to hatred or what is done or said is not likely to incite hatred. This is an important protection for democratic processes, where it is essential that opinions can be freely expressed. However, whenever anyone incites hatred against a person or any group of persons on the basis of a personal characteristic such as their gender or religion, that is an offence.

question: 2195. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department, or any body under its aegis, has assessed the evidence base for the effectiveness of unconscious bias training prior to any endorsement of the recommendation for mandatory, continuous unconscious bias training across all public sector staff; if his Department is aware of the decision taken in 2020 to phase out such training across the United Kingdom civil service on the basis of a commissioned evidence review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60949/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Recommended Public and Civil Service-wide training is developed and delivered through OneLearning, in partnership with the Institute of Public Administration (IPA). OneLearning delivers a range of training programmes for public and civil servants and supports the ongoing development of capability across the Civil Service. The Department is aware of the decision taken by the UK Civil Service in 2020 to discontinue mandatory standalone unconscious bias training following a review of the available evidence. However, the Department does not provide standalone mandatory unconscious bias training. Instead, unconscious bias is addressed within the wider context of intercultural awareness and inclusive workplace practices. While the Department provides a suite of Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (ED&I) training programmes, including mandatory programmes such as Equality and Human Rights in the Public Service and Intercultural Awareness – Building Competence for Inclusive Workplaces, the Department recognises that sustainable behavioural change is achieved through a combination of leadership, organisational culture, practical workplace measures and skills development. The Intercultural Awareness programme is informed by research and practical approaches to developing intercultural competence and fostering inclusive workplaces. It equips staff with the knowledge, skills and tools required to work effectively in increasingly diverse environments and to contribute to a culture of respect, inclusion and belonging across the organisation. Strengthening intercultural competence across the organisation supports the delivery of responsive, inclusive and accessible services for all. With regard to the agencies under the remit of my Department, I am informed that, similarly, they do not provide standalone mandatory unconscious bias training. Instead, unconscious bias is addressed within the wider context of intercultural awareness and inclusive workplace practices. As the Deputy will be aware, under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána, including Garda training matters. I am informed by their HR Directorate that unconscious bias training is undertaken. It has not yet been assessed.

question: 2196. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the estimated cost of introducing mandatory, continuous anti-racism, cultural competency and unconscious bias training across all public sector staff, as recommended in the first annual report of the Special Rapporteur on Racial Equality and Racism; the providers through which such training will be delivered; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60961/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The First Annual Report of the Special Rapporteur on Racial Equality and Racism contains a number of recommendations for Government consideration. My Department's consideration of the recommendations is ongoing and forms part of broader work to strengthen the State's response to racism, promote equality, and support the implementation of the National Action Plan Against Racism 2023-2027. As such, no decision has been taken regarding the introduction of mandatory, continuous anti-racism, cultural competency and unconscious bias training across all public sector staff. Accordingly, I do not have an estimate of the cost of introducing such training. Under section 42(1) of the Public Sector Equality and Human Rights Duty, public bodies must have regard to the need to eliminate discrimination, promote equality of opportunity, and protect human rights, for employees, service users, members and policy beneficiaries, across all their function areas. Individual Departments and public bodies are responsible for meeting their obligations in this regard and for determining the measures necessary to support compliance with those obligations.

question: 2199. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if provision exists within the Domestic Violence Judgments Register Act 2026 to ensure that a person cannot circumvent discovery of their inclusion on the register through changing their name, for example, by deed poll; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61007/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) is a priority for this Government and one that is reflected in a range of policies and legislation, as well as unprecedented increases in budget allocations. The Domestic Violence Judgments Register Act 2026 provides a mechanism whereby those convicted of domestic violence against a partner or former partner can be included on a Register of Judgments. A publicly available Register of Judgments will assist people who are in a relationship, or considering a relationship with a person, to ascertain whether they have a history of serious domestic violence convictions. The legislation inserts a Part 3A into the Domestic Violence Act 2018 and applies to convictions on indictment for serious domestic violence offences. It creates a structure through which relevant judgments may be published to supplement the existing means of publicity, such as through media attendance and reporting on proceedings. It does not constitute an additional form of punishment. The trial judge has discretion to issue a judgment in an appropriate case, which will contain details of conviction and sentence, as well as any other information relevant to the offence that the judge deems appropriate. Only in cases where the victim consents to publication will this step be considered. Judgments will be published online by the Courts Service, under a specific heading of “Domestic Violence Register Judgments”. The legislation includes a procedure whereby a convicted person in respect of whom a Register Judgment has been published may apply for removal from the Register, no earlier than three years following conviction. However, such removal will be at the discretion of the Court. Judgments produced by the Courts are a snapshot of the situation on the day the judgment is produced. It is not normal practice to update judgments delivered by any court, and doing so could present operational and legal complexities. It should be noted that the Register is one of a number of initiatives being progressed to address DSGBV. It sits alongside and complements other preventative and protective measures such as Operation Devise and the Sex Offenders Register. The information will be presented in a way that is linked insofar as possible with domestic violence services, to ensure that anyone consulting the Register will be directed towards appropriate supports, whether for themselves or for another person that they are concerned about. In relation to a change of name more generally, all Deed Polls enrolled in the High Court are included on a register and the last ten years of enrolled deed polls are publicly accessible on the Courts Service website at: www.courts.ie/hubs/deed-poll. This lists both the old and new versions of the names used by any persons who have changed their name by Deed Poll.

question: 2200. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total amount his Department and departmental agencies have spent in 2025 and to date in 2026 on social media and web advertising; the proportion this is of his Department's advertising budget; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60923/26]

question: 2201. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of FOI requests his Department, and each agency under his auspices, received in each year 2020 to 2025, and to date in 2026; the number that were refused on original decision; the number for which reviews were sought and the number of those reviews whereby the original decision was amended; the number for which subsequent appeals were submitted; the number of those appeals which resulted in an amendment to the original decision; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61047/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department is committed to fulfilling its obligations under the Freedom of Information Act 2014 and to ensuring that requests are processed in an open, fair and timely manner. The volume of FOI requests received by the Department has increased significantly in recent years. My Department received 1,522 FOI requests in 2025, representing an increase of 25% on the 1,216 requests received in 2024, which itself represented an increase of almost 30% on 2023 levels. Despite this substantial growth in demand, my Department continues to process a high volume of requests while maintaining robust review and appeals mechanisms. Consideration of all requests under the Act are made in accordance with the relevant provisions, exemptions and administrative refusal mechanisms as set out in the Freedom of Information Act 2014. Decisions to refuse release of a record will often be on the basis that requested records do not exist within my Department or because the records are already in the public domain. My Department ensures that where a decision is made to refuse, the reason for such refusal is clear in the decision letter and the individual requester is made aware of their appeal rights. Details of the number of FOI requests received by my Department, the number refused at original decision stage, the number of internal reviews sought and resulting in amendments to the original decision, and the number of appeals made to the Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC) and resulting changes are set out in the attached, at Appendix 1. It should be noted that figures presented in Appendix 1 are recorded on the basis of the year in which the FOI request was received. As a result, internal reviews and appeals may be concluded in a subsequent year but are attributed to the year of receipt of the original request. Details of FOI requests received by agencies under the remit of my Department are attached in Appendix 2.

question: 2202. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends to compile and publish data concerning the number of applications for international protection submitted by persons who had initially or previously entered the State broken down by immigration permission categories (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61105/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department takes all necessary steps to manage the international protection process efficiently and effectively while ensuring that the integrity of those processes is maintained at all times. The number of international protection applications has been rising over the past number of years, reaching 18,500 in 2024. In 2025, application numbers fell by approximately one-third. Application numbers to the end of July 2026 show a further reduction compared to 2025. There has been a significant increase in investment in the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process re-engineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand. In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions, compared with approximately 14,100 in 2024, representing a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed, from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. As of 16 August this year, IPAT has already closed 5,858 appeals and is on track to significantly exceed the number of appeals closed in 2025. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable, and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases. The new system has been in place for two months and is operating as intended. The Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement, developing and resourcing new processes and procedures to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact. The table below provides a yearly breakdown of international protection applications made from 2022 to 2026. Year of Application Total 2022 13,642 2023 13,271 2024 18,553 2025 13,143 2026* 7,401 *to 23 August 2026. Combined IP Act 2015 and IP Act 2026 data. Figures are correct at time of issue; however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. Data on the number of persons who applied for international protection and who entered the State on any category of visa has not historically been compiled on a systemic basis. Under the new Pact processes, however, this information is now collected as part of the international protection application process and, as the dataset matures, will support future analysis and reporting on migration and protection trends.

question: 2203. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will commit to implementing ask 2 of a framework (details supplied) by ensuring that bereaved families in manslaughter cases are entitled to receive a written explanation of sentencing decisions upon request, as operates in England and Wales; whether this could be achieved through amendment to the Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017 or through a direction to the DPP; and the proposed timeline for implementation. [59780/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is important to emphasise that the conduct of any court case is a matter entirely for the presiding judge. The courts are, subject only to the Constitution and the law, independent in the exercise of their judicial functions, including sentencing. While judges are not required by statute to provide reasons for their sentencing decisions, they are required to have regard to certain factors and typically explain how they balance the gravity of the crime, aggravating factors, and mitigating personal circumstances in reaching their decision. The Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017, which transposed the EU Victims’ Rights Directive into Irish law, sets out a framework of rights and entitlements for victims. This includes access to information, support services, and protection measures. Section 8 of the Act relates to a victim’s right to receive information in relation to their case and primarily concerns information provided during the investigation and prosecution phases of the criminal justice process. The section also distinguishes between general information about rights and supports, and additional case-specific information which may be provided where requested by a victim. The relevant competent authority is responsible for providing such information, depending on the nature of the information sought. While the Courts Service is not one of the bodies that are obliged to provide information under the 2017 Act, in appropriate cases, victims can obtain information relating to the courts process and outcomes where appropriate from responsible agencies including An Garda Síochána or the Director of Public Prosecutions. Directive (EU) 2026/1472, which amends and updates the Victims’ Rights Directive, came into force in July 2026. Ireland actively engaged in negotiations on this Directive, aiming to ensure at EU level that supports for victims are further entrenched. Ireland will be obliged to transpose the new Directive into Irish law by 2 July 2028 for most of its provisions, aside from those relating to the use of information and communication technologies to support victims, which have a transposition date of 2 July 2030. As part of this process, officials in my Department will review our victims’ rights legislation and will consider any further improvements that may be needed.

question: 2204. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of prisoners released from each prison under the community return scheme in each of the years 2020 to 2025, and to date in 2026; the numbers of prisoners that had been in custody for under one month, under two months, under three months, three to six months, six months to one year, between one to two years, between two to five years, over five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61126/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2204 and 2210 together. The Community Return Scheme is a supervised and structured scheme, introduced in August 2011, that supports persons subject to it, during an initial period of release from prison. This is a critical period of time where they adjust to community based living. Community Return involves the person making reparation through community work which is of benefit to the community and to themselves. Engagement in the scheme offers these people an opportunity to avail of early release from prison; reintegration opportunities with their families; results in improved resettlement outcomes; structure and routine in daily life; promotes the development and maintenance of a work ethic and improved sense of self and skills development that supports future employability. I am advised that compliance rates have remained consistent since the introduction of the scheme. These validate the assessment process and the systems implemented for the day to day management by Community Service Supervisors on work site. The Initial Pilot Assessment had a compliance rate of 90%. An evaluation from 2014 indicated a compliance rate of 89% and up to date data indicates the same compliance rate. In order to be considered for Community Return Scheme persons must be serving a period of imprisonment of 1 to 8 years; they must have demonstrated a willingness to engage in authorised structured activities and rehabilitative opportunities while in prison; they must be deemed to be of good behaviour while in prison. All persons released under the scheme must reside at an agreed address, be of good behaviour, report back to a stated prison on a set date, be of sober habits and not convey messages into prisons. There is also a requirement to report to a Garda station on the days they are not on site or back at the prison. Extra conditions may attach in any individual case such as attendance at a training or addiction service, to stay away from a particular area or produce wage slip as evidence of employment. To date, since 2020, over 1,400 prisoners have been released from custody to the Community Return Scheme with a compliance rate of 89%. If a person is non-compliant with the conditions of their temporary release to the Community Return Scheme they have their temporary release revoked and return to custody to serve out the remainder of their sentence. I am advised that the attached tables outline the number of persons who were either granted temporary release or full temporary release during the years requested. Prisoners who are granted full temporary release are prisoners who are in the very latter stages of their sentence and in the vast majority of cases they will receive 2- or 3-days early release to access medical, social welfare or accommodation services, particularly if their release date falls on a Friday, Saturday or Bank Holiday. Investment in An Garda Síochána has increased year on year since 2020 and a Garda budget of €2.74 billion will fund the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí and 200 more Garda staff in 2026. question: 2206. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will outline the legislation originating from the European Union which he is obliged to, but has not yet, transposed into domestic law; the deadline for transposition; the consequences arising from not meeting the transposition deadline; the timeframe in which he intends to transpose, by directive, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61152/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2206 and 2207 together. The European Commission monitors the application of EU law in the Member States and may initiate infringement proceedings if a Member State fails to transpose an EU directive into national law by the prescribed deadline. The infringement procedure follows several steps laid out in the EU treaties (Article 258 of the TFEU), each ending with a formal decision. If an EU Member State fails to transpose or communicate a complete transposition to the Commission following a reasoned opinion, the Commission may refer the matter to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) to confirm the principle of the infringement and propose that the court impose financial penalties. In March 2026, the Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence, Thomas Byrne TD, launched an EU law transparency initiative with a dedicated section on Ireland.ie focused on highlighting how Ireland implements EU law. Details of infringement proceedings against Ireland are listed. Details of directives which are due to be transposed into Irish law this year are also included in this section. A link to the website can be found at the following address - www.ireland.ie/en/eu/implementation-of-eu-law-in-ireland/. The following table provides details of measures under the remit of my Department which have a transposition date since 1 January 2023. No financial penalties have arisen in respect of the late transposition of measures under the remit of my Department during that timeframe. question: 2208. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the details of the policy, criteria or decision-making process used by the Irish Prison Service for determining whether an individual will be placed on a basic, standard or enhanced regime upon committal; the policy, criteria, and decision-making process for changing the regime a person is on; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60602/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised that the Irish Prison Service operates an incentivised framework in line with their Incentivised Regimes policy. The Policy is available on the Irish Prison Service website www.irishprisons.ie/about-us/care-and-rehabilitation/incentivised-regimes-policy/. The Incentivised Regimes policy provides for a differentiation of privileges between people in custody, according to their level of engagement with services and behaviour. The objective is to provide tangible incentives to those in prison to participate in constructive activities and to encourage good behaviour, leading to a safer and more secure environment. There are three levels of regime – basic, standard and enhanced, with different privileges associated with each regime level. All people on committal enter the system at standard regime level and have the opportunity to become eligible for the enhanced regime status once they have met the required criteria for the preceding two months. There are three fundamental requirements which must, at a minimum, be met before a person in custody can be considered for progression to the Enhanced Level of the Prison Privilege Regime. These include: 1. Actively participating in at least five constructive activities per week 2. Have spent a minimum of 56 days on Standard Privilege Level 3. Demonstrate exemplary behaviour and/or be a positive influence on their peers. People in custody may be moved to the Basic Level of the Prison Privilege Regime where they are in breach of the Prison discipline rules or where they fail to meet the requirements of either the Standard or Enhanced Level. Where a person in custody has two unacceptable weeks within a 56 day period, their placement on the regime may be reviewed and they may be considered to be moved from the Standard Level to Basic Level. I am further advised that recommendations and decisions on regime levels are made by the Class Officer and accepted or rejected by the Assistant Chief Officer following consultation with those responsible for co-ordinating or delivering services. Decisions on regime level are confirmed by a Chief Officer. Assistant Chief Officer’s audit at least ten percent of cases weekly to ensure consistent high standards. Chief Officers review the appropriateness of people in custody regime levels at least quarterly. People in custody who are on remand are treated in the same way as those who have been sentenced for the purposes of the Incentivised Regimes policy.

question: 2209. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of convictions for murder in each of the past 15 years arising from unprovoked assaults or one-punch attacks; the number of offenders convicted in each year who had previous convictions; the gender of victims and convicted persons; the county or Garda division in which the offences occurred; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59908/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2209, 2213 and 2214 together. Management of the courts, operational matters and logistical functions including the recording of conviction data is the responsibility of the Courts Service who are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998. As Minister, I have no role in these independent matters. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. However, to be of assistance, I am advised by the Courts service that convictions are recorded on Courts Service case management systems by reference to the offence concerned. The systems do not record the circumstances surrounding the offence such as an unprovoked assault or a one-punch attack. In addition, the Courts Service does not record victim details such as gender. It should also be noted that the Central Statistics Office is the national statistics agency, established under the Statistics Act 1993. The CSO role includes the collation and publication of recorded crime and re-offending statistics. This data is available from the CSO website at the following link. www.cso.ie/en/statistics/crimeandjustice/.

question: 2210. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of prisoners granted early release from the prison estate in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026, disaggregated by the scheme under which release was granted including reviewable temporary release, the community return programme, the community support scheme, and any temporary release scheme introduced or expanded to address overcrowding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61182/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2204 and 2210 together. The Community Return Scheme is a supervised and structured scheme, introduced in August 2011, that supports persons subject to it, during an initial period of release from prison. This is a critical period of time where they adjust to community based living. Community Return involves the person making reparation through community work which is of benefit to the community and to themselves. Engagement in the scheme offers these people an opportunity to avail of early release from prison; reintegration opportunities with their families; results in improved resettlement outcomes; structure and routine in daily life; promotes the development and maintenance of a work ethic and improved sense of self and skills development that supports future employability. I am advised that compliance rates have remained consistent since the introduction of the scheme. These validate the assessment process and the systems implemented for the day to day management by Community Service Supervisors on work site. The Initial Pilot Assessment had a compliance rate of 90%. An evaluation from 2014 indicated a compliance rate of 89% and up to date data indicates the same compliance rate. In order to be considered for Community Return Scheme persons must be serving a period of imprisonment of 1 to 8 years; they must have demonstrated a willingness to engage in authorised structured activities and rehabilitative opportunities while in prison; they must be deemed to be of good behaviour while in prison. All persons released under the scheme must reside at an agreed address, be of good behaviour, report back to a stated prison on a set date, be of sober habits and not convey messages into prisons. There is also a requirement to report to a Garda station on the days they are not on site or back at the prison. Extra conditions may attach in any individual case such as attendance at a training or addiction service, to stay away from a particular area or produce wage slip as evidence of employment. To date, since 2020, over 1,400 prisoners have been released from custody to the Community Return Scheme with a compliance rate of 89%. If a person is non-compliant with the conditions of their temporary release to the Community Return Scheme they have their temporary release revoked and return to custody to serve out the remainder of their sentence. I am advised that the attached tables outline the number of persons who were either granted temporary release or full temporary release during the years requested. Prisoners who are granted full temporary release are prisoners who are in the very latter stages of their sentence and in the vast majority of cases they will receive 2- or 3-days early release to access medical, social welfare or accommodation services, particularly if their release date falls on a Friday, Saturday or Bank Holiday. question: 2211. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the legal authority that permits the State to decline to determine an asserted directly effective Article 20 TFEU right directly, and instead determine the matter solely under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015; if such authority exists, to identify the specific legal authority relied upon; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59876/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I understand that the Deputy has clarified that the question refers to a specific immigration case. I can advise the Deputy that the applicant concerned applied for permission to remain in the State pursuant to the Chen/Teixeira/Ibrahim judgments. These judgements apply in circumstances where an EU citizen child has moved to reside in a Member State other than that of their nationality and is accompanied by their primary carer. These judgments set out rights that are not expressly provided for in the Free Movement of Persons Directive. The application referred to by the Deputy was based on a child who is an Irish citizen. Accordingly, the above judgments were not applicable in the circumstances of the case and the application was refused both at first instance and following review. The decision letter issued to the applicant on 20 July 2026 sets out the reasons for refusal in this regard. As the parent of an Irish citizen child, it is open to the applicant to apply for permission to reside in the State on that basis. More information is available on the Immigration Service Delivery web site at: www.irishimmigration.ie/my-situation-has-changed-since-i-arrived-in-ireland/the-parent-of-an-irish-citizen-child/.

question: 2212. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if supports are available for a victim of domestic violence seeking a divorce who is above the income threshold for legal aid but can not afford divorce proceedings. [61163/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2126, 2212, 2509 and 2524 together. The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both. A range of civil legal issues are covered by the scheme, including domestic violence applications, which are prioritised by the Board. While contributions from those legally aided are an aspect of the scheme, the Civil Legal Aid Regulations 2017 provide that no contribution is payable for those who are applying solely for orders under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. The Family Law Legal Aid panels include a District Court Private Family Law Panel covering matters in the District Court and on appeal to the Circuit Court under the Domestic Violence Act 2018. In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people. In particular, the majority report recommends increasing the disposable income threshold from €18,000 to €23,500. Having the Civil Legal Aid Scheme and a Legal Aid Board which is equipped to meet the changing needs of society is critical to ensuring access to justice, particularly for those who have very modest means. However, any changes must be considered in the round and the potential implications that such changes might have on the operation of the Scheme. A critical aspect will therefore be the careful sequencing of reforms. Officials in my Department are examining the recommendations and are working closely with the Legal Aid Board to ensure any proposed reforms are developed as part of the annual budgetary Estimates process. Potential implications on the operation of the Scheme and broader government policy will be taken into account. The recommendations from the Review will also have to be considered with due regard to the findings from Ireland’s first legal needs survey, recently completed with the support of the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). This survey will provide invaluable insights into the extent of legal need in Ireland. While preliminary results of the survey have been released on gov.ie, further analysis is underway, with officials in my Department working closely with the OECD on final outputs. I will revert to Government in due course with proposals to reform the Scheme.

question: 2215. question: 2216. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide details of any programmes, education initiatives, behavioural interventions or awareness campaigns currently operated by or within the Irish Prison Service, the Probation Service, the Parole Board and the Garda Youth Diversion Programme which are designed to address violent behaviour, raise awareness of the impact of physical assaults on victims and families, promote non-violence and reduce reoffending; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59946/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2153 and 2216 together. This Government has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026. Following a significant increase of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding as part of Budget 2026, the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. Part 4 of the Children Act 2001 provides the statutory basis for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. The intention of this programme is to divert children, aged 12-17 years old, who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the criminal justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices. Young people who are deemed suitable by the Director of the Garda Youth Diversion Programme are referred to local youth diversion projects, where, in collaboration with a Garda Juvenile Liaison Officer, these projects provide supports to children to address their behaviour, engage in positive self-development, and connect with their communities. While there has been an approximate 25% increase in the population of 12-17 year olds over the past ten years, I am advised that the number or children coming to the attention of the Garda National Youth Diversion Bureau has remained steady, pointing to an actual reduction in youth offending. I am advised that between 2012 and 2022, there has been a drop in total criminal incidents involving children of 35% and a reduction of 31% in the number of children in detention over the past ten years. With the official opening of POINT YDP on 18th June 2026, youth diversion is available to all children and young people across the country. There are currently 92 youth diversion projects and 4 targeted youth diversion projects across the country that are funded by my Department. In 2025, these youth diversion projects and targeted youth diversion projects engaged with 4,786 young persons. Details of the projects and participant numbers are contained in Table 1. The locations of 2 specialist targeted YDPs are excluded in Table 1 for confidentiality, to protect the identity of the young people engaged in their services. The department, in collaboration with the Probation Service, also operates a number of initiatives distinctly designed to address serious and prolific youth offending for those who may be deemed unsuitable for diversion, these are: the Greentown Programme, the Bail Supervision Scheme and targeted interventions for children who are harder to reach in terms of addressing prolific and serious offending. The Department also funds specialised Youth Justice Workers and Programmes in youth diversion projects catering to Early Intervention, Family Support and Harder-to-Reach, serious and prolific young offenders. Within the Irish Prison Service, I am advised that measures to prevent and manage violence include early intervention, rehabilitation and multidisciplinary responses within individual prisons. The Irish Prison Service Psychology Service provides specialist, proactive interventions for people convicted of general and sexual violence, young people at increased risk of recidivism, people serving life sentences, and people convicted of violent offences who are serving sentences of more than two years. The Psychology Service provides primary and secondary care mental health interventions, alongside assessment and intervention for people presenting with neurodivergence, histories of trauma and personality difficulties. Irish Prison Service Healthcare and Merchants Quay Ireland also provide healthcare and addiction interventions, including opioid agonist treatment (OAT) and addiction counselling. The National Forensic Mental Health Service provides specialist psychiatric care to people in custody experiencing major mental illness. Collectively, these services address a range of factors that may contribute to the risk, occurrence or management of violent behaviour and support broader rehabilitation and efforts to reduce re-offending. I am advised that 2,786 individuals were referred in 2025 to the Irish Prison Service Psychology Service, across all interventions, of whom 1,619 were seen for intervention. The Alternatives to Violence Project (AVP) is a voluntary organisation comprising trained volunteers from within prisons and the wider community. Teams deliver workshops in Irish prisons aimed at helping participants build better relationships and develop ways of resolving conflict without resorting to violence. During 2025, I am advised that AVP delivered 43 full workshops across 11 prisons, accounting for 402 participations. A further 11 support sessions were delivered across 10 prisons, accounting for 93 participations and encompassing taster, debrief and refresher sessions. The Traveller Mediation Service (TMS) is a partnership initiative supported by Restorative Justice in the Community and funded by the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. It provides mediation and conflict-skills training within the community, including mediation between Travellers, and between Travellers, agencies and the Settled Community. I am advised that since establishment, the peer-mediation programme has worked with 412 people in custody, with 160 participants attending the programme in 2025. The National Violence Reduction Unit (NVRU), based in the Midlands Prison, accommodates some of the most complex and high-risk men in custody with significant histories of violence. It is a psychologically informed, co-led unit specifically designed to reduce and manage violence. The capacity of the unit is 9 and there are currently 9 prisoners accommodated on the unit. The Irish Prison Service also operates a number of other initiatives that contribute to violence prevention. The Community-Based Health and First Aid (CBHFA) programme, which has operated since 2009, uses trained peer volunteers to deliver health and wellbeing initiatives within prisons. In 2025, 272 CBHFA volunteers implemented 252 projects addressing areas including mental health, anti-bullying, violence prevention and health awareness. The Irish Prison Service has also established a Violence Management Steering Group in 2025. The Group aims to reduce violence in all its forms across the prison estate and to ensure that effective prevention and response mechanisms are in place. Given the breadth of these interventions, and the extent to which violence prevention and reduction are embedded within wider clinical, rehabilitative and multidisciplinary work, the IPS have advised that it is not possible to provide a single accurate figure representing the total number of people who engaged in work specifically directed towards all of the objectives referenced in the Deputy’s question. I am further advised that with regard to the Probation Service, work was undertaken with 17,686 people in the community. At every level of engagement, the focus on re-offending and the impact of crime on victims is paramount. question: 2217. Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider legislative amendments to ensure that deliberate misrepresentation of qualifications, insurance, accreditation or business identity by contractors can be better prosecuted as fraud rather than treated solely as a civil matter; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61227/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The deliberate misrepresentation of qualifications, insurance, accreditation, or business identity is not solely a civil matter under Irish law. Where an individual dishonestly makes false representations with the intention of securing business, making a financial gain, or causing a loss to another, such conduct may, depending on the circumstances, be addressed under existing criminal fraud legislation. Under Sections 6 and 7 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, it is an offence to dishonestly induce a person by deception to do or refrain from doing an act, with the intention of making a gain or causing a loss to another, or to dishonestly obtain services by deception with the intention of making a gain or causing a loss to another. On conviction on indictment, a person guilty of an offence under Section 6 or 7 is liable to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or both. Where the conduct involves the making or use of a false instrument, offences of forgery and using a false instrument under Sections 25 and 26 of the Act may also be applicable. A person guilty of an offence under Section 25 or 26 is liable, on conviction on indictment, to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years, or both. It should also be noted that should a report be submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), that office is responsible for deciding whether a person should be prosecuted and, if so, for which offence. The DPP is wholly independent of my role as Minister and the Department of Justice under the Prosecution of Offences Act 1974 (as amended). I have no role in the operations, functions, oversight or governance of the Office of the DPP and cannot provide any information relating to the decisions made by that Office.

question: 2221. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to address the issues raised correspondence (details supplied); the supports available to make the transition into private accommodation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61252/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2221 and 2223 together. Following the Government decision in May of this year, my department is progressing the next phase of withdrawal of state-supported commercial accommodation for people benefitting from Temporary Protection who arrived in Ireland before March 2024. This is being progressed on a phased basis over the coming months and people who are residents in state-supported Ukraine accommodation will be given a notice period on changes to their accommodation. My department recognises that there will be people who, for various reasons may require continued accommodation which may be in an alternative setting. An application process has opened to people in these centres who can demonstrate that they continue to require temporary accommodation post-commercial accommodation wind-down. The self-declaration application process is open from August 4th – September 11th 2026 online. Successful applications will be offered accommodation in a designated accommodation centre. Anyone not availing of continued accommodation will be required to vacate the centres by the agreed date. People with Temporary Protection continue to have access to public services in accordance with the Temporary Protection Directive and Irish law, including access to healthcare and, where eligible, social protection supports such as rent supplement administered by the relevant Departments. Integration supports are provided by a number of stakeholders and supports will be further mobilised and coordinated to harness inputs and support the integration of people with Temporary Protection and to assist them in moving to independent living. Local Authorities coordinate the supports of wider agencies through their Community Integration Forums. Supports are provided by: • The HSE on health • Department of Social Protection on PPSN and Social Welfare supports • Intreo on employment supports and jobs advice • Department of Education, ETBs and Regional Education and Language Teams (REALTs) for schooling, youth services and English Language supports. Further supports are also provided by the Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM). A blended model of online and in-person engagement are being delivered by the IRC and IOM to inform people of policy changes and give guidance on options available to people. For more information on these supports please visit www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/state-contracted-commercial-accommodation-en/. People with Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own private arrangements for accommodation through their own means, using supports provided by the Department of Social Protection, or by asking their Local Authority or Irish Red Cross for alternative accommodation offered by hosts. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation in any given area should contact the Local Authority in that area or the Irish Red Cross. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted by email at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or by phoning 1800 753 343. I have also obtained Government approval to develop an alternative permission for people with Temporary Protection in Ireland, which will be granted for a period of up to two years, renewable for periods of two years thereafter. This permission is known as the Temporary Protections Transition Scheme. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a requirement to be earning a minimum of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be continuously resident in Ireland for a period of one year as person with Temporary Protection prior to the opening of the application process. Applicants who are self-employed must provide satisfactory evidence such as revenue records that they were, and continue to be, self-employed for 6 months prior to the opening of the Scheme. There is no time requirement on how long an applicant is living independently from state supported accommodation prior to applying. However, an applicant must provide evidence of independent accommodation at the time of application. Further information is available at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. This webpage will be updated over the next few weeks to include details of the application process. It is also important to note that the alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Persons who cannot meet the requirements of the scheme remain entitled to and benefit from the Temporary Protection Status while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. For the avoidance of doubt, the eligibility requirements for the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme do not apply to those remaining under Temporary Protection. While Temporary Protection is currently in place until March 2027, an extension until March 2028 has recently been agreed by the Council of the European Union. Those granted Temporary Protection in Ireland will remain entitled to this protection and associated rights to include employment and education while the Directive is in effect.

question: 2222. Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration regarding the family reunification visa system whether he acknowledges the concerns of healthcare assistants who work full-time, pay tax, and serve the needs of Irish society but who are refused reunification visas as their income is deemed insufficient under the terms of the scheme; whether he accepts the view that Ireland accepts healthcare labour as essential, but the immigration system often treats family reunification as unaffordable; and his plans to examine the fairness of the thresholds. [60049/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2491, 2515 and 2615 together. I recognise the difficulties faced by workers who are separated from their spouses and children while working in Ireland, and I can assure the Deputy that the Government recognises the immense contribution migrants make to our society and economy. The issues raised, including waiting periods, income requirements and the impact that separation can have on children and families, were carefully considered as part of the recent review of the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy. Following that review, I introduced a revised Family Reunification Policy on 26 November 2025. Further changes were made on 12 June 2026, including a commitment to review financial thresholds annually to ensure they remain aligned with living costs and consistent with the new statutory family reunification arrangements introduced under the International Protection Act 2026. A key issue considered during the review was family reunification for General Employment Permit holders, including Healthcare Assistants. Extensive consultation took place with Government Departments, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on this matter. A key principle of the policy is that individuals who bring family members to Ireland should be in a position to support them without reliance on State income supports. For this reason, financial thresholds remain part of the assessment process. Following the review, the Government decided that any future changes to these requirements should be linked to wage growth rather than reducing them below the income threshold used for the Working Family Payment. The review also introduced changes designed to make family reunification more accessible for General Employment Permit holders. In particular, the effective waiting period was reduced from 24 months to 12 months by reducing the amount of income evidence required from two years to one year. The review concluded that a further reduction in the waiting period could lead to a significant increase in applications and longer processing times. The policy continues to provide more favourable arrangements for Critical Skills Employment Permit holders. This reflects the State's objective of attracting workers whose skills are in short supply. Immediate family reunification is one of a number of measures that support this objective. While there are currently no plans to align the family reunification arrangements for General Employment Permit holders with those available to Critical Skills Employment Permit holders, the policy will continue to be kept under review to ensure that it remains fair, effective and responsive to changing circumstances. For information, the policy review report is available at: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf. The Family Reunification Policy is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf. I can further advise that current processing times and visa decisions at Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be viewed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing teams is intended to streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 2225. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the strategies he has in place to address the growing problem of shoplifting; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61280/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2225 and 2306 together. I take any risk to retailers, retail staff and communities very seriously and I am acutely aware of the personal and economic impact that retail crime is having on businesses, retail workers and communities. I recognise that shoplifting and organised retail crime pose a significant threat to the economic welfare of Irish retailers and that retail theft is not a victimless crime. The Government is taking a number of strategic, tactical and integrated measures to address retail crime. The Programme for Government makes several commitments in relation to retail crime. Together with the ongoing roll-out of high visibility policing by An Garda Síochána, further measures are also under consideration. These include: • Improving data sharing between retailers and Gardaí to support enforcement; • Expanding the use of community sanctions for retail crime; and • Updating the Public Order Acts to allow prolific offenders to be excluded from retail premises for a certain period of time. My Department is in the process of drafting a Retail Crime Strategy and work is well advanced. I expect to receive a draft copy of this strategy in the coming weeks for my consideration. The Government intends to publish the Strategy within the next few months. An Garda Síochána commenced a dedicated operation in 2023, ‘Operation Táirge’, to tackle organised retail crime. Under ‘Táirge’, Gardaí nationwide use an intelligence-led approach to identify criminals engaging in retail crime. The approach is to disrupt the most prolific groups using organised crime legislation and proceeds of crime legislation and to work with retailers to strengthen their security and prevent them becoming victims of this criminality. It should also be noted that my Departments work in relation to community safety, youth justice interventions, probation supervision schemes and antisocial behaviour, as well as securing funding for more Garda recruitment and increasing high visibility policing, will also contribute to the aim of supporting retailers, their staff and their customers. Additionally, An Garda Síochána is currently developing a new Crime Prevention and Reduction Strategy for 2026-2029. On a tactical level, getting more Gardaí on our streets is my first priority. The overall Garda workforce has increased from 15,980 in 2016 to over 18,500 in 2026. With three recruitment competitions to join An Garda Síochána in the last 18 months, there is a strong pipeline of recruits regularly entering and attesting from the Garda College. More Gardaí proactively patrolling in our cities, towns and rural areas as well as more Garda staff will help to maintain law and order and make everyone feel safer.
