question: 2227. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will report on operation of naturalisation via Irish association; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60460/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2141, 2227, 2311 and 2312 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Last year, my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. These guidelines set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or has Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department's website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/. In April 2025, 1,358 fair procedures letters were issued to applicants, affording them the opportunity to provide a submission or submit additional documentation in support of their Irish Association application. All submissions received have been reviewed and added to the relevant applications. I can advise the Deputy that, in devising and introducing the new guidelines, full policy and operational consideration was undertaken, including transitional arrangements. Under the provisions of Section 16 of the Act, the Minister is afforded absolute discretion. I can inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide statistics on the number of applications and decisions based on Section 16 'Irish Association' received each year, during the past four years. This would require the manual examination of hundreds of cases. Such an examination would require a disproportionate amount of time to compile. Following the recent introduction of the new Section 16 'Irish Association' guidelines, arrangements to separately record such applications have been put in place. The total number of decisions issued on Irish Association applications since the introduction of the guidelines in April 2025 is 444, of which 300 were refusals and 144 were approvals.

question: 2228. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fines issued at a static speed camera (details supplied) from 1 July 2026 to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60107/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, the use of technology is a vital component of reducing speeding on our roads. The aim of road safety cameras across Ireland is to encourage safer driving practices, reduce collisions and protect road users by promoting compliance with speed limits. Nine static speed safety cameras are in operation across the country since 2024. The locations of these cameras were selected based on fatal and serious injury collision data and speed data, as well as feedback from stakeholders. I am informed by Garda Authorities that there has been 4,569 Fixed Charge Penalty Notices (FCPN) issued for speeding for the month of July 2026 for this camera. All information contained in this report is based upon operational data from the FCPS system as was available on 14 August 2026 and is liable to change.

question: 2229. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who have been required to leave, or have otherwise left, State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022, the number who left Ireland, including the number who returned to Ukraine, where this information is available; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61305/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2229, 2230, 2231, 2232, 2233, 2234, 2235, 2240 and 2365 together. My department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My department has no role in private accommodation arrangements and cannot assist with long-term housing matters. Those granted Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own accommodation arrangements through their own means, with the support of schemes and services provided by other bodies where appropriate. People may seek private rented accommodation independently and, where eligible, may avail of Rent Supplement administered by the Department of Social Protection to assist with rental costs. Further information on Rent Supplement is available through local Intreo Centres and Department of Social Protection offices. Alternatively, people with Temporary Protection may seek hosted accommodation through their Local Authority or through the Irish Red Cross. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation should contact their Local Authority or the Irish Red Cross directly. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or on 1800 753 343. Information on the Offer a Home scheme is available at www.offerahome.ie. Once a person with Temporary Protection leaves State-provided accommodation, my department does not have a role in, or visibility of, their subsequent private accommodation arrangements. Accordingly, my department cannot track whether an individual has returned to Ukraine, secured accommodation through private means, or accessed accommodation supports through other agencies. Further information regarding accommodation supports and policy updates is available at gov.ie under the Ukraine Updates portal.

question: 2236. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in light of the Government's decision that the accommodation recognition payment, ARP, scheme will end on 31 March 2027 and the phased withdrawal of State-contracted accommodation for beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine, the protections, accommodation supports and transition arrangements the Government intends to put in place for beneficiaries of temporary protection who remain dependent on ARP-supported accommodation when the scheme ends. [61320/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2236, 2238 and 2242 together. The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced in July 2022 to recognise the generosity of people who have opened their homes to provide accommodation to people arriving in Ireland from Ukraine under the Temporary Protection Directive. It is intended that the ARP will end on 31 March 2027. From 1 September 2026, the ARP monthly contribution rate will be reduced from €600 per month to €400 per month per eligible property. As the payment is made monthly in arrears, the first payment at the reduced rate will be made in October 2026. S.I. No. 368 of 2026 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/si/368/made/en/pdf) gives effect to this change. The planned reduction in the contribution rate is expected to reduce the numbers participating in the scheme. However, as the scheme is demand-led, it is not possible to produce a robust estimate of the numbers expected to remain in the scheme. The previous reduction from €800 per month to €600 per month in June 2025 did not have a significant impact on numbers engaged in the scheme. The number of active claims continued to increase in the months following the reduction until December 2025 when it plateaued. However, participation in the scheme is currently trending downward. The impact of the reduction will be monitored. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, I would like a situation whereby people will have the ability to continue to share their homes with beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine. Other measures are in place in this regard, including the rent a room scheme. Hosts and beneficiaries of temporary protection will hopefully make agreements to continue their private arrangements that will enable this valuable source of accommodation to be retained beyond the termination of the scheme. In recognition of the valuable contribution many people who have come from Ukraine since the outbreak of the war have made, Ireland is introducing an alternative permission to live and work here. This alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation.

question: 2241. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applicants from Palestine for student visas for the 2026/2027 academic year; the number that were granted; the number refused; the primary reasons for refusal; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61119/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. question: 2243. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether discussions have taken place with local authorities, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Department of Social Protection, and relevant housing and homelessness services regarding the potential consequences of the withdrawal of the accommodation recognition payment, ARP; if he will publish a detailed transition plan setting out the accommodation and support pathway available to each category of beneficiary currently dependent on ARP before the scheme terminates; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61328/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Since the outbreak of the conflict in Ukraine on 24 February 2022, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration continues to work as part of the whole-of-Government response with a focus on meeting the immediate needs of those fleeing the conflict. A number of Government decisions and actions that I have taken on the gradual phasing out of accommodation supports have involved discussion with other Departments and Local Authorities as referenced by the Deputy. These include: The monthly contribution rate per property was reduced from €800 to €600 from 1 June 2025. (S.I. No. 228 of 2025 www.irishstatutebook.ie/2025/en/si/0228.html). This reduction aimed to ensure that temporary and timebound supports for temporary protection beneficiaries from Ukraine are proportionate and equitable. From 10 November 2025 Ireland’s accommodation offering to newly arriving people fleeing the war in Ukraine was reduced to a maximum of 30 days. They will be provided with food, laundry, other services and integration supports in Designated Accommodation Centres. From the 1 January 2026, I made regulations to limit the period that retrospective claims for the ARP scheme can be made to six months from the date of application. S.I. No. 672 of 2025 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2025/si/672/made/en/print?q=21&years=2025) gives effect to this change. This intended to support more effective administration of the scheme and compliance matters. Under Part 3 of the Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/act/3/enacted/en/) from 3 March 2026, new applications for properties that have been registered with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) at any time since March 2022 no longer meet the ARP scheme’s eligibility criteria. Tenants in rental properties are no longer eligible to make new applications for the scheme. In March 2026, following approval of both Houses of the Oireachtas, I made a regulation [ S.I. No. 120 of 2026 ] (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/si/120/made/en/print)to set the ARP scheme termination date to 31 March 2027. Following the Government decision of May 2026 concerning the coordinated approach to transition from Temporary Protection, i made regulations in S.I. No. 368 of 2026 to confirm a reduction of the monthly ARP contribution rate from €600 to €400 from September 2026. The Government continues to support Ukraine in its long-term recovery. This will include a new alternative permission to live and work here, under the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme, for those who wish to remain in Ireland. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, hosts can continue to have private arrangements with Ukrainians if they so wish. Measures such as the rent a room scheme are also available. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation.

question: 2244. [61331/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2244, 2273, 2349, 2351, 2363, 2384, 2386 and 2387 together. Most of the information sought by the Deputy is unavailable at this time. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2245. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of a naturalisation application by a person (details supplied), that has been pending since 2022 and has reportedly reached final processing; when the applicant can expect a final decision; the estimated date for completion, given the exceptional length of time the application has remained outstanding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60979/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation applications referred to by the Deputy continue to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2246. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of farm theft incidents in each county in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60218/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2246 and 2248 together. This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country. Rural crime covers a range of issues, ranging from burglary and theft, to animal crime and road traffic offences. An Garda Síochána are committed to tackling all these forms of crime. The Rural Safety Plan 2025-2027 brings together and strengthens all of the various strands of work being carried out in relation to rural safety. It has been developed by my Department, in conjunction with the National Rural Safety Forum. The Plan's vision is to ensure people and communities in rural Ireland feel safe and are safe in their homes, places of work and their local environments. It does this by identifying four key priority areas that we will focus on to achieve this goal. These areas are Community Safety and Engagement, Property Crime, Roads Policing, and Animal and Wildlife Crime. A number of Garda operations support these objectives, including Operation Thor, which provides an intelligence-led response to burglary and related offences. Gardaí also conduct high-visibility patrols and checkpoints in identified hotspot locations, gather intelligence on known offenders, and regularly engage with rural communities on crime prevention measures. Local Garda Crime Prevention Officers also provide practical advice to farmers, businesses and householders on securing property and reducing opportunities for theft. I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that there is no specific incident type or crime classification of "farm theft" and therefore no corresponding definition. An Garda Síochána compiled figures using a combination of incident types, object categories and location information to provide an indication of theft-related incidents affecting farms. Specifically, the figures include incidents involving the theft of livestock, poultry, farming equipment or vehicles from locations such as farmland, fields, yards and outhouses/sheds, as well as incidents where the term "farm" was identified in the incident narrative. Crime counting rules were applied. The figures provided by An Garda Síochána for County Kerry are set out below for each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026. question: 2247. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, in light of the particular circumstances of elderly beneficiaries of temporary protection, TP, who remain dependent on State-supported accommodation and who have limited or no capacity to supplement their income through employment, he will seek a review of the categories exempted from the revised weekly payment of €38.80, with a view to including persons of pensionable age; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60901/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2247 and 2249 together. question: 2250. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the current responsibilities of his Department in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection, TP, in Ireland; the responsibilities which now rest with other Departments in relation to their accommodation, income supports, housing and integration; and if he will provide clarity as to the lead Department responsible for the overall co-ordination of Government policy concerning beneficiaries of temporary protection. [60897/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2250, 2253 and 2254 together. My Department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My Department also registers arrivals at points of entry and provides Temporary Protection Certificates. Under the Local Integration Model, my Department funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including those with Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in 2025. Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Other Departments and Agencies are also involved in the whole-of-Government response to this crisis: The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage and local authorities provide assistance to people with Temporary Protection in sourcing hosted accommodation. The Department of Health has responsibility for policy relating to the healthcare needs of people fleeing the conflict. The Department of Social Protection has responsibility for the provision of access to social welfare benefits and income supports. The Government has approved the phased withdrawal of State-funded accommodation for people from Ukraine who arrived before March 2024 and who have been in receipt of State accommodation on an ongoing basis. Ireland's State-funded accommodation model for people fleeing Ukraine has been more extensive than that available in many other EU Member States. There are currently over 13,000 people in non-time bound State-contracted commercial accommodation who will be affected by the accommodation wind-down. An application process for people currently residing in State-contracted commercial accommodation who require ongoing State accommodation support and who meet specified criteria opened on 4 August 2026 and will remain open until 11 September 2026. Individuals seeking continued State-supported accommodation are required to self-declare their need for support and provide appropriate documentary evidence in support of their circumstances. As the application process remains open, data on the number of applicants seeking ongoing State accommodation will not be available until the application period has closed and all applications have been assessed and processed. Accordingly, the number of people with Temporary Protection who will remain eligible for State-supported accommodation on grounds such as age, disability or other vulnerability criteria is not yet available. My Department will remain in contract with a number of accommodation centres to accommodate those who are eligible for ongoing accommodation support. The changes are being introduced on a phased basis to allow residents who are impacted time to access the information and supports available to them. My Department is not currently procuring any further new accommodation centres for use as Designated Accommodation Centres. Based on current assessments of accommodation demand, my Department is satisfied that sufficient accommodation capacity is available at present and will continue to keep requirements under review as applications are processed. People with Temporary Protection who are no longer eligible for State-supported accommodation may apply for housing and income supports, subject to the statutory eligibility criteria applying to those schemes. Responsibility for the administration of these supports and any guidance relating to their operation rests with the relevant Department. My Department will continue to work closely with all relevant Government Departments to ensure a coordinated approach to supporting beneficiaries of Temporary Protection in Ireland.

question: 2251. Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when applications for tourism or visit a family and-or friend received in Dublin on 2 June 2026 may be completed. [60893/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2251 and 2252 together. I can assure the Deputy that, while processing times vary across Visa Offices and Irish Embassies, the majority of visa applications are processed within the published target timeframes. The average processing time for all Type C short-stay visas in 2025 was 37 days. My Department's website recommends that visa applications be submitted three months before the intended date of travel. While applications may be submitted earlier than this, applicants are advised to ensure that all supporting documentation is as up to date as possible. Applicants may also use my Department's Customer Service Portal to upload updated documentation after an application has been submitted. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. In 2025, approximately 206,000 visa applications of all types were received by the Visa Division of my Department. This represented an increase of 2% compared with 2024, with more than 3,900 additional applications received. This followed a 21% increase in applications in 2024 compared with 2023. During the first six months of 2026, the Visa Division received approximately 102,000 visa applications and issued approximately 85,200 decisions. Processing times are influenced by a range of factors, including the type and complexity of the application, the individual circumstances of the applicant, peak application periods such as holiday seasons or the beginning of the academic year, and, importantly, the quality and completeness of the application submitted. Verification of application details is a critical component of the immigration system, and the necessary checks can take time to complete. Information on current processing times for visa applications being processed in Dublin is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/. The website currently indicates that tourism and visit family/friend visa applications received by the Dublin Visa Office on 11 August 2025 are being processed. It should be noted that the date published on the website represents the oldest application currently under consideration within a particular category. Visa officers continue to process and decide applications received after the published processing date. Where an individual application requires additional examination and takes longer to finalise, the published processing date may remain unchanged for a period. This should not be interpreted as indicating that processing of applications within that category has ceased. Unfortunately, it is not possible to provide a definitive date for the finalisation of any individual application. Applications are generally processed in chronological order based on their date of receipt. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This enables applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency.

question: 2257. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of emails received through the dedicated helpdesk at ipasinbox@justice.ie from persons applying for international protection regarding concerns in relation to their accommodation in each year from 2020 to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60815/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The safety and well-being of all residents and staff in our accommodation centres is a priority for the Department and IPAS. IPAS is always available to deal with any complaints from residents and residents are encouraged to engage with IPAS if they are unhappy with any aspect of their accommodation. Each resident has access to details of the IPAS complaints procedure, and how residents can submit complaints about issues and problems in their accommodation. Complaints are handled sensitively and in confidence. Residents can make complaints verbally or in writing to the centre manager. If residents are not satisfied with how a centre has dealt with a complaint, they can submit a formal written complaint to IPAS. Residents can also submit written complaints directly to IPAS if they prefer. If a resident is not comfortable contacting centre management or the Department directly, the Jesuit Refugee Service (JRS) operate a confidential support helpline for all residents being accommodated by IPAS. If a resident is not satisfied with the outcome of a complaint submitted to IPAS, a complaint can be submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman or the Office of the Ombudsman for Children. The following number of emails were received by the IPAS Helpdesk from residents regarding concerns in relation to their accommodation in each year since 2020. To note, the number of IPAS residents in IPAS accommodation has grown from 7,000 in 2020 to 33,000 in 2026. Year Emails 2020 213 2021 244 2022 564 2023 889 2024 1,668 2025 1,703 2026 YTD 1,172 These issues are raised with centre management and most can be resolved locally or with IPAS support. Residents are also offered the opportunity to proceed with a formal written complaint. The IPAS customer services team conduct clinics at IPAS accommodation centres and individual residents may raise a query or complaint directly with IPAS at any time by email through a dedicated contact centre, and may also seek support from external advocates as needed. All IPAS Accommodation Centres, whether state-owned or contracted emergency accommodation, are subject to oversight arrangements through the Department's Centre Management and Compliance Team, and inspected either by HIQA, department officials, or by external inspectors commissioned by the Department. HIQA reports are available online here: www.hiqa.ie/reports-and-publications/inspection-reports. Reports of IPAS inspections are available online here: www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/publications/ipas-inspection-reports/.

question: 2261. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the organisations, persons and stakeholders that have been consulted to date with respect to the formulation and drafting of the national Migration and Integration Strategy due to be published in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60792/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands and the opportunities facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy later this year. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level. The ten Departments represented on the SMPG are: • Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Chair) • Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment • Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science • Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage • Department of Finance • Department of Social Protection • Department of an Taoiseach • Department of Health • Department of Education and Youth • Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht Each Department is in a position to convey the perspectives of the agencies under their remit which have also provided inputs to the Group as required. The SMPG and its working group has now met on 14 occasions for detailed discussions on different aspects of the Strategy. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs. With specific regard to integration, work previously undertaken, including a detailed consultation process with stakeholders, will be taken into account in the development of this strategy. The first phase of consultation consisted of a public survey, stakeholder submissions, and stakeholder workshops to gather insights into the needs, challenges, and opportunities for supporting migrant integration. Further engagement will take place as the strategy is developed.

question: 2262. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether passport control checks at ports of entry automatically identify individuals who are subject to Irish entry bans, exclusion orders, deportation orders or other immigration restrictions; the systems used to facilitate such checks; the number of alerts generated in each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60778/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2262, 2504 and 2526 together. The Border Management Unit (BMU) is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. Immigration officers are responsible for carrying out border management functions in order to protect the integrity of the State's immigration system and ensure compliance with immigration law. For security reasons and to protect the integrity of the immigration system, neither I nor my Department can comment on specific operational procedures of the BMU or the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB). However, I can assure the Deputy that all persons arriving at ports of entry are examined, and their travel documentation verified, using a range of border management and security systems. This includes checks against relevant national and international databases to assist in confirming identity, detecting fraudulent documentation, and identifying people who may be the subject of immigration, law enforcement, or security alerts. In relation to the sharing of biometric data with the UK, I can advise the Deputy that, at the UK-Ireland Summit in March, it was agreed that further steps would be taken to ensure that the CTA remains secure by working together to expand immigration data-sharing arrangements, particularly to prevent abuse of CTA free movement by those not entitled to its benefits.

question: 2263. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a contract (details supplied) for IPAS accommodation will be renewed; if there has been engagement with the property owners in terms of its future use; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60768/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Providing reception conditions, including accommodation and other basic supports, to international protection applicants is a requirement of Irish and EU law. There are currently 298 IPAS Accommodation Centres located around the country, with over 32,000 residents.? The Department has a contract in place to provide accommodation seeking international protection at this location, which is due to expire in March 2027. This location was previously used to provide accommodation to people fleeing the war in Ukraine. Details of individual contractual processes are treated as confidential and commercially sensitive while they are ongoing. With respect to potential for contract renewals, the provision of accommodation for international protection applicants is demand-led, which remains high, and each premises is considered on a case-by-case basis to decide if the contract will be renewed as it approaches its end date. At potential renewal stage, consideration will be given to the current and projected demand for accommodation, the provider's performance under contract, and compliance with standards and legal obligations.

question: 2264. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to report on progress to meet his commitments under the National Human Rights Strategy for disabled people; the measures taken since the strategy was introduced; the key metrics identified to measure progress; and if he will make a statement on the matter [60743/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 commits Government Departments and public bodies to lead by example in creating meaningful employment opportunities for disabled people. Since the introduction of the Strategy, my Department has implemented a range of measures designed to advance the inclusion, participation and progression of disabled people. Details of my Department's progress under the commitments of the Strategy relevant to the Department's work are outlined below. Commitment 4: Civil & Public Sector Under Commitment 4, the Government has committed to maximising opportunities and access for disabled people to obtain meaningful work in the civil and public sector, enhancing disability inclusion policies and practices, supporting career progression, and providing clear pathways to permanent employment for participants in work placement programmes who perform well. Strengthening Workplace Supports My Department has appointed a full-time Disability Liaison Officer (DLO) who acts as a central point of contact for staff and managers on disability and accessibility matters. The DLO provides guidance to employees and managers and coordinates reasonable accommodations to support disabled staff in carrying out their roles effectively. My Department has also committed to implementing the forthcoming cross-Civil Service Reasonable Accommodation Policy once finalised by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. This will further strengthen and standardise workplace supports available to disabled employees. Establishment of a Disability Staff Network In 2025, my Department established a Disability Staff Network to support disabled employees across the organisation. The network: • Promotes peer support and connection among disabled staff; • Provides a structured forum for engagement and feedback; • Supports the development of a more inclusive workplace culture; and • Assists the Department in identifying opportunities for continuous improvement in disability inclusion. This measure directly supports the Strategy's objective of strengthening workplace inclusion and employee engagement. Inclusive Recruitment and Assignment Practices My Department continues to ensure that recruitment and onboarding processes are accessible and inclusive. Measures include: • Offering reasonable accommodations at all stages of recruitment and selection; • Providing accommodations throughout onboarding and induction; • Early engagement by the Disability Liaison Officer with successful candidates who require supports; and • Assigning staff, where possible, to roles that maximise opportunities for success, development and career progression. These arrangements are intended to reduce barriers to entry and support long-term retention and advancement. Supporting Pathways to Employment My Department continues its participation in the Willing Able Mentoring (WAM) Programme, a national initiative that provides work experience opportunities for disabled graduates and supports progression to employment. Since 2016, my Department has hosted WAM placements and has continued this commitment following publication of the Strategy. I am informed my Department currently employs two former WAM graduates at Executive Officer level, demonstrating progress in creating routes from placement programmes to permanent employment. This directly contributes to the strategic objective of providing clear pathways to sustainable employment for disabled people. Workforce Representation Percentage of staff who identify as disabled • 2025 Disability Census result: 15% • Public sector statutory target: 6% My Department's disability representation rate significantly exceeds the statutory target and provides strong evidence of success in attracting and retaining disabled employees. While the National Human Rights Strategy provides that detailed Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) will be set out in subsequent Programme Plans of Action, several measurable indicators are already being used or can be identified to track progress in the Department. The Strategy states that Programme Plans will specify delivery actions, timelines and relevant KPIs for each commitment. My Department has identified the following metrics as indicators of progress: Recruitment and Accessibility Metrics Indicators include: • Number of applicants requesting reasonable accommodations; • Number of accommodations provided during recruitment and onboarding; • Number of disabled candidates recruited; • Employee retention rates among disabled staff; and • Participation rates in disability inclusion initiatives. Career Progression Metrics Indicators include: • Promotions achieved by disabled staff; • Representation of disabled employees at different grades; and • Employee engagement through the Disability Staff Network. Employment Pathway Metrics Indicators include: • Number of WAM placements offered annually; • Number of WAM participants progressing to employment; • Number of former WAM participants retained in the Department; and • Conversion of placement opportunities into permanent roles. Assessment of Progress Against Commitment 4 The measures introduced by the Department demonstrate substantial progress towards the objectives of commitment 4. Achievements include: • Dedicated disability leadership through the appointment of a full-time DLO; • Enhanced workplace supports and accommodation processes; • Creation of a Disability Staff Network; • Inclusive recruitment and onboarding practices; • Continued participation in the WAM programme and support for pathways to employment; and • Exceeding the statutory public sector disability employment target, with 15% of staff identifying as disabled. Collectively, these actions show that my Department is progressing the Strategy's commitment to lead by example within the civil and public service and is working to ensure that disabled people can access, participate in and progress within employment on an equal basis with others. Commitment 13: Criminal Justice System The National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 commits to ensuring that disabled people can access justice on an equal basis with others, that they do not unnecessarily enter the criminal justice system, and that disabled people in custody can access appropriate services and supports. Since the introduction of the Strategy, my Department has been progressing actions under Commitment 13. Criminal Justice Pathways In circumstances where a specific need has been identified and ongoing treatment is required on release, I am advised that the Irish Prison Service and in-reach services will take all reasonable steps to ensure that the necessary links are made with community services prior to release. The Irish Prison Service and Health Service Executive continue to engage in relation to improved care pathways from prison to community across all areas of clinical need, including disability through various fora including ‘Sharing the Vision’ and the ‘High-Level Taskforce on Mental Health and Addiction Challenges of persons interacting with the Criminal Justice System. Registered Intermediaries My Department supported the establishment of the Registered Intermediaries Scheme through a pilot programme, which concluded earlier this year. As part of the pilot, the Department funded several cohorts of eligible applicants (registered Speech and Language Therapists, Occupational Therapist or Social Workers) to undertake a Professional Diploma in Intermediary Studies at the University of Limerick in successive academic years from 2022 to 2026. As a result of this Scheme, Registered Intermediaries are available to support vulnerable witnesses with communication difficulties to engage effectively with the criminal justice system. The Registered Intermediaries Register is administered by the Courts Service, and information on the Scheme, including details of registered intermediaries, is available on the Courts Service website. A review of the pilot programme is currently underway to assess its operation and effectiveness and to inform the future development of the Scheme, including consideration of measures to increase awareness of its availability.

question: 2265. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the anticipated impact of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact on Ireland's border control, immigration screening and security procedures; the preparations being undertaken for its implementation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60638/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. The Pact is designed to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for the standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for applicants who have previously applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. In addition, under the International Protection Act 2026, people who apply for international protection are subject to initial security and identity checks and will be registered on the Eurodac system. The Eurodac Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1358) expands the data collection requirements to individuals aged six and over. It broadens data collection beyond fingerprints to include facial images and travel documents. Those seeking to claim asylum attend a designated Screening Centre at Citywest, where they lodge an application for international protection. During the screening process, applicants undergo further security, identity, health and vulnerability checks. The Screening Centre has staff from asylum processing, appeals, returns, reception, the HSE, the Department of Social Protection, legal representatives and other agencies co-located on site to engage with applicants. The new system has been in place since 12 June and is operating as intended. My Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact.

question: 2266. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland's current position in relation to European Union initiatives on migration management, border security and protection of the EU's external borders; the specific measures Ireland is advocating at EU level to reduce undocumented migration; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60635/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland has shown its commitment to a common EU-wide solution to migration through opting in to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the measures of the Pact which Ireland has opted into, and provides for appropriate alignment with the Schengen measures of the Pact. The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in the EU. Harmonisation in the area of returns is equally important and it is the Government’s preference that Ireland would participate in the Returns Regulation. Additionally, the Deputy may wish to know that the Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands and the opportunities facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy in the coming months. The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision including housing, amongst other issues relating to migration. As of the 1 July of this year, Ireland took over the Presidency of the Council of the European Union and for six months from that date, we will be driving an ambitious programme of work to advance the interests of the Union. Under the Justice and Home Affairs Council, which I Chair, one of the three overarching priorities for our Presidency is advancing a fair, firm, rules-based approach to migration, asylum and returns. Central to this is of course the effective implementation of the Pact, as well as preparing for the implementation of the recently agreed returns measure. I will also focus on the external dimensions of migration, including through partnerships with third countries and using the tools at our disposal to improve the rate of return and readmission of those with no right to remain in the Union. The Irish Presidency will also prioritise advancing actions that support Member States to secure our borders, fight serious and organised crime and respond to new and emerging threats.

question: 2267. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the resources and supports provided to local authorities and communities affected by the accommodation and processing of persons admitted to the State through international protection and immigration procedures; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60630/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department runs a number of funding schemes to support communities and enable migrant integration in Ireland. In 2025, the Integration Fund was established combining the former International Protection Integration Fund (IPIF) and Communities Integration Fund (CIF). The results of the 2025 Integration Fund were announced in November 2025, with 117 projects receiving a total of €3.6 million in funding. Separately, the National Integration Fund (NIF), a multi-annual funding programme open to organisations operating at regional and national level. The results of the NIF 2023 call were announced in April 2024, with 18 projects awarded grants totalling more than €2.8 million over a three-year period. Building on these initiatives, the 2026 Integration Fund now includes a new multi-annual funding stream that replaces the NIF. The 2026 fund closed to applicants on 2 September 2026, with €4.5 million made available, and the results will be announced later this year. My Department also manages two EU funding schemes aimed at migrant integration. Firstly, my Department is the managing authority for the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF). AMIF provides a range of supports for International Protection applicants, programme refugees, individuals granted Temporary Protection and other third country nationals arriving in Ireland. Since 2023, two open calls for proposals were published for projects suitable for funding under the AMIF 2021-2027 national programme. Arising from these two Open Call for Proposals, €11.5m of grant funding has been awarded to 19 successful projects to provide reception and integration supports and rehabilitative services to third country nationals. The second EU funding scheme to assist migrants is the Integration and Employment of Migrants action under the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) 2021-2027 programme. This action is aimed at legally resident migrants who are experiencing barriers to participation and employment because of language difficulties, lack of training or social exclusion. A total allocation of €5.4m was assigned to this action for the period 2021-2027, which is now fully committed. In 2022, seven projects were approved total. funding of €2.7m for a three-year period. In December 2025, a further eight projects were approved for funding to the value of €2.7m. Under the Local Integration Model, my Department funds teams of staff in the 31 Local Authorities to provide orientation and community integration supports to a range of humanitarian migrants, including individuals granted Temporary Protection. The Model was developed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth in conjunction with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the County and City Management Association, and the LGMA. Responsibility transferred my Department in 2025. The Model makes use of existing organisations and initiatives, supported by co-ordination and collaboration across government bodies, agencies and NGOs. The Local Government Management Agency (LGMA) is responsible for coordinating and supporting the Local Authorities in the delivery of integration services. The approach rests heavily on interrelated and complementary work carried out by a DJHAM-funded network of Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) and Community Integration Fora (CIFs) in each Local Authority across the country, via programmes aimed at supporting the long-term integration into local communities of: • Individuals granted Temporary Protection • Applicants for International Protection • Persons granted Refugee status, Subsidiary Protection status, or Permission to Remain • Refugees resettled under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) LAITs provide information, advice and guidance to facilitate access to supports required to participate in Irish life and live independently. They provide connection to services, e.g. healthcare, English language supports, employment and volunteering opportunities, that can help new arrivals to live independently in their community. LAITs do not replace mainstream service provision but support persons in accessing services appropriate to their needs. Communication and collaboration between the actors in the integration space is facilitated by a Community Integration Forum (CIF) in each Local Authority. CIFs bring together a network of Government and Non-Government Organisations, voluntary and community groups, including LAITs, to collaborate on a community-led integration approach. CIFs are chaired at a senior level within the Local Authority and provide strategic oversight for the promotion of integration, social inclusion and civic participation of the relevant cohorts. My Department's Community Engagement Team (CET) was established in late 2023 to engage directly with elected representatives, local authorities, An Garda Síochána, community members, and other service providers in advance of a new accommodation centre opening. The CET team also links with other stakeholders outside of immediate openings of centres to build relationships and networks with key groups. This includes meetings with Community Integration Fora, Local Development Companies (LDCs) and other non-governmental organisations. Finally, the Programme for Government 2025 provides a commitment to developing a new Migration and Integration Strategy for Ireland, detailing how we intend to meet the demands and the opportunities facing our society and economy over the next decade. Work is well advanced on this project, with a view to the Strategy being launched later this year.

question: 2268. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the penalties, sanctions or enforcement actions available in respect of airlines or carriers that transport passengers to the State without valid travel documentation; the number of such actions taken in each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60625/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2173, 2268, 2269, 2270, 2276, 2307 and 2374 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted permission to land and enter the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. The establishment of a person's identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. People arriving at a port of entry will have their travel documents inspected either by an Immigration Officer or, in certain limited categories, by an electronic system (e-gates). They will also be subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. Under this system, Ireland sends and receives SIS II information (termed "alerts") on persons and objects; for example, persons wanted for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial purposes. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused permission to land. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, arriving without the correct documentation. When a person is refused permission to land at Dublin Airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to An Garda Síochána for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available flight to their last point of embarkation. If a person indicates, or is identified as being, in need of international protection, they are admitted to the international protection process. I can advise the Deputy that the EU Migration Pact introduces mandatory processing times for international protection applications. Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.

question: 2271. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the Garda resources assigned to Operation Tombola in 2026 to combat the illegal importation, sale and use of fireworks; whether these resources have been increased or decreased from previous years; and if he will make a statement on the matter [60471/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2271 and 2310 together. An Garda Síochána’s Operation Tombola combats the illegal importation, sale and use of fireworks through a nationwide policing plan focused on the prevention and detection of the sale of fireworks and associated public order and anti-social behaviour issues during the Halloween period. The operation encompasses all aspects of policing the Halloween period each year. It combats the importation, sale and distribution of illegal fireworks, through intelligence-led operations, searches and seizures, as well as focusing on preventing associated public disorder and anti-social behaviour. The penalties for importing, selling or using unlicensed fireworks are significant and Part 6 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 gives Gardaí power to arrest people found with unlicensed fireworks and sets out significant penalties on conviction, including fines up to €10,000 or up to five years imprisonment for possession with intent to sell or supply. These penalties, which can also apply to those convicted of throwing an ignited firework at a person or property, demonstrate the seriousness attached to breaches of the legislation governing the importation and use of fireworks. I am advised that a key component of Operation Tombola is active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each Garda Division. Gardaí collaborate closely with community stakeholders. Operation Tombola is actively implemented in the lead-up to and during the Halloween period, with each Chief Superintendent overseeing measures to address the sale, supply, and possession of fireworks, as well as anti-social behaviour. These measures include increased overt and covert patrols in key areas, including usual gathering locations for young people and areas likely to stockpile bonfire materials, as well as regular patrols on Dublin Bus, LUAS, and DART services in the days leading up to Halloween, ensuring a visible presence to deter anti-social behaviour continues. An Garda Síochána also conduct talks and sessions in schools and youth services throughout the region, specifically targeting young individuals who may be involved in the sale, supply, or use of firework continues, and there is active monitoring of open-source media to identify potential locations where individuals were engaging in the illegal sale and supply of fireworks continues. An Garda Síochána co-ordinates with local authorities to remove any stockpiled bonfire materials before Halloween will take place. A key component of Operation Tombola involves active engagement with local authorities and partner agencies in each division. Gardaí have collaborated closely with these stakeholders to ensure a unified approach to preventing anti-social behaviour during the Halloween period. I am advised that since 2016 Gardaí have sized 1,883 fireworks, with an estimated value of €347,516. These seizures have undoubtedly contributed to reducing harm associated with the illegal use of fireworks. The attached table counts the number of fireworks offences reported, the number of those sanctioned (charge/summons/caution), the number of objects seized and the estimated value thereof, for the period 2016 to 26 August 2026. question: 2272. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to examine the case of a person (details supplied); the reason that after three years a decision has not yet been made on the application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61405/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2273. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the proposed voluntary return and re-integration programme for Ukrainian beneficiaries of TP, the number of persons his Department estimates may avail of the programme in 2027. [61329/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2244, 2273, 2349, 2351, 2363, 2384, 2386 and 2387 together. Most of the information sought by the Deputy is unavailable at this time. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2274. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of beneficiaries currently in ARP-supported accommodation who are not in employment or self-employment and therefore may not meet the proposed eligibility criteria for the temporary protection transition scheme. [61325/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced in July 2022 to recognise the generosity of people who have opened their homes to provide accommodation to people arriving in Ireland from Ukraine under the Temporary Protection Directive. The eligibility criteria for the temporary protection transition scheme sets out that the principal applicant must be employment or self-employment for six months, with a minimum yearly salary of €29,432. More information on the criteria can be found at Ukraine Updates (EN) on www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. I am unable to provide the current numbers for those hosted in ARP accommodation who are unemployed or self-employed. This information is not compiled as part of the administration of the ARP scheme and is not separately compiled. From the ARP scheme’s launch on 26 July 2022 to date approx. 29,500 hosts have hosted approx. 67,500 people with Temporary Protection. Currently, there are approx. 22,500 active claims in payment in respect of hosting approx. 40,000 people granted Temporary Protection from Ukraine. Recent CSO data shows that for the 31,069 BoTPs in employment, the mean weekly earnings in May 2026 for these employments was €573: www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/fp/p-aui/arrivalsfromukraineinirelandseries19/. Based on this data, it is likely that a large proportion of these can meet the income requirement. However, it is not possible to pre-empt the number of people in ARP supported accommodation who may not meet the proposed eligibility criteria for the temporary protection transition scheme.

question: 2276. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to clarify issues regarding current border control operations, airport security and immigration procedures in Ireland (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60265/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2173, 2268, 2269, 2270, 2276, 2307 and 2374 together. When a non-EEA national presents at a border, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted permission to land and enter the State. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the circumstances of the individual at the time of entry. The establishment of a person's identity and nationality is an important feature of our immigration process. The Border Management Unit (BMU) of my Department is responsible for frontline immigration functions at Dublin Airport only. Other airports and ports of entry are the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. People arriving at a port of entry will have their travel documents inspected either by an Immigration Officer or, in certain limited categories, by an electronic system (e-gates). They will also be subject to a Schengen Information System (SIS) check. Under this system, Ireland sends and receives SIS II information (termed "alerts") on persons and objects; for example, persons wanted for criminal purposes, missing persons, and objects that have been stolen or are sought as evidence for judicial purposes. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the full range of grounds on which a person may be refused permission to land. People can be refused for more than one reason. These include, but are not limited to, arriving without the correct documentation. When a person is refused permission to land at Dublin Airport, the Immigration Officer will arrange for the person to be referred to An Garda Síochána for removal from the State. The priority is to return them on the next available flight to their last point of embarkation. If a person indicates, or is identified as being, in need of international protection, they are admitted to the international protection process. I can advise the Deputy that the EU Migration Pact introduces mandatory processing times for international protection applications. Ireland, along with other Member States, will be required to process certain applications within three months under an accelerated procedure. This will apply to, amongst others, people who have misled authorities, for example by destroying identity documents. Carriers that permit a passenger to travel with their airline or ferry company without the necessary documentation, including where a passenger travels without documents, with false documents, without a visa, or by improperly using genuine documents, may be issued with carrier liability fines by An Garda Síochána. My Department and the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) are working closely with airlines on a range of measures to ensure that passengers have the necessary documentation when boarding. This includes delivering in-person training to relevant airline ground-handling staff on immigration requirements and the detection of false travel documentation. Following the delivery of this training, the BMU provides ongoing support to ensure compliance with immigration requirements and to strengthen capability in detecting false documents and other indicators of irregular migration. The BMU and GNIB have an ongoing intelligence-led programme of operations on aircraft to detect passengers who have destroyed documents in flight and to identify the point of embarkation of undocumented passengers. Up to the end of July this year, the BMU had carried out 3,653 doorstop operations at Dublin Airport. Implementing effective border security arrangements is a priority for me as Minister. The Programme for Government commits to developing a border security strategy to deliver stronger border security, ensuring that technology supports border screening, and reviewing the potential for extending pre-clearance mechanisms, such as electronic travel authorisation, to travel from designated third countries. This work is under way.
