question: 2334. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to expand capacity within the criminal justice system to deal effectively with youth delinquency; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61626/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2334 and 2345 together. The Children Act 2001, and the Government’s approach to addressing youth offending is rooted in the principle that detention of young people should only be used as a measure of last resort. The focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. While this principle underpins the approach to youth offending, it does not mean that young people do not face consequences when they engage in offending behaviour. To address and prevent youth crime, the Government operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime. My Department has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives; the budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, and the total allocation is now €43 million. With these funds, Youth Diversion Projects employ dedicated youth justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country; over 570 full-time equivalent youth justice workers have been recruited in recent years. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service. There are currently 92 Youth Diversion Projects and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects. The programmes offered by these YDPs primarily provide young people between the ages of 12 and 17 years with suitable activities to facilitate their personal development, promote civic responsibility, encourage pro-social behaviour in their communities and improve their educational outcomes and long-term employability prospects. The minimum core ‘package’ for a YDP includes two youth justice workers, together with what may be appropriate in the specific locality: a family support youth justice worker, an early intervention youth justice worker, an outreach youth justice worker to engage with harder-to-reach young people, and a team leader where the number of other staff requires such a post. My Department funds these posts based on the needs, size and population base of each YDP catchment area, and as feasible given the annual budget allocation. My Department recently commissioned the development of a toolkit to provide support for youth justice workers in addressing harmful masculinity norms and discouraging male-to-male violence among adolescents and young adults. This will be an evidence-informed training programme and tools for youth justice workers in Youth Diversion Projects and Targeted Youth Diversion Projects. These resources are intended to support them in navigating difficult topics with young people engaged in their services, specifically themes of masculinity, racism, radicalisation/far-right extremism and misogyny/gendered violence in both online and offline dimensions. This toolkit will be developed over the course of 2026 in collaboration with the Dublin City University Observatory on Cyberbullying, Cyberhate and Online Harassment and the University of Limerick Research Evidence into Policy, Programmes and Practice (REPPP) team. The toolkit’s design will allow for application in the youth justice sphere, and also across a wide variety of organisations, agencies and institutions (e.g. youth clubs, schools, etc.) that engage with children and young people on a regular basis. While effective in their work, there are some young people who are not suitable for diversion through a Youth Diversion Project, based on either the severity of their crimes or if they fail to accept responsibility for their offending. In such cases, An Garda Síochána refers these young people to the Director of Public Prosecutions. If prosecuted, the Courts can then determine if the young person should engage with the Bail Supervision Scheme (available in Cork, Dublin and Limerick) to prevent reoffending while on remand. Where a child is convicted, there a range of options available to the Court ranging from community sanctions, supervision by the Probation Service, and where necessary, detention in Oberstown Children Detention Campus. All of these interventions continue to focus on rehabilitation, addressing the underlying causes of the offending behaviour and breaking the cycle of crime.

question: 2336. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for international protection that have been received under each procedure since the International Protection Act 2026 became operational by nationality and outcome, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61730/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2323, 2327 and 2336 together. My Department takes all necessary steps to manage the international protection process efficiently and effectively, while ensuring the integrity of those processes is maintained at all times. The number of International Protection applications have been rising over the past number of years, reaching 18,500 in 2024. In 2025, application numbers reduced by approximately a third. There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand. In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024, a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. As of 16 August 2026, IPAT has already completed 5,858 appeals and is on track to significantly exceed the number of appeals closed in 2025. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 entered into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. The Pact provides a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. While the new system has only been in place since 12 June, it is operating as intended. My Department engaged in significant preparation work prior to commencement to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact. Under the new International Protection Act 2026, 1,638 people have made applications for international protection since 12 June. The table below outlines pathway outcomes for the 1,314 applicants who have completed screening under the IP Act 2026 up to 24 August. My Department does not provide detailed statistics on international protection grant and refusal rates by nationality. First instance decisions under IP Act 2026 2026* Granted Refugee Status (RS) and Subsidiary Protection (SP) 49 (9.67%) Refused Refugee Status (RS) and Subsidiary Protection (SP), or Decision to Transfer under AMMR, Inadmissible, Implicit Withdrawal) 458 (93.33%) Total first instance decisions 507 *to 2nd Sept, IP Act 2026 data only As of 31 August 2026, there are 195 appeals pending before the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA), with three appeals completed since its establishment on 12 June 2026. In relation to departures from the State following refusal or other negative decisions under the International Protection Act 2026, one person has been removed from the State as of 31 August 2026 and four applicants have been recorded as having availed of voluntary return as of 2 September 2026. Given the recent commencement of the new legislative framework, the volume of completed returns remains limited. The Department will continue to monitor outcomes arising under each procedure as the new system matures and larger datasets become available. question: 2337. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for international protection that have been received under each procedure since the International Protection Act 2026 who presented a valid passport or other recognised travel document when making their application; the number who did not, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61731/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 commenced on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. The Pact provides for a more streamlined and harmonised asylum procedure across the European Union, including standardised processing timeframes for applications examined under the standard, accelerated and border procedures. The table below outlines pathway outcomes for applicants who had completed screening under the International Protection Act 2026 as of 30 August 2026. Pathway Outcome Count % of Total Border Procedure 313 23.20% Accelerated Procedure 319 23.6% Standard Procedure 343 25.40% AMMR 128 9.50% Inadmissible 216 16.00% Screening completed - awaiting pathway assignment 32 2.40% TOTAL 1,351 100.00% The International Protection Office records information relating to the identity documentation presented by applicants during the screening and lodgement process. Since commencement of the Act, original hard-copy identity documentation, including passports, national identity cards, convention travel documents, birth certificates and driving licences, has been recorded as having been presented in respect of 602 applicants. Digital copies of identity documents presented by applicants may also be taken into account during the pathway determination process and are not included in the figure above. In determining the appropriate procedure under which an application should be processed, the International Protection Office considers a range of factors, including the documentation presented by an applicant, the reliability of that documentation, security or criminality concerns, and any identified vulnerabilities or medical needs. Under the International Protection Act 2026, applicants who deliberately withhold or conceal documentation relevant to establishing their identity or nationality may, depending on the circumstances of the case, be considered for processing under the accelerated procedure or the border procedure. Such decisions are made on a case-by-case basis and in accordance with the requirements of the Act and relevant EU legislation. Ireland is required to maintain adequate capacity for the operation of the asylum border procedure. Accordingly, assignment to that procedure is not determined solely by the presentation or non-presentation of documentation but involves consideration of all relevant legal and operational factors.

question: 2338. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for international protection that have been received under each procedure since the International Protection Act 2026 who entered IP accommodation services upon making their application; the number that subsequently left that accommodation following determination of their application, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61732/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection system is robust, and rules based, and that our borders are protected. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact provides a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for inadmissible cases. The new system has been in place for two months and is operating as intended. The Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement, developing and resourcing new processes and procedures, to ensure readiness for new timelines required under the Pact. The State is currently providing accommodation to over 32,000 people who have applied for international protection, and over 9,000 of these are children. Accommodation is provided in 298 centres nationwide. It is a legal obligation of the State to provide this accommodation and other basic supports to people seeking international protection. IPAS does not collate information on residents by stage of the application process. Between 12 June 2026 and 24 August 2026, 1,638 people started the screening process under the new legislation. The table below outlines pathway outcomes for the 1,314 applicants who have completed screening: Pathway Outcome Total Border Procedure 290 Standard Procedure 301 Accelerated Procedure 284 Inadmissible 186 AMMR (replacing Dublin Regulations) 120 No Pathway Assigned 133 Total 1314 IPAS releases weekly statistics in relation to international protection applicants. This includes a per county breakdown of where applicants are residing, an accommodation overview, and a wide range of other details. These statistics are located on the Gov.ie website: www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/collections/statistics-2004-to-2026/.

question: 2339. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether consideration has been given to a centralised vetting model or "vetting passport" as a means of reducing duplication and administrative burden on individuals and organisations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61636/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. In relation to vetting, that Department, together with Tusla, engages directly with the Garda National Vetting Bureau in An Garda Síochána on operational matters affecting the sector. While the delivery of vetting services is an operational matter or An Garda Síochána, in addition to the work to update the Garda vetting system, my Department engages on an ongoing basis with other Departments and stakeholders in relation to any relevant policy issues that may be raised or identified, as they arise.

question: 2340. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the key measures taken to tackle crime and improve community safety nationally since January 2025; his priorities for same for the rest of 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61633/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2325, 2340 and 2341 together. This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 includes unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion which will support the continued recruitment of Garda personnel. This will ensure that the Commissioner has additional resources to deploy to divisions nationwide. It will also support the expansion of the High Visibility Policing Plan introduced in Dublin City Centre in March 2025, which has since been rolled out to Cork, Limerick City Centres, Galway City Centre and Salthill, as well as areas of South Dublin, including Tallaght and Dún Laoghaire. An Garda Síochána introduced a High Visibility Policing (HPV) Plan in Dublin City Centre (North Central, Store Street and South Central and Pearse Street Garda Community Engagement Areas) in March 2025. During the period from April 2025 to March 2026, there were nearly 6,500 arrests made, over 13,500 charges/summonses and over 1,000 Adult Cautions/ Juvenile Diversion Referrals. The operation coincided with a 23% drop in theft, a 33% reduction in robbery from the person, and assaults causing harm were down by 18%. The Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced in April 2025, provides for the establishment of 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships (Safety Partnerships) within each local authority area. I have appointed members to all 36 of these Safety Partnerships. The Safety Partnerships bring together a broad range of relevant stakeholders to address community safety issues in their area, including residents, community representatives, business and education representatives, local councillors, and a range of public services including senior representatives of the HSE, Tusla, An Garda Síochána and the local authority. Each local partnership is responsible for developing a tailored and prioritised plan specific to that area in conjunction with the community and the relevant public services. Safety Partnerships leverage local and national policies, planning and funding to ensure service delivery is aligned with local needs. Drawing together the collective resources of partners at the table, they will ensure interventions are delivered proactively by the service best placed to deliver it and in a joined up, integrated way with other services. Many of these Safety Partnerships, including the five in Dublin City Centre have already undertaken consultation with their community in preparation for developing local community safety plans. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is providing support and guidance to Safety Partnerships in the performance of their functions and to monitor the implementation of local community safety plans. It is also a statutory function of the National Office to commission research and evaluations relating to the operation of Safety Partnerships. Such monitoring and evaluations will be guided by the strategic pillars of the National Strategy for Improving Community Safety. This strategy is currently being finalised following public consultation, ensuring our research is evidence-led and responsive to the safety concerns of communities across Ireland. I am very pleased that this Government has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026. Following a significant increase of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding as part of Budget 2026, the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. There are currently 92 Youth Diversion Projects and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects across the country that are co-funded by my Department and the European Union. With these funds, these projects employ dedicated youth justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country. With the official opening of POINT Youth Diversion Project on 18 June, Youth Diversion is available to all children and young people across the country. The Programme for Government commits to publishing a Retail Crime Strategy with targeted actions to reduce retail crime and support affected businesses. Work on the Strategy is well advanced and I expect to receive a draft in the coming weeks for detailed consideration. I look forward to engaging with its proposed objectives, priorities and recommendations to ensure that the final Strategy reflects the priorities of the Government and the needs of retailers, workers and communities. The Government intends to publish the Strategy within the next few months. The Community Safety Fund (CSF) redirects proceeds of crime seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána back into communities. Applications to the CSF are invited from community safety initiatives as well as groups co-funded with local authorities, NGOs and community organisations working on issues relevant to community safety and youth justice. On 13 April 2026, I announced the opening of this year’s funding call of €4.75 million for the CSF. This is a significant increase since the initial allocation of €2 million in 2022. This call closed on 18 May 2026 and successful projects will be announced later this year. The Fund has supported 127 community safety projects to date all across Ireland. Putting this money back into the community is a tangible way of showing that there can be a direct link between the activities of law enforcement and building stronger, safer communities.

question: 2342. Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of an application for "Without Condition as to Time" (Stamp 5 permission) submitted on 16 February 2026 by an individual residing in County Longford (details supplied); if he is aware that the individual's prior Stamp 4 permission expired on 15 March 2026, resulting in the loss of their employment; the timeline for the processing team to review the requested documentation covering the past eight years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61630/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Domestic Residence and Permissions (DRP) Division is experiencing very high volumes of applications for Without Conditions As To Time (Stamp 5). As a consequence there is currently a delay in processing applications. The application referred to by the Deputy is currently under consideration. Applications are dealt with in chronological order of when they are received. The applicant can be assured that there will be no avoidable delay in finalising their application and will be contacted as soon as a decision has been reached. The onus is on the applicants to keep their current permission in date as there is no guarantee of a positive outcome for any application. The DRP Division issues decisions based on existing immigration policies, all of which can be found on our immigration website: www.irishimmigration.ie. It is only in exceptional circumstances where a WCAT application will be approved outside of these given policies.

question: 2343. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of any proposals to streamline the Garda vetting process by introducing a system whereby individuals can use a single Garda vetting disclosure across multiple organisations, where appropriate; the measures being considered to reduce duplication in vetting applications; the expected timeline for implementation of any such reforms; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61736/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. In relation to vetting, that Department, together with Tusla, engages directly with the Garda National Vetting Bureau in An Garda Síochána on operational matters affecting the sector. While the delivery of vetting services is an operational matter or An Garda Síochána, in addition to the work to update the Garda vetting system, my Department engages on an ongoing basis with other Departments and stakeholders in relation to any relevant policy issues that may be raised or identified, as they arise.

question: 2345. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the national initiatives, programmes or strategies are currently in place to address male-to-male violence among adolescents and young adults; the bodies responsible for delivering such initiatives; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59875/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2334 and 2345 together. The Children Act 2001, and the Government’s approach to addressing youth offending is rooted in the principle that detention of young people should only be used as a measure of last resort. The focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. While this principle underpins the approach to youth offending, it does not mean that young people do not face consequences when they engage in offending behaviour. To address and prevent youth crime, the Government operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime. My Department has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives; the budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, and the total allocation is now €43 million. With these funds, Youth Diversion Projects employ dedicated youth justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country; over 570 full-time equivalent youth justice workers have been recruited in recent years. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service. There are currently 92 Youth Diversion Projects and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects. The programmes offered by these YDPs primarily provide young people between the ages of 12 and 17 years with suitable activities to facilitate their personal development, promote civic responsibility, encourage pro-social behaviour in their communities and improve their educational outcomes and long-term employability prospects. The minimum core ‘package’ for a YDP includes two youth justice workers, together with what may be appropriate in the specific locality: a family support youth justice worker, an early intervention youth justice worker, an outreach youth justice worker to engage with harder-to-reach young people, and a team leader where the number of other staff requires such a post. My Department funds these posts based on the needs, size and population base of each YDP catchment area, and as feasible given the annual budget allocation. My Department recently commissioned the development of a toolkit to provide support for youth justice workers in addressing harmful masculinity norms and discouraging male-to-male violence among adolescents and young adults. This will be an evidence-informed training programme and tools for youth justice workers in Youth Diversion Projects and Targeted Youth Diversion Projects. These resources are intended to support them in navigating difficult topics with young people engaged in their services, specifically themes of masculinity, racism, radicalisation/far-right extremism and misogyny/gendered violence in both online and offline dimensions. This toolkit will be developed over the course of 2026 in collaboration with the Dublin City University Observatory on Cyberbullying, Cyberhate and Online Harassment and the University of Limerick Research Evidence into Policy, Programmes and Practice (REPPP) team. The toolkit’s design will allow for application in the youth justice sphere, and also across a wide variety of organisations, agencies and institutions (e.g. youth clubs, schools, etc.) that engage with children and young people on a regular basis. While effective in their work, there are some young people who are not suitable for diversion through a Youth Diversion Project, based on either the severity of their crimes or if they fail to accept responsibility for their offending. In such cases, An Garda Síochána refers these young people to the Director of Public Prosecutions. If prosecuted, the Courts can then determine if the young person should engage with the Bail Supervision Scheme (available in Cork, Dublin and Limerick) to prevent reoffending while on remand. Where a child is convicted, there a range of options available to the Court ranging from community sanctions, supervision by the Probation Service, and where necessary, detention in Oberstown Children Detention Campus. All of these interventions continue to focus on rehabilitation, addressing the underlying causes of the offending behaviour and breaking the cycle of crime.

question: 2346. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the facilities that he has put in place to carry out biometric testing in third countries for the purposes of the Humanitarian Admissions Programme 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59708/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2131, 2132, 2133, 2137, 2145, 2146, 2147, 2148, 2149, 2152, 2156, 2157, 2346, 2347 and 2567 together. As the Deputy may be aware, the 2026 Humanitarian Admissions Programme, which operates under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) within my Department, commenced on 1 July 2026. For 2026, The Open Community has been appointed to administer the Humanitarian Admissions Programme, supporting the admission of 50 individuals through a community sponsorship (CS) framework. The deadline for submission of expressions of interest under the 2026 Programme has now elapsed. As the process of examining the applications received under the Programme is ongoing, the Deputy will appreciate that I am not in a position to comment on individual applications or pre-empt the decision making process. The Deputy will be aware that the EU Migration and Asylum Pact came into effect from 12 June 2026. The Pact contains a number of provisions around humanitarian admissions including a definition of ‘humanitarian admissions’, provisions around eligibility and the admissions procedure as well as requirements to be fulfilled in advance of admission under humanitarian admissions programmes. The Humanitarian Admissions Programme for 2026 was designed having regard to these requirements. In addition, when setting out the arrangements for the 2026 Programme, my officials were informed by issues including the presence of an Irish diplomatic presence in potential countries of first asylum, discussions with colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade around visa eligibility requirements in particular countries and the feasibility of facilitating travel to Ireland. As a result of these considerations, and given the shortened time period for completion of the 2026 Programme, applications from those persons in Pakistan and Türkiye will be considered for admission under the Programme this year. The Pact also sets out particular requirements in the area of collection of biometric data for all persons over the age of six years. These provisions will be applied to all such persons whose applications will be progressed under the 2026 Humanitarian Admissions Programme. Discussions are ongoing with relevant partners around arrangements for the collection of such data under this Programme.

question: 2348. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeframe within which an approved employment permit is notified from the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for the purposes of a visa application; the average time currently taken between employment permit approval and visa processing commencing; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [59584/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that in order to work in Ireland a non-EEA National, unless they are exempted, must hold a valid Employment Permit. The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (DETE) administers the Employment Permits system. DETE do not notify my Department that an Employment Permit has been granted for an individual. Once a visa required applicant receives their employment permit they must apply for a Type D Long Stay Employment visa from my Department before they seek to enter the State. Any person that wishes to make a visa application must do so online at: www.visas.inis.gov.ie/avats/OnlineHome.aspx. Visa processing cannot commence until the relevant fee and supporting documentation are lodged with the Irish Embassy/Consulate/Visa Office. Applicants are advised to do this as soon as possible. In 2025, the average processing time for an employment visa was 44 days. Work is underway to introduce a single permit for people coming to Ireland to live and work. Currently, employment permits, visas and residency permits are all processed separately. This is a significant technical project involving the integration of two IT systems. In the short term, we are streamlining the existing process by removing duplication, aligning online information and introducing a single payment model. These improvements will make the system simpler and more efficient. The project is progressing through a phased development with ongoing cross-departmental engagement. A pilot is also currently being scoped out to test the proposed new approach to delivering the single permit directive. Changes introduced in 2024 also mean that spouses and partners of employment permit holders can now take up employment without requiring separate employment authorisation. These initiatives support the long-term sustainability of our economy while recognising the important contribution that legal migrants make to our society.

question: 2349. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the role his Department and Ireland's diplomatic and consular services are expected to have in supporting the proposed voluntary return and re-integration programme for Ukrainian beneficiaries of TP; whether additional demand for travel documentation, consular assistance or liaison with Ukrainian authorities is anticipated; the additional resources that may be required; whether provision has been made for these requirements in the 2027 Estimates; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61207/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2244, 2273, 2349, 2351, 2363, 2384, 2386 and 2387 together. Most of the information sought by the Deputy is unavailable at this time. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2350. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the assessment his Department has made of the anticipated workload for immigration service delivery arising from applications under the temporary protection transition scheme; the estimated number of applications expected; the additional staffing and administrative resources required to process the applications; whether additional staff have been recruited or will be recruited in advance of the September 2026 opening of applications; the estimated processing time for applications; and the contingency arrangements in place should application volumes exceed current processing capacity. [61749/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government has approved the development of an alternative immigration permission for people with Temporary Protection in Ireland. This permission, known as the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme, will be granted for an initial period of up to two years and may be renewed for further two-year periods. The application process is expected to open in the coming weeks. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a minimum income of €29,432 per year, having independent accommodation, and being continuously resident in Ireland for a period of one year. The principal applicant must demonstrate they meet each criterion to be granted the permission under the scheme. As of June 2026, the CSO estimates that approximately 84,739 (69%) of those who registered for Temporary Protection continue to be active in/reside in Ireland. 31,069 persons fleeing the war in Ukraine who are currently residing in the state are in employment, with mean weekly earnings in May 2026 for these employments of €573: Arrivals from Ukraine in Ireland Series 19 - Central Statistics Office: (www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/fp/p-aui/arrivalsfromukraineinirelandseries19/). Based on this data, it is likely that a large proportion of these can meet the income requirement. However, it is not possible at this stage to predict the number of applications that may be received or to provide an estimate of processing times. This is due to to a number of factors, including variations in family composition and the individual circumstances and complexities of each case. The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme forms part of the Government’s wider preparations for an orderly transition from Temporary Protection and is in line with the EU Council recommendation for a co-ordinated approach to transition people out of Temporary Protection across the EU. This transition is being implemented on a phased basis. Planning for the implementation of the Scheme is ongoing within my Department. Workload requirements and operational arrangements continue to be assessed in advance of the opening of applications. At present, I am satisfied that sufficient resource capacity is available in my Department to implement each stage of the Government decision and for an orderly transition from Temporary Protection. The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme is expected to open for applications in the coming weeks. Further information is available on the Department's Ukraine Updates webpage, which will be updated in advance of the launch of the Scheme with details of the application process.

question: 2352. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procedures in place within the international protection process to identify a person who may be under 18 years of age where that person presents to the State accompanied by an adult who identifies them as a spouse, partner, child or other family member; whether the age, identity and claimed relationship of each person are independently verified where there is reason to doubt the information provided; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61753/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2352, 2353, 2366 and 2367 together. The International Protection Act 2026 has set out the legislative basis for carrying out an age assessment in line with the best interests of the child. Both this Act and the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum set out a series of safeguards in relation to presumed minors, including the procedures governing age assessment. Prior to the 2026 Act, a practice developed whereby, if an individual presented for asylum and claimed to be a minor, they were generally referred to Tusla, the Child and Family Agency. The International Protection Office (IPO) accepted Tusla's determination as to whether an individual was entitled to access its services as a proxy for an age assessment process. Under the 2026 Act, where doubts arise regarding the applicant's claimed age, an age assessment is scheduled. Each applicant is required to provide any identity documents in their possession. In conducting an age assessment, the Determining Authority (the International Protection Office) may consider statements made by the applicant to an officer of the Minister, a member of An Garda Síochána, their appointed representative, an immigration officer, a member of staff of Tusla, and any documentary evidence available. The applicant is provided with an opportunity to receive legal counselling and/or to appoint a legal representative, and a dedicated child representative supports them throughout all procedures. A professionally trained social care worker carries out a psychosocial assessment to support the age assessment decision. If the applicant is deemed to be a minor, they are referred by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to Tusla. Tusla will then undertake its own internal eligibility-for-services process. If, following completion of this process, Tusla disagrees with the Department's decision and believes the applicant to be an adult, it may refer the applicant back to the Department for a subsequent age assessment under Section 60 of the 2026 Act. In cases where Tusla has determined that an individual is not eligible to access its services, the individual's application is managed through the international protection process as an adult and they are accommodated accordingly. Individuals who apply as unaccompanied minors, undergo the age assessment process, and are subsequently determined to be adults are not subject to any further investigation on that basis. Their applications are progressed in the normal way as adult applications and, as with all applications, all relevant factors are taken into account before a decision is made. In terms of verification of familial relationships, the IPO team will seek documentary evidence of the relationship and observe behaviours between the child and the accompanying adult. Where concerns arise, the child is referred to Tusla for a comprehensive review of the child's wellbeing. Tusla can work with the child to initiate family tracing where the parent is not in Ireland. The table below shows the number of referrals from the IPO to Tusla for individuals claiming to be under 18 years of age from 2021 to 2025. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 39 181 186 233 353 The Department does not retain statistics on the number of individuals deemed ineligible for Tusla services. The table below shows the number of international protection applications made by Tusla on behalf of unaccompanied minors from 2021 to 2025. Please note that the difference between the number of IPO referrals to Tusla and the number of international protection applications made on behalf of unaccompanied minors does not equate to the number of referrals that were determined not to be minors. Decisions on whether to apply for international protection on behalf of an unaccompanied minor are carefully considered by Tusla on a case-by-case basis. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 53 58 189 250 224

question: 2354. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procedures used to verify the identity, age and claimed familial relationship of persons who enter or reside in the State on the basis of a claimed relationship to another person (details supplied); whether each person's identity, age and claimed relationship are independently verified; whether his Department records cases in which the claimed relationship is subsequently found to be incorrect, including cases involving claimed spouses or partners and claimed parent-child relationships; if so, the number of such cases from 2021 to 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61755/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that proof of a family relationship is required for a spouse, civil partner, or de facto partner, and for all children included in any immigration application, including the children of a spouse, civil partner, or de facto partner. Applicants are responsible for providing the documentation required to demonstrate compliance with the criteria of the scheme. The relevant division of my Department verifies identity and family relationships through official documents such as passports, birth certificates, and marriage certificates. In certain cases where reasonable doubt exists, applicants may be asked to provide DNA evidence to establish the relationship. Only DNA evidence obtained through a recognised service provider will be accepted, and the applicant must bear the cost of the DNA test. There is no obligation to submit a DNA test if requested. However, if an applicant decides not to submit a DNA test, a negative inference may be drawn and taken into account when a decision is being made on the application. Any State-issued official documents, such as birth certificates, marriage certificates, death certificates, or divorce certificates, that were issued by a State outside the EEA or Switzerland must be attested or apostilled as genuine by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or equivalent authority, in the State that issued the document before they can be accepted as evidence for Irish visa purposes. Such documents must also be translated into English or Irish where necessary. Applicants must provide a full certified translation into English or Irish of any documents that are not in either language. They must submit both the original documents and the certified translations. My Department will also accept an extract of a European marriage certificate, issued in accordance with the Convention on the Issue of Multilingual Extracts from Civil Status Records, as proof of a marriage within the EEA or Switzerland. Further details on how to obtain a certified translation of a document are available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-make-a-certified-translation-of-a-document/ Any applicant who submits false, fraudulent, or misleading information or documentation: - May have their application refused; - May not be permitted to appeal that decision; and - May be prevented from making any further Irish visa or preclearance application for up to five years from the date of the decision. My Department does not collect statistics on the number of instances in which false, fraudulent, or misleading information or documentation is submitted.

question: 2355. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the assaults perpetrated in Ireland in each of the years 2022 to 2025, where the victim was female; to include the perpetrator’s nationality and ethnicity if recorded, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61784/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO) is the national statistical agency and is responsible for the compilation and publication of all recorded crime statistics. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded on An Garda Síochána’s PULSE system and makes releases in relation to various crime statistics. The data on recorded female crime victims and perpetrators from 2022 to 2025 are available on their website at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/CVA03. I am advised by the Garda authorities that while information on a person's nationality, where known, may be recorded on their PULSE record, it does not systemically or mandatorily collect data related to nationality or ethnicity. I am further informed that An Garda Síochána is aligned with the practice of the Central Statistical Office of not publishing or compiling crime statistics based on nationality, ethnicity or citizenship. As Minister, I am committed to improving the collection and strength of data which may support the functioning of the criminal justice system, including data which may inform policy consideration; which can support our understanding of those who are victims of crime or who may be disproportionately represented within the system; and which may support crime prevention measures. My officials are currently working to fulfil a Programme for Government commitment to introduce a unique identifier for use across all criminal justice agencies. This would provide an invaluable source of data, without having to ask individuals to identify protected characteristics; and will provide a statistically robust way to understand ethnicity within the criminal justice system. While the Central Statistics Office (CSO) is not a body under my aegis and I have no role in its operations, functions, oversight or governance, my officials are engaged with it to consider how criminal justice sector data may be enhanced with its support.

The data on recorded female crime victims from 2022 to 2025 are available on their website at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/CVA03. I am advised by the Garda authorities that while information on a person's nationality, where known, may be recorded on their PULSE record, it does not systemically or mandatorily collect data related to nationality or ethnicity. I am further informed that An Garda Síochána is aligned with the practice of the Central Statistical Office of not publishing or compiling crime statistics based on nationality, ethnicity or citizenship. As Minister, I am committed to improving the collection and strength of data which may support the functioning of the criminal justice system, including data which may inform policy consideration; which can support our understanding of those who are victims of crime or who may be disproportionately represented within the system; and which may support crime prevention measures. My officials are currently working to fulfil a Programme for Government commitment to introduce a unique identifier for use across all criminal justice agencies. This would provide an invaluable source of data, without having to ask individuals to identify protected characteristics; and will provide a statistically robust way to understand ethnicity within the criminal justice system. While the Central Statistics Office (CSO) is not a body under my aegis and I have no role in its operations, functions, oversight or governance, my officials are engaged with it to consider how criminal justice sector data may be enhanced with its support.

question: 2361. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department records the number of protected disclosures referred to An Garda Síochána by Ministers, prescribed persons or public bodies each year; the number of such referrals have been made since the commencement of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022; and whether the subsequent outcomes of those referrals are monitored. [61412/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department fully complies with the protected disclosure reporting requirements established by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation and makes annual statistical returns to the Protected Disclosures Commissioner. This return includes referrals by my Department to An Garda Síochána for follow up. The reporting requirements however do not extend to my Department collating reports of wrongdoing referred to An Garda Síochána by other Ministers, prescribed persons or public bodies each year. question: 2362. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 534 on 7 July 2026, if he has received the relevant information from Garda authorities. [61383/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I refer to Parliamentary Question No. 534 of 7 July 2025 where you sought the estimated cost in 2027 if 1,250 new recruit Gardaí were recruited. Under section 33 of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2025, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the administration and management of An Garda Síochána. This includes the recruitment, training and appointment of members of Garda personnel. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under section 34 of the Act. I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that the first year estimated payroll and fixed subsistence cost of recruiting 1,250 Garda is in the region of €40.97 million. This sum includes a basic training allowance for 35 weeks along with 17 weeks of post attestation salary in year one of employment, and an estimation of certain fixed allowances and variable unsocial hours’ allowance, employer’s PRSI and an estimate of subsistence paid during the trainees’ deployment to an operational station. Other costs, including the cost of equipment, training and accommodation are not included as these are covered and facilitated by the Garda college. It should also be noted that the estimated figures do not take account of potential overtime costs in excess of estimated briefing time payments or potential future pension costs. For the purposes of this estimation it is assumed that the 1,250 recruits commence training on 1 January 2027.

question: 2363. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the proposed voluntary return and re-integration programme for Ukrainian beneficiaries of TP the estimated total cost of operating the programme in 2027, including travel, re-integration assistance; the estimated average cost per participant; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61330/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2244, 2273, 2349, 2351, 2363, 2384, 2386 and 2387 together. Most of the information sought by the Deputy is unavailable at this time. Ireland is not currently supporting voluntary returns to Ukraine. People considering returning to Ukraine, do so of their own volition and by their own means. Consideration is being given at EU level to the possible development of a voluntary return and reintegration initiative. Ireland remains engaged in ongoing discussion with EU Member States and will continue to monitor developments in this area. It is expected that information on a dedicated voluntary return and reintegration programme will be available in the coming months.

question: 2364. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number who may not meet the minimum income requirement for that scheme; the accommodation options will be available to such persons following the termination of ARP; whether any alternative housing support or transitional financial assistance is being considered for households that cannot secure private accommodation. [61326/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Following a recent Government decision, my Department is progressing to develop an alternative permission for people with Temporary Protection in Ireland. This is known as the Temporary Protections Transition Scheme. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a requirement to be earning a minimum of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be continuously resident in Ireland for a period of one year as a beneficiary of temporary protection prior to the opening of the application process. Applicants must provide evidence of independent accommodation at the time of application. Each application will be considered on a case-by-case basis. Further information is available at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/. This webpage will be updated over the next few weeks to include details of the application process. Recent CSO data shows that for the 31,069 BoTPs in employment, the mean weekly earnings in May 2026 for these employments was €573: Arrivals from Ukraine in Ireland Series 19 - Central Statistics Office: (www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/fp/p-aui/arrivalsfromukraineinirelandseries19/). Based on this data, it is likely that a large proportion of these can meet the income requirement. However, the principal applicant can apply on behalf of a family unit and as such It is not possible to pre-empt the number of people who will not be eligible under the income requirement for the scheme due to the unknown family composition of each applicant. Following the termination of the ARP scheme, hosts can continue to have private arrangements with Ukrainians if they so wish. Other measures, such as the rent a room scheme are also available. Beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine are free to explore private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of Rent Supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection to help meet the cost of private rented accommodation. Following Council Implementing Decision 2026/1912 of 30 July 2026, the Temporary Protection Directive is currently in place across the EU until March 2028. Those granted Temporary Protection in Ireland will remain entitled to this protection and associated rights under Section 60 of the International Protection Act 2015 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/66/section/60/enacted/en/html) and Section 237 of the International Protection Act 2026 www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/act/9/section/237/enacted/en/html). (while the Directive remains in effect. These rights, include access to the labour market, access to education and training, and access to medical care in the State in the like manner and to the like extent in all respects as an Irish citizen. Similarly, such persons (other than persons resident in Designated Accommodation Centres), may apply for social welfare benefits in a like manner and subject to the same eligibility criteria as Irish Citizens.

question: 2365. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who have been required to leave, or have otherwise left, State-provided or State-contracted accommodation since January 2022, the number for whom his Department has no recorded accommodation outcome following departure from State-provided accommodation. [61306/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2229, 2230, 2231, 2232, 2233, 2234, 2235, 2240 and 2365 together. My department is responsible for providing access to emergency temporary accommodation to persons who have fled the war in Ukraine and received Temporary Protection in Ireland. My department has no role in private accommodation arrangements and cannot assist with long-term housing matters. Those granted Temporary Protection are entitled to make their own accommodation arrangements through their own means, with the support of schemes and services provided by other bodies where appropriate. People may seek private rented accommodation independently and, where eligible, may avail of Rent Supplement administered by the Department of Social Protection to assist with rental costs. Further information on Rent Supplement is available through local Intreo Centres and Department of Social Protection offices. Alternatively, people with Temporary Protection may seek hosted accommodation through their Local Authority or through the Irish Red Cross. Those wishing to avail of hosted accommodation should contact their Local Authority or the Irish Red Cross directly. The Irish Red Cross can be contacted at migrationcrisis@redcross.ie or on 1800 753 343. Information on the Offer a Home scheme is available at www.offerahome.ie. Once a person with Temporary Protection leaves State-provided accommodation, my department does not have a role in, or visibility of, their subsequent private accommodation arrangements. Accordingly, my department cannot track whether an individual has returned to Ukraine, secured accommodation through private means, or accessed accommodation supports through other agencies. Further information regarding accommodation supports and policy updates is available at gov.ie under the Ukraine Updates portal.

question: 2366. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in respect of persons who presented or were assessed as being under 18 years-of-age and were subsequently determined to be adults, whether any cases in each of the years 2021 to 2025 were identified as involving suspected deliberate misrepresentation of age or identity; the number of such cases referred to An Garda Síochána or another relevant authority for investigation; the number resulting in any legal proceedings; the outcome of any such proceedings; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61228/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2352, 2353, 2366 and 2367 together. The International Protection Act 2026 has set out the legislative basis for carrying out an age assessment in line with the best interests of the child. Both this Act and the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum set out a series of safeguards in relation to presumed minors, including the procedures governing age assessment. Prior to the 2026 Act, a practice developed whereby, if an individual presented for asylum and claimed to be a minor, they were generally referred to Tusla, the Child and Family Agency. The International Protection Office (IPO) accepted Tusla's determination as to whether an individual was entitled to access its services as a proxy for an age assessment process. Under the 2026 Act, where doubts arise regarding the applicant's claimed age, an age assessment is scheduled. Each applicant is required to provide any identity documents in their possession. In conducting an age assessment, the Determining Authority (the International Protection Office) may consider statements made by the applicant to an officer of the Minister, a member of An Garda Síochána, their appointed representative, an immigration officer, a member of staff of Tusla, and any documentary evidence available. The applicant is provided with an opportunity to receive legal counselling and/or to appoint a legal representative, and a dedicated child representative supports them throughout all procedures. A professionally trained social care worker carries out a psychosocial assessment to support the age assessment decision. If the applicant is deemed to be a minor, they are referred by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to Tusla. Tusla will then undertake its own internal eligibility-for-services process. If, following completion of this process, Tusla disagrees with the Department's decision and believes the applicant to be an adult, it may refer the applicant back to the Department for a subsequent age assessment under Section 60 of the 2026 Act. In cases where Tusla has determined that an individual is not eligible to access its services, the individual's application is managed through the international protection process as an adult and they are accommodated accordingly. Individuals who apply as unaccompanied minors, undergo the age assessment process, and are subsequently determined to be adults are not subject to any further investigation on that basis. Their applications are progressed in the normal way as adult applications and, as with all applications, all relevant factors are taken into account before a decision is made. In terms of verification of familial relationships, the IPO team will seek documentary evidence of the relationship and observe behaviours between the child and the accompanying adult. Where concerns arise, the child is referred to Tusla for a comprehensive review of the child's wellbeing. Tusla can work with the child to initiate family tracing where the parent is not in Ireland. The table below shows the number of referrals from the IPO to Tusla for individuals claiming to be under 18 years of age from 2021 to 2025. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 39 181 186 233 353 The Department does not retain statistics on the number of individuals deemed ineligible for Tusla services. The table below shows the number of international protection applications made by Tusla on behalf of unaccompanied minors from 2021 to 2025. Please note that the difference between the number of IPO referrals to Tusla and the number of international protection applications made on behalf of unaccompanied minors does not equate to the number of referrals that were determined not to be minors. Decisions on whether to apply for international protection on behalf of an unaccompanied minor are carefully considered by Tusla on a case-by-case basis. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 53 58 189 250 224

question: 2368. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported suspected drink-spiking cases in County Kerry and throughout the country; the number that were investigated; the number that were brought before the courts; the number that were convicted in the past five years and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61187/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2368 and 2369 together. Spiking is a crime that preys on vulnerability, that undermines consent and that can have devastating consequences for victims. As Minister, I am committed to fostering a zero-tolerance approach to all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). Spiking a person’s drink or spiking someone by injection are, in effect, poisoning, which is a criminal offence under section 12 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, that can result in a three-year prison term. Section 12 applies to anyone who intentionally or recklessly administers a substance which is capable of interfering substantially with another person’s bodily functions, which explicitly includes inducing unconsciousness or sleep. Depending on the nature of the substance that is administered, it may be possible to charge a perpetrator with endangerment under section 13 of the Non-Fatal Offences against the Person Act 1997. This provides that it is an offence to intentionally or recklessly engage in conduct which creates a substantial risk of death or serious harm to another. The offence of endangerment carries a maximum penalty of seven years imprisonment. Where spiking is perpetrated in order to facilitate the commission of a further substantive offence (for example rape, sexual assault or theft), the perpetrator may also be charged with that offence or, where that offence was not completed, an attempt to commit that offence. An Garda Síochána has clear protocols in place in responding to reports of any crime. Gardaí undertake comprehensive investigations into each case, including toxicology analysis where necessary, to determine the circumstances and nature of the incident. Where evidence indicates a criminal offence linked to suspected spiking, the investigation will be conducted by local Gardaí, supported by or working in conjunction with Divisional Protective Services Units. An Garda Síochána takes all reports of spiking seriously and thoroughly investigates to determine the exact nature of each incident including results of toxicology reports in each case. I would advise any victims of similar incidents or any form of spiking to come forward and report same. On the measures in place to ensure timely Garda statements and preservation of evidence where a victim is incapacitated, I’m informed that on receipt of a report of any crime, Gardaí are duty bound to gather and seize evidence at a crime scene. Statements form part of the evidence-gathering process and will be taken from injured parties at an appropriate time and in a timely manner by the investigating member or the Senior Investigating Officer, if it is an SIO led investigation. Considerations such as the victim’s health and welfare, readiness and availability to provide a statement will be considered in preparing to take a statement of evidence. Preliminary notes and details may however be taken from the injured party and witnesses if available at the earliest time possible to initiate the investigation with a view to the early gathering of evidence and identification of the suspect(s). All victims of crime are dealt with by Gardaí in line with the Victims Charter: (www.garda.ie/en/victim-services/garda-victim-service/victims-charter.pdf) I’m informed by the Courts Service that there is no specific offence on the statute book for spiking. As a result, there is no offence code on their case management systems and therefore there is no data available in relation to spiking. I am advised by An Garda Síochána that the following publication may be of assistance to the Deputy and provides an analysis of spiking incidents reported between 2010 and 2023: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/spiking-incidents-may-2024.pdf. I am further advised that, according to the published data, there were 107 reported spiking incidents in 2022 and 52 reported incidents in 2023. An Garda Síochána has advised that there were 61 reported incidents in 2024 and 58 reported incidents in 2025. Each of these reported incidents was investigated. An Garda Síochána has advised that volumes were not sufficient to summarise beyond a regional breakdown. Data relating to spiking incidents will continue to be made available through annual proactive publications by An Garda Síochána.

question: 2370. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to expedite an application (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60572/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2372. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a response will issue to matters raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [60413/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Matters in regard to court fees are set by Statutory Instrument made by the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, with the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. The court fee structures currently in place are designed to be proportionate and balanced to ensure continued access to justice, while supporting appropriate contribution to the efficient running of the court system overall. The current fees system reflects the need to ensure the interests of applicants, as well as considering the public interest in the smooth operation of the court system. This balance of interests, as well as applicable administrative considerations, is evident in the extensive range of existing exemptions from court fees already in place in regard to specific categories of proceedings and by some State bodies. Matters arising relating to court fees are kept under consideration by my Department.
