answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I have requested the information sought by the Deputy from the Garda authorities. Regrettably, this was not available in time and I will write to the Deputy once the information is to hand.

question: 2418. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if owning a home would satisfy the accommodation requirement under the temporary protection transition scheme; if beneficiaries who secure a mortgage and purchase a home prior to applying for the scheme will be deemed compliant with the accommodation criteria; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62300/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The eligibility criteria in relation to accommodation as part of the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme is that a person must not be availing of state supported accommodation such as commercially provided, rapid build programme or hosted accommodation supported by the Accommodation Recognition Payment at the time of application. A person who purchases a home and is living in that home will meet the accommodation criteria for the scheme.

question: 2419. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if beneficiaries of temporary protection residing in modular accommodation at Clonminch may remain in situ while arranging a mortgage and purchasing a home, provided they vacate the accommodation before formally applying for the temporary protection transition scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62301/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The rapid build sites, including the site at Clonmich, referred to by the Deputy, are currently outside of the scope of the commercial accommodation wind down. As such, residents are free to make future plans for accommodation while remaining in their rapid build units. This can include the necessary measures to source and purchase their own homes. Rapid build residents will be able to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process becomes available. It is anticipated that the application process will be available soon. Updates and details of eligibility criteria will be available on Gov.ie. In order to meet the conditions of the scheme, however, they must first surrender their unit and leave state-provided accommodation. This same requirement also applies to those in commercial accommodation.

question: 2420. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the guidance issued to local authorities regarding the accommodation requirements for beneficiaries of temporary protection transitioning to independent housing; if this guidance has been communicated to Offaly County Council; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62302/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Department has and continues to communicate with local authorities regarding accommodation arrangements for beneficiaries of temporary protection who are transitioning from State-supported accommodation. The information provided to local authorities is consistent with that being communicated directly to affected beneficiaries through the Irish Red Cross (IRC) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM). This information outlines the accommodation options available to beneficiaries, including sourcing accommodation independently or applying for continued State-supported accommodation where specific needs arise. Local authorities in areas where accommodation centres are impacted, including Offaly County Council, are kept informed through ongoing engagement and communications issued by the Department. The Community Engagement Team circulated information about the changes to local elected representatives and officials in Offaly County Council on 21 July and 01 September 2026. These communications provide updates on the phased transition from State-supported accommodation, available supports and the application processes for continued accommodation. Relevant information relating to accommodation, available supports and the application processes for ongoing accommodation are published on www.gov.ie/ukraineupdates. The Department will continue to engage with local authorities and other stakeholders to ensure they are kept informed of developments as the transition from State-supported accommodation progresses.

question: 2421. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí and Garda staff assigned to the Cork city Garda division, and to Mayfield Garda station, as of the latest date available; the equivalent figures for each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62330/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the allocation and deployment of Garda resources throughout the state. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally, including a breakdown of Gardaí and Garda Staff assigned by division and station. Figures for the end of July 2026, the latest available, and for previous years, that can be viewed by accessing the data for December 2025 can be found at the following links: 2010-2025 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html. 2026 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/july-2026.html. As of the end of July 2026, the latest date for when figures are available, there were 3,565 Garda Staff within An Garda Síochána, accounting for about 19% of the overall Garda workforce, This represents an increase of over 75% since 2015 when there were approximately 2,000 Garda Staff. Garda Staff are an integral part of our policing service and they are involved in the provision of a wide range of administrative, professional and technical services. As well as providing clerical support and financial management functions in Garda stations and offices across the country Garda Staff also carry out a range of specialised support roles. The significant increase in Garda Staff has enabled 900 Gardaí to be freed up for frontline duties.

question: 2422. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the role of Local Community Safety Partnerships in responding to localised, persistent public disorder; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62335/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 includes unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion which will support the continued recruitment of Garda personnel. This will ensure that the Commissioner has additional resources to deploy to divisions nationwide. It will also support the expansion of the High Visibility Policing Plan introduced in Dublin City Centre in March 2025, which has since been rolled out to Cork, Limerick City Centres, Galway City Centre and Salthill, as well as areas of South Dublin, including Tallaght and Dún Laoghaire. The Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced in April 2025, provides for the establishment of 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships (Safety Partnerships) within each local authority area. I have appointed members to all 36 of these Safety Partnerships. The Safety Partnerships bring together a broad range of relevant stakeholders to address community safety issues in their area, including residents, community representatives, business and education representatives, local councillors, and a range of public services including senior representatives of the HSE, Tusla, An Garda Síochána and the local authority. Each local partnership is responsible for developing a tailored and prioritised plan specific to that area in conjunction with the community and the relevant public services. Safety Partnerships leverage local and national policies, planning and funding to ensure service delivery is aligned with local needs. Drawing together the collective resources of partners at the table, they will ensure interventions are delivered proactively by the service best placed to deliver it and in a joined up, integrated way with other services. Many of these Safety Partnerships have already undertaken consultation with their community in preparation for developing local community safety plans. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is providing support and guidance to Safety Partnerships in the performance of their functions and to monitor the implementation of local community safety plans. It is also a statutory function of the National Office to commission research and evaluations relating to the operation of Safety Partnerships. Such monitoring and evaluations will be guided by the strategic pillars of the National Strategy for Improving Community Safety. This strategy is currently being finalised following public consultation, ensuring our research is evidence-led and responsive to the safety concerns of communities across Ireland.

question: 2425. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of prisoners accommodated above the official operational capacity in each prison as of the latest available date, in tabular form. [62339/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am acutely aware of the capacity constraints in our prisons and the resulting challenges faced by those who work and live in our prisons. The Irish Prison Service (IPS) must accept into custody all people committed to prison by the courts and has no control over the numbers committed to custody at any given time. I am pursuing a dual approach to address the issue of prison overcrowding by both increasing prison capacity and pursuing further measures to support increased use of non-custodial sanctions. Since 2024, 265 spaces have been constructed across the Prison Estate, with 126 finished in 2024, 106 in 2025 and a further 33 so far in 2026. A further 32 spaces will be built this year, and 70 in 2027 The Government has allocated funding for a significant building programme in the prison estate. On conclusion of the NDP Review in July 2025, I secured a record capital investment of €528 million from 2026 to 2030, of which €495 million is being invested in building projects to further increase capacity, with an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031. This includes a large extension to the existing Cork Prison, a new block in Wheatfield, and an additional block extension at Midlands prison. This is in addition to spaces created at Castlerea, Mountjoy and the Dóchas Centre. Measures to support non-custodial sanctions are also important. The Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 will amend the Criminal Justice (Community Service) Act 1983 to support and encourage greater use of community service orders (CSOs). It includes an amendment to oblige the courts to consider a CSO in lieu of a prison sentence of up to 24 months’ duration (the current such threshold being 12 months) and to give reasons where they consider that a CSO should not be imposed in such a case. This amendment will oblige judges to demonstrate that they have considered this alternative. The Bill will further amend the 1983 Act to increase the maximum community service hours that a judge may order from 240 to 480. Budget 2026 also provides for a 13% increase in funding for the Probation Service. This additional funding will be used to increase the use of supervised community sanctions in the criminal courts, expand restorative justice services, and expand supervised temporary release schemes nationally. The Programme for Government commits to implement electronic tagging for appropriate categories of people, including those on temporary release and on bail. Under Budget 2026, I secured funding of €2.1 million for the project and anticipate electronic monitoring will be operational in 2026. Additionally, a Prison Overcrowding Response Group (PORG) was established in July 2023, composed of officials from my Department and representatives from relevant agencies. The Group considers measures to address capacity issues in the prison estate. In June 2024, following a report from this Group, a range of actions was agreed. Actions agreed by the PORG include developing new responses to deliver structured temporary release for suitable prisoners, actions to encourage greater use of community service, and advancing legislative changes to support delivery of community-based sanctions. The PORG continues to meet and work to implement these actions is ongoing. question: 2431. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he plans to intervene in relation to Palestinian students who have obtained scholarships to universities in Ireland for this academic year but who have been refused visas to come to Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62353/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. question: 2436. Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the assessment has been undertaken before assigning Ukrainian families to different counties; if a child's disability and specialist educational needs and ongoing medical treatment are considered as part of that decision; if these families fall within the commitment regarding established HSE care plans and continuity of care; and if not, the reason. [62371/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2436 and 2437 together. The phased wind-down of state contracted commercial accommodation for people from Ukraine follows a Government decision of 26 May 2026. This approach is consistent with the Council Recommendation adopted by the European Union encouraging EU Member States to support an orderly transition from Temporary Protection, while providing protection to those displaced by the conflict. Recognising that this is a significant change for residents, my Department, the Irish Red Cross and the International Organization for Migration has commenced dedicated engagement with those affected, providing information and practical support regarding available options. My Department also recognises that there are those who have a continued requirement for state-contracted commercial accommodation due to individual circumstances. For this reason, a self-declaration application process has been made available to residents who believe they continue to require temporary accommodation following the ending of accommodation at their property. Before my Department allocates accommodation to beneficiaries, available information regarding the composition of a family is considered, including any identified vulnerabilities or medical requirements, where known. My Department works with relevant agencies, including the HSE, to ensure that these factors are taken into consideration, insofar as practicable, when allocating accommodation. While every effort is made to continue to accommodate those with established HSE care plans to remain in the relevant Community Health Organisation area for continuity of care, there is no guarantee continued accommodation will be in the same area in which a person currently lives. My Department seeks however, insofar as practicable, to match accommodation to identified needs and remains committed to ensuring that vulnerable persons continue to receive appropriate supports throughout this transition. With specific reference to the review of an allocation prior to the date of transfer, it should be noted that the appeals process in place only allows for appealing the application decision to grant accommodation or not, rather than the location of the onward accommodation provided. Such an approach is in keeping with the way in which transfers of this nature have always been completed. While additional supporting documents can be submitted, unless they contain new and relevant information which renders the current allocation unsuitable, it is unlikely to change. Even in such a case, the State accommodation portfolio is very limited in what it might be in a position to offer as it continues to be wound down. It should be noted that it is standard practice to try to retain children with special needs in the same area where possible. In cases however where documented medical needs present along with special educational needs, medical requirements are considered to be the priority in the accommodation allocation process. In this context, medical requirements may necessitate relocation to a specific accommodation centre, even if it is not in immediate proximity to the current location. Relevant HSE Social Inclusion teams are kept informed of the allocations to ensure transfer of care packages and equipment within the timeframe.

question: 2439. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average processing times fors Stamp 4 visa renewals, broken down by the applicant’s nationality; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62413/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2439, 2440, 2441, 2442, 2443, 2444 and 2641 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience exceptionally high demand for first-time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended waiting times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every available avenue to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers in processing both first-time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact, and waiting times are reducing. I expect them to reduce further over the coming months. I am happy to inform the Deputy that the time taken for a Stamp 4 renewal application to be reached for processing after submission has been significantly reduced in recent weeks, from over 17 weeks to fewer than 11 weeks. Work is continuing to further reduce this timeframe. The processing times for individual nationalities are not recorded by my Department. Immigration renewal applications are processed chronologically based on permission stamp type rather than nationality. The Registration Office provides a live processing date for each stamp category, which is updated every Monday and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing. Customers may submit their renewal application up to 12 weeks prior to the expiry of their permission to allow sufficient time for the application to be reached and processed before their current permission expires. The standard 12-week provision remains in place, as does the notice to employers regarding any concerns individuals may have about their eligibility to work while their application is being processed. Further information is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.

This is having an impact, and waiting times are reducing. I expect them to reduce further over the coming months. I am happy to inform the Deputy that the time taken for a Stamp 4 renewal application to be reached for processing after submission has been significantly reduced in recent weeks, from over 17 weeks to fewer than 11 weeks. Work is continuing to further reduce this timeframe. The processing times for individual nationalities are not recorded by my Department. Immigration renewal applications are processed chronologically based on permission stamp type rather than nationality. The Registration Office provides a live processing date for each stamp category, which is updated every Monday and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing. Customers may submit their renewal application up to 12 weeks prior to the expiry of their permission to allow sufficient time for the application to be reached and processed before their current permission expires. The standard 12-week provision remains in place, as does the notice to employers regarding any concerns individuals may have about their eligibility to work while their application is being processed. Further information is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.

question: 2446. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the percentage of those in IPAS granted working permission and access to the labour market that have entered employment within twelve months of receiving the permission. [62495/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2446, 2447 and 2448 together. It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. Labour market access permission for international protection applicants gives eligible applicants the opportunity to work and helps them to integrate into Irish society while providing for themselves and their families outside of the State’s directly provided services and supports. It also helps people to plan and prepare for their future in Ireland if they receive a positive decision on their application for international protection. Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018), people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if: * They are an international protection applicant; and * They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and * They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a recommendation must not be attributable to the applicant. Following that, a person may be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application. The permission allows a person to access both employment and self-employment. They may work for most employers, however they are not permitted to be employed in the Defence Forces, An Garda Síochána, the Civil Service, the Public Service, or one of the other bodies listed in Schedule 6 of the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018. The granting of a labour market access permission does not necessarily confirm that the applicant has found employment. Data on IPAS Accommodation residents and their employment status is not collated by the International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) in the manner requested by the Deputy. The table below shows the number of labour market access permission applications made and granted from 2020 to 28 July 2026. - Applications made Applications granted 2020 6,284 5,721 2021 6,688 6,091 2022 7,511 6,732 2023 10,939 10,102 2024 18,868 17,004 2025 23,748 20,336 2026* 12,113 10,534 *to 23 July 2026.

question: 2449. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration To ask the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the age, sex, year of death and recorded cause of death of each person who died while resident in direct provision or IPAS accommodation since 2002, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62480/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2449 and 2450 together. Any death of a resident in International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) accommodation is a tragic event for their family, friends and neighbours, and also for the accommodation centre staff who know them. The Department publishes information on deaths of people staying in IPAS centres on Gov.ie, with the most recent publication reporting on the period to January-June 2026. www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/publications/statistics-on-deaths-of-international-protection-accommodation-service-residents/. The data provided shows that 10 residents died in the period from January to June 2026. In 2025, 23 IPAS residents died and 15 IPAS residents died in 2024, compared to 9 in 2023. It is relevant to note that from 2023 to 2024, the number of people resident in IPAS increased by more than 25%. The statistical breakdown of deaths and information on cause of death is grouped to protect the identity of the people concerned and their families. Where the cause of death is not publicly available or has not been confirmed by the General Registration Office (GRO), it is noted as “Not Available”. The Department does not have any input into the process of reporting or recording of deaths by the GRO. This publication is in line with the Department's policy on 'Recording & Reporting of Deaths of Residents in International Protection and Accommodation Centres’, a copy of which is published on Gov.ie, as follows: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/policy-on-the-recording-reporting-of-deaths-of-residents-in-international-protection-a.pdf.

question: 2451. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the number of applications for naturalisation currently being processed; the expected average waiting period for a person applying for naturalisation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62431/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2397, 2398, 2399, 2400 and 2451 together. It is important to note that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of Irish citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place in respect of each application. Unfortunately, some checks, including international enquiries and verifications, can take a considerable amount of time and are largely outside the control of Immigration Service Delivery. While I expect that, going forward, most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in every case due to the individual circumstances and complexity of applications. The Citizenship Division currently has 81 staff assigned across all grades. Staffing levels are kept under constant review, taking account of operational needs, application volumes and available resources, and additional staff have been assigned to the team as required. The number of naturalisation applications received by the Department in recent years is set out in the table below. Table 1. Citizenship applications received 2021-2026 Year Applications Received 2021 11,975 2022 17,202 2023 22,690 2024 27,032 2025 41,511 2026 (to date) 22,055 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. Citizenship Division has taken a significant number of steps in recent years to improve the application process and support more efficient case processing. These measures include the introduction of an online citizenship application process, online payment facilities and eVetting arrangements. These initiatives continue to improve the customer experience and support more streamlined processing. Approximately 6,000 applicants who have recently been approved for naturalisation are awaiting attendance at a citizenship ceremony. Each such applicant has received an invitation to attend the Citizenship Ceremonies being held on 17 and 18 September 2026. In 2025, 25 citizenship ceremonies were held and 29,300 certificates of naturalisation were conferred (adult and minor). In 2026 to date, 5 ceremonies have been held and 6,750 certificates have been conferred (adult and minor). My Department does not maintain statistics on the average length of time between the issue of an approval letter and an applicant's attendance at a citizenship ceremony. The scheduling of ceremonies is dependent on a range of operational factors, including venue availability and the number of applicants to be accommodated. The timeframe is also affected by the time taken by an applicant making the payment. There is no statutory processing time for naturalisation applications. However, the general objective of the Citizenship Division is to process straightforward applications as efficiently as possible. Citizenship processing remains a significant operational priority for my Department and I am committed to ensuring that the necessary resources and process improvements continue to be put in place to support the timely delivery of decisions. As of 31 August 2026, there were 51,882 active naturalisation applications being processed by the Citizenship Division of my Department. Of these, 38,748 applications (74%) had been in the system for less than 12 months, while 8,064 applications had been in the system for between 12 and 24 months and 5,070 applications had been in the system for more than 24 months.

question: 2454. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a list of all of the community dialogue events being arranged by his community engagement team; to provide the full list of participants and invitees to the community dialogue event in Tipperary; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62539/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Department’s Community Engagement Team (CET) was established in 2023 to engage directly with community stakeholders like elected representatives, local authorities, community members and service providers, in advance of a new accommodation centre opening for international protection applicants, or for people fleeing the war in Ukraine. As part of the Programme for Government 2025, Securing Ireland’s Future, there is a commitment to provide for detailed discussions with communities and to plan more effectively for delivery of public services. The Department has been progressing this commitment since early 2026, and part of this process includes community meetings being convened, in partnership with each of the 31 Local Authorities, to seek feedback on accommodation, migration and integration initiatives in each local authority area. Participants are identified by the Local Authority and drawn from existing local authority structures including the PPN, Community Integration Forums, Local Community Development Committees, Local Community Safety Partnerships etc. In general, the CET does not issue the invitations and does not retain a record of the names of participants at the community dialogues. As of 01/09, 17 Local Authorities have collaborated with the Community Engagement Team to host community dialogues in their areas. The CET continues to engage with Local Authorities to schedule community dialogues. The Community Engagement Team is collaborating with Tipperary Local Authority to convene a community dialogue which will take place in October.

question: 2455. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total amount spent by his Department, the International Protection Accommodation Services, and any State agency under his remit on security services at international protection accommodation centres in each of the past ten years; the companies that received such payments in each year; and the amount paid to each company annually. [62527/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In all IPAS accommodation centres, whether they are commercially provided or State-owned, centre management and providers are responsible for day-to-day operational arrangements on the site, including catering, health and safety, utilities and security arrangement. Security costs and service provision for commercially contracted centres are included in the overall contracted rate with the service provider. All contracts negotiated now provide for an all-inclusive rate, that covers all services on the site, including security. Security for occupied State-owned IPAS centres is also provided as part of each site's facilities management contract. As such, the Department does not hold details of individual security contracts and service providers, and would not procure or pay for these services directly. Security is maintained at two State-owned centres that are currently unoccupied: the Midlands Accommodation Centre, Lissywollen in Westmeath and River Lodge, Newtownmountkennedy in Wicklow. The need for security at these sites is informed by previous instances of criminal damage at these locations. In February 2026, the Department undertook a review of security services at both sites. Following appraisal, efficiencies were identified which resulted in cost savings at the site. question: 2458. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the contract for the provision of IPAS accommodation at a facility (details supplied); whether the contract review has concluded; the date on which the current contract expires; whether a decision has been made regarding its renewal; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62593/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2458, 2461, 2462, 2463, 2464, 2465, 2466, 2468 and 2469 together. The Department has a contract in place to provide accommodation to up to 120 people seeking international protection at this location, which is currently going through a contract review process for potential renewal. The Department treats the individual details of contractual arrangements and processes as confidential and commercially sensitive while they are ongoing. In relation to your questions about resident profile, since 2024, IPAS has not published details of the specific locations, resident profile, and occupancy of our accommodation centres. This is to preserve the privacy, safety and wellbeing of residents and staff. In relation to your question about broader community services, the provision of supports and services to people seeking international protection is a whole of Government response. Under the requirements of the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations, people applying for international protection are entitled to basic supports including accommodation, which is provided by my Department through IPAS accommodation. Other supports including healthcare and education which are accessed through mainstream services that are outside of the remit of the Department of Justice. These community services are available to all IPAS residents in centres located in communities all over Ireland. The contracted accommodation provider at an International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centre is obliged to ensure provision of staffing and all services at the centre, including 24 hour security services. Security and supervision arrangements are provided for under the contract and include the need to comply with the licensing requirements of the Private Security Authority (PSA). In relation to inspections, all IPAS Accommodation Centres are subject to oversight arrangements through the Department's Centre Management and Compliance Team, and inspected either by HIQA, department officials, or by external inspectors commissioned by the department. Across the wider network of IPAS Accommodation Centres, emergency accommodation centres are inspected by the department through officials or through an external contractor, and these reports are published regularly on gov.ie. The inspections examine the quality of the accommodation services, looking at food quality, fire safety, appropriate signage and information for residents, the condition of communal areas and sleeping quarters and adherence to hygiene and other health and safety measures. Centres are inspected at intervals every year and all inspections are unannounced. These inspections also check on whether centres are fulfilling their overall contractual obligations. Where any centre, following an inspection, has areas of partial or non-compliance identified, a bespoke compliance plan is agreed, noting the specific and time-bound measures which will be taken in order to ensure full compliance. This centre was inspected in February 2026 and the report for this inspection is available here. www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/publications/ipas-inspection-reports/. IPAS releases weekly statistics in relation to international protection applicants. This includes a per county breakdown of where applicants are residing, an accommodation overview, and a wide range of other details. These statistics are located on the Gov.ie website: www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/collections/statistics-2004-to-2026/.

question: 2467. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current processing time for an application type (details supplied); the number of applications currently in processing for the years 2024, 2025 and 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62620/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration A non-EEA parent of an Irish citizen child may be eligible for permission to remain in the State. To apply for this permission, the child must hold an Irish passport and the applicant must provide evidence that they are the child's biological parent and are substantially involved in the child's care. More information is available on the ISD website at: www.irishimmigration.ie/my-situation-has-changed-since-i-arrived-in-ireland/the-parent-of-an-irish-citizen-child/. In circumstances where a non-EEA parent of an Irish citizen child holds a valid permission to reside in the State, or has recently entered the State on a valid Join Family visa, they may make an appointment to attend my Department's Registration Office with their child to register their permission. If an applicant has a current permission, they may renew it online as the Parent of an Irish Citizen Child through the ISD Online Registration Portal. Processing timelines for renewals under this scheme are published on the ISD website at: www.irishimmigration.ie/information-on-online-renewal-timelines/. For all other applicants, the time taken to process an application for immigration permission as the Parent of an Irish Citizen Child depends on the complexity of the case. I can advise the Deputy that Irish Citizen Child applications are assessed on an individual basis and processing times may vary. The processing of this type of application can be complex in certain cases and, therefore, my Department does not record the average processing time for Irish Citizen Child applications. The table below outlines the number of Irish Citizen Child applications on hand for the years requested by the Deputy. Table 1: ICCA applications on hand Year Total 2024 15 2025 85 2026 191 Total 291

question: 2471. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 2312 on 28 July, if he has received the relevant information from Garda Authorities required to provide an answer to this question; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62567/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am informed by the Garda authorities that there are currently 5,328 live bench warrants in the Blanchardstown Community Engagement Area, formerly known as the K District. I am further informed by the Garda authorities that a bench warrant does not expire and is only removed from the PULSE system when cancelled by the Court. Furthermore the execution of warrants, including bench warrants, can be impeded by people actively seeking to evade detection and where limited identification information might be available to support enforcement. Local management in An Garda Síochána monitor the number of warrants (including bench warrants) under their area of responsibility. I am advised that there are currently two full-time Gardaí attached to the warrants unit in the Blanchardstown Community Engagement Area. Applications may be made by An Garda Síochána to the court to cancel bench warrants following consideration of a number of factors, including: an error on the warrant, the death of the defendant, previous failed attempts to execute the warrant, the age of the warrant or evidence that there is now an inability to prosecute the substantive charge.

question: 2472. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fixed charge notices, prosecutions or other enforcement actions taken in respect of e-bike users and e-scooter users failing to comply with traffic lights in each of the years 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, broken down by category of road user and Garda division where available, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62566/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by the Garda authorities that failure to comply with traffic lights is dealt with by way of FCN (Fixed Charge Notice). As outlined in the table provided below the offence can arise in the context of pedal cycles (including e-bikes) and separately for e-scooters. I am further advised that An Garda Síochána can only prosecute these alleged offences on an intercept basis, e.g. where the Garda stops the alleged offender at the time of or shortly after the alleged offence. Locations where alleged breaches are commonly reported at busy pedestrian crossings and junctions are the subject of local enforcement in their respective Divisions. An Garda Síochána also proactively use ‘ Days of Action’ to enforce and improve compliance. All identified breaches are dealt which by way of FCN. The below table provides the number of FCNs issued for the relevant offences in 2024, 2025 and to 2026, as of 1 September: Offence 2024 2025 2026 Cyclist Cycling Past A Red Traffic Light. Contrary to Section 35(5) of the Road Traffic Act, 1994 362 589 417 Failure by driver of a Powered Personal Transporter to obey traffic lights 13 132 108 The Garda authorities have advised that the data have been provided at a national level as divisional breakdown would have resulted in significant redactions. The Deputy may be interested to note however that the vast majority of FCNs issued for both categories of offence occurred in the Dublin Metropolitan Region with approximately 90% of FCNs issued in the period. Data provided is correct as of 1 September 2026, is operational and is liable to change.

question: 2473. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether there is currently a limit or operational target of approximately 25 Stardust compensation/redress payments per week; if so, the reason for this level of processing; the number of outstanding eligible applicants; the projected date by which all applications currently received will have been assessed and paid; whether he considers the current rate of processing acceptable given the age of many of those affected and the length of time that Stardust survivors and families have already waited for redress; and the measures being taken to expedite outstanding applications and payments. [62563/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2473 and 2474 together. On 16 February last, I announced the details of the Stardust Recognition Payment Scheme. The scheme was available to all survivor beneficiaries of the original Stardust Victims Compensation Tribunal established in 1985. The Scheme remained open for the receipt of applications for six months and it closed to new applications on 17 August 2026. Applications under the scheme were accepted online or by post. A Stardust Recognition Payment Helpline was also set up. The Scheme remains open for queries on existing applications. Applicants may contact the Stardust Recognition Payment team by emailing sdrqueries@justice.ie or by telephone at 01 8592268. In the processing of applications, all applications are reviewed by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit for completeness. In making an application, applicants consent to providing any relevant information requested by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit that is required to validate their application. Once all criteria are met, the applicant is then contacted to finalise arrangements and information for payment. A total of 555 applications have been received by the Scheme. As of 28 August 2026, the validation process for 243 applications has concluded and these have been authorised for payment. Payments to these applicants have been made to their designated bank account. The remaining applications are pending the completion of the validation process and I expect the number of payments to increase further in the coming weeks.

answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2473 and 2474 together. On 16 February last, I announced the details of the Stardust Recognition Payment Scheme. The scheme was available to all survivor beneficiaries of the original Stardust Victims Compensation Tribunal established in 1985. The Scheme remained open for the receipt of applications for six months and it closed to new applications on 17 August 2026. Applications under the scheme were accepted online or by post. A Stardust Recognition Payment Helpline was also set up. The Scheme remains open for queries on existing applications. Applicants may contact the Stardust Recognition Payment team by emailing sdrqueries@justice.ie or by telephone at 01 8592268. In the processing of applications, all applications are reviewed by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit for completeness. In making an application, applicants consent to providing any relevant information requested by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit that is required to validate their application. Once all criteria are met, the applicant is then contacted to finalise arrangements and information for payment. A total of 555 applications have been received by the Scheme. As of 28 August 2026, the validation process for 243 applications has concluded and these have been authorised for payment. Payments to these applicants have been made to their designated bank account. The remaining applications are pending the completion of the validation process and I expect the number of payments to increase further in the coming weeks.

question: 2475. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the movement of responsibility of the MUDS Act to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. [62556/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2475, 2506, 2507 and 2508 together. The Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 (MUDs Act) was enacted with the primary objective of reforming the law relating to the ownership and management of common areas of multi-unit developments, and facilitating the fair, efficient and effective management of owners' management companies (OMCs). The MUDs Act includes provisions relating to: • the setting of the annual service charge payable by apartment owners in a MUD; • the establishment of a sinking fund, to fund any non-recurring expenditure; and • the development of house rules for the operation and maintenance of their multi-unit development. Under Section 18 of the Act, the OMC must establish and maintain a scheme for annual service charges to fund ‘ongoing expenditure reasonably incurred’ on the maintenance, insurance and repair of common areas within its control and for the provision of common services (security, legal, accounting etc.) to unit owners. It is a matter for each individual OMC to determine the amount of the service charge on an annual basis. Section 18 of the Act requires OMCs to establish and maintain a scheme of annual service charges from which they may discharge expenditure incurred on the provision of common or shared services to the owners and occupiers of residential units in the development, including insurance, waste management, and security services. The Act sets out clearly that the service charge must be calculated on a transparent basis and be equitably apportioned between the residential unit owners. To ensure transparency and accountability, both the annual service charge and the services to be provided must be approved by a general meeting of the members of the OMC. Under section 19 of the MUDs Act, the OMC must establish a sinking fund for the purpose of ‘discharging expenditure reasonably incurred’ on refurbishment, improvement, or maintenance of a non-recurring nature, of the multi-unit development. Section 19(3) obliges the owner of each unit in the multi-unit development to make payment to the sinking fund of the amount of contribution fixed in respect of the unit concerned. Section 17 of the Act imposes obligations on OMCs: specifically, it provides that OMCs must prepare an annual report and hold a meeting at least once a year to consider the report. That report must contain details of the annual service charges as well as planned expenditure on maintenance and repair; insurance cover and contracts entered into by the company. The MUDs Act acknowledges the risk of disputes arising in the enforcement of rights and the performance of obligations imposed by its provisions on OMCs. Section 24 of the Act makes provision for the resolution of such disputes. This section provides that a person, including any member of an OMC, may apply to the Circuit Court for an Order to enforce any rights conferred or obligations imposed by the Act. Section 24(2) allows the Court to take into account whether the parties have tried to resolve their differences by mediation or other alternative dispute resolution. Section 27 provides for court-directed mediation if the court considers that a ‘mediation conference’ between the parties would assist in reaching a settlement of the matter. The Housing Agency which is a statutory body under the aegis of the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, already provides extensive information and guidance relevant to residents and OMCs in dealing with their obligations and rights under the MUDs Act. Further information can be found on the Housing Agency website - www.housingagency.ie/housing-information/multi-unit-developments-managed-estates. OMCs are also subject to company law provisions, including their own memorandum of association, and are subject to oversight by the Companies Registration Office and the Corporate Enforcement Authority. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission also plays a role in providing information and advice to intending purchasers of residential units in multi-unit developments. Under the Programme for Government, Securing Ireland’s Future, responsibility for the regulation of owner management companies (OMCs) and the Multi-Unit Development Act (MUDs) is to be transferred from my Department to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. This will streamline support for OMCs and improve oversight. The transfer has been enabled by legislative amendments which were necessary to avoid a conflict of Ministerial responsibility as arose in the Mulcreevy case. These necessary amendments were made by the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026, following this enactment, a Transfer of Functions order will then be necessitated. A timeline for this work and the transfer of functions is currently being advanced and engagement between the Departments is ongoing in this regard. The Department is currently working with relevant stakeholders to deliver this commitment in the coming weeks.

question: 2476. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the categories of personnel who will have access to the real-time location data of monitored individuals; the safeguards in place to prevent unauthorised access to or disclosure of that data; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62438/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2476, 2477, 2478, 2479, 2480, 2481, 2483, 2484, 2485 and 2486 together. The contract for electronic monitoring (EM) was awarded to Allied Universal Electronic Monitoring (AUEM). AUEM were selected through an open procurement competition carried out in accordance with Irish and EU public procurement rules. Three tenders were received by the deadline of 14 April 2026. AUEM was assessed against the published selection, mandatory and award criteria and was found to be compliant with all mandatory requirements. All tender responses were evaluated on a cost and quality basis (i.e. Most Economically Advantageous Tender (“MEAT”) basis). The Department has awarded a contract to the service provider for a 12-month pilot phase, with a possibility to extend for a further period of up to 12 months, with a maximum of one such extension. In line with Public Procurement Regulations, details of the awarded contract, including the contract value, will shortly be made publicly available via a Contract Award Notice published on eTenders. Under Budget 2026, €2.1 million has been secured to support staffing, procurement and set-up costs for the project. The exact cost breakdown under the contract is commercially sensitive. The pricing schedule can be viewed in the RFT that was issued on eTenders, and it is made up of a number of components, including installation and removal costs, monitoring costs, and a monthly monitoring fee. Electronic monitoring is provided for under a number of pieces of legislation. Two of these cohorts will be progressed for the initial pilot. The relevant pieces of legislation are Section 108 of the Criminal Justice Act, 2006 (for people on Temporary release) and Section 6B, 6C and 6D of the Bail Act of 1997, as amended by Criminal Justice Act (2007), s. 11 (for people on bail, provisions not yet commenced). The pilot rollout will initially provide for EM services for the temporary release cohort, followed by the bail cohort. The specific provisions of the Bail Act 1997 relating to EM will be commenced as part of the pilot. In line with the existing decisions on temporary release, consideration will be given on a case-by case basis to the profile of offender and the nature, type and seriousness of the offence and other relevant considerations of suitability and public safety. In relation to electronic monitoring for persons on bail, where the subject has been charged with a serious offence, certain decisions such as curfew and exclusion zones will be made on a case-by-case basis by the Judge. Electronic monitoring necessarily involves the processing of personal data, however, only data necessary for the operation, supervision and management of the service will be processed, and this will be subject to applicable Irish and EU data protection laws, including GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive. The Department completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment in advance of procurement. This assessment is a live document, subject to ongoing reviews, for the duration of the project. As outlined in the Request for Tender (RFT), all data must be stored, hosted, and processed only in data centres located within the European Economic Area (EEA). All required cyber security standards and security certifications required of the provider are outlined in the RFT. The provider is required to maintain independently certified ISO 27001 information security standards (or equivalent) for the systems and services used to deliver the service. The contract also specifies a range of technical and organisational security requirements, including secure data hosting, encryption, multi-factor authentication and role-based access controls. The pilot will use both radio frequency (RF) and GPS technology. Real-time location data will only be available where a GPS tag is used, and such data will only be accessed where required for the operation, management, oversight or support of the electronic monitoring service. Appropriate data protection, and contractual and security arrangements will be in place governing how information is accessed, used, stored and shared. Appropriately authorised officials of the Department and relevant agencies, including people involved in the monitoring process, will be Garda vetted and only have access to certain data if required. The experience of other jurisdictions was analysed by the project team during the discovery phase of the project. The learnings were taken into consideration in the design and planning of the project. The pilot approach will allow for processes and procedures to be tested before a wider scale national rollout, while also supporting the agencies involved to build capability and knowledge of the EM system. The pilot will inform future decisions and provide the evidence necessary to assess value for money, cost, operational impacts and outcomes in advance of any decisions on wider implementation.

question: 2483. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the contingency arrangements in place to ensure continuity of monitoring and preservation of data of the electronic monitoring service in the event that the service provider fails to deliver the service or the contract transfers to another provider; whether his Department has examined failures in electronic monitoring systems in other jurisdictions, including the loss of location data during a change of contractor in Spain, in designing these safeguards; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62439/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2476, 2477, 2478, 2479, 2480, 2481, 2483, 2484, 2485 and 2486 together. The contract for electronic monitoring (EM) was awarded to Allied Universal Electronic Monitoring (AUEM). AUEM were selected through an open procurement competition carried out in accordance with Irish and EU public procurement rules. Three tenders were received by the deadline of 14 April 2026. AUEM was assessed against the published selection, mandatory and award criteria and was found to be compliant with all mandatory requirements. All tender responses were evaluated on a cost and quality basis (i.e. Most Economically Advantageous Tender (“MEAT”) basis). The Department has awarded a contract to the service provider for a 12-month pilot phase, with a possibility to extend for a further period of up to 12 months, with a maximum of one such extension. In line with Public Procurement Regulations, details of the awarded contract, including the contract value, will shortly be made publicly available via a Contract Award Notice published on eTenders. Under Budget 2026, €2.1 million has been secured to support staffing, procurement and set-up costs for the project. The exact cost breakdown under the contract is commercially sensitive. The pricing schedule can be viewed in the RFT that was issued on eTenders, and it is made up of a number of components, including installation and removal costs, monitoring costs, and a monthly monitoring fee. Electronic monitoring is provided for under a number of pieces of legislation. Two of these cohorts will be progressed for the initial pilot. The relevant pieces of legislation are Section 108 of the Criminal Justice Act, 2006 (for people on Temporary release) and Section 6B, 6C and 6D of the Bail Act of 1997, as amended by Criminal Justice Act (2007), s. 11 (for people on bail, provisions not yet commenced). The pilot rollout will initially provide for EM services for the temporary release cohort, followed by the bail cohort. The specific provisions of the Bail Act 1997 relating to EM will be commenced as part of the pilot. In line with the existing decisions on temporary release, consideration will be given on a case-by case basis to the profile of offender and the nature, type and seriousness of the offence and other relevant considerations of suitability and public safety. In relation to electronic monitoring for persons on bail, where the subject has been charged with a serious offence, certain decisions such as curfew and exclusion zones will be made on a case-by-case basis by the Judge. Electronic monitoring necessarily involves the processing of personal data, however, only data necessary for the operation, supervision and management of the service will be processed, and this will be subject to applicable Irish and EU data protection laws, including GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive. The Department completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment in advance of procurement. This assessment is a live document, subject to ongoing reviews, for the duration of the project. As outlined in the Request for Tender (RFT), all data must be stored, hosted, and processed only in data centres located within the European Economic Area (EEA). All required cyber security standards and security certifications required of the provider are outlined in the RFT. The provider is required to maintain independently certified ISO 27001 information security standards (or equivalent) for the systems and services used to deliver the service. The contract also specifies a range of technical and organisational security requirements, including secure data hosting, encryption, multi-factor authentication and role-based access controls. The pilot will use both radio frequency (RF) and GPS technology. Real-time location data will only be available where a GPS tag is used, and such data will only be accessed where required for the operation, management, oversight or support of the electronic monitoring service. Appropriate data protection, and contractual and security arrangements will be in place governing how information is accessed, used, stored and shared. Appropriately authorised officials of the Department and relevant agencies, including people involved in the monitoring process, will be Garda vetted and only have access to certain data if required. The experience of other jurisdictions was analysed by the project team during the discovery phase of the project. The learnings were taken into consideration in the design and planning of the project. The pilot approach will allow for processes and procedures to be tested before a wider scale national rollout, while also supporting the agencies involved to build capability and knowledge of the EM system. The pilot will inform future decisions and provide the evidence necessary to assess value for money, cost, operational impacts and outcomes in advance of any decisions on wider implementation.

question: 2489. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on whether the new financial threshold for non-EEA family reunification visas is discriminatory against a person in receipt of carer’s allowance (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62719/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Policy Document on Non-EEA Family Reunification sets out a comprehensive framework to facilitate applications for family reunification strike a balance between the right to family life and the economic interests of the State. It is a core principle of the Policy that a sponsor must assume primary financial responsibility for any joining family members, thereby minimising the risk ofreliance on State resources. The recent adjustments to the financial criteria, including the gross cumulative income threshold of €75,000 over a three-year period for an Irish citizen sponsoring a spouse, reflect significant changes in the cost of living and the cost of essential services. I wish to state clearly that the financial thresholds outlined in the policy do not operate as an automatic bar, nor do they discriminate against individuals in receipt of Carer's Allowance. In accordance with standard practice under Section 10 of the Policy, the baseline assessment focuses on primary earned income, exclusive of State welfare payments. However, the Policy does not impose rigid prohibitions in this area. Every application for family reunification is subject to a case-by-case assessment. Where a sponsor is a full-time carer and in receipt of Carer's Allowance, the application is not summarily refused. Instead, decision-makers conduct a full qualitative review of the applicant’s overall material circumstances. In a case such as that described, immigration officers evaluate the broader context of the application. This includes: • Assessing any supplementary income or declared and verifiable savings by the sponsor/family member • Reviewing the sponsor's employment history in the State; • Assessing potential future employability or changes in income; and • Examining the specific caregiving responsibilities and unique vulnerabilities within the immediate family unit. Furthermore, exceptional circumstances are provided for in Section 13 of the Policy. However, the consideration of rare and exceptional circumstances will always be subject to the application establishing that the family relationship is valid and genuine; and one where there is dependency. The exceptional circumstances must refer to the specific exceptional circumstances of the sponsor/family member concerned. The revised Policy Document is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf

question: 2490. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken to address lengthy Garda vetting delays for childcare workers, which providers report are contributing to staffing shortages and room closures; whether consideration is being given to a transferable vetting system for childcare employees moving between services; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62139/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. In relation to vetting, that Department, together with Tusla, engages directly with the Garda National Vetting Bureau in An Garda Síochána on operational matters affecting the sector. While the delivery of vetting services is an operational matter or An Garda Síochána, in addition to the work to update the Garda vetting system, my Department engages on an ongoing basis with other Departments and stakeholders in relation to any relevant policy issues that may be raised or identified, as they arise.

question: 2491. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider reviewing the family reunification rights for healthcare assistants and home care assistants who have completed two years of lawful full-time employment in Ireland in order that they can access family reunification rights similar to those available to critical skills employment permit holders; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62740/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2222, 2491, 2515 and 2615 together. I recognise the difficulties faced by workers who are separated from their spouses and children while working in Ireland, and I can assure the Deputy that the Government recognises the immense contribution migrants make to our society and economy. The issues raised, including waiting periods, income requirements and the impact that separation can have on children and families, were carefully considered as part of the recent review of the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy. Following that review, I introduced a revised Family Reunification Policy on 26 November 2025. Further changes were made on 12 June 2026, including a commitment to review financial thresholds annually to ensure they remain aligned with living costs and consistent with the new statutory family reunification arrangements introduced under the International Protection Act 2026. A key issue considered during the review was family reunification for General Employment Permit holders, including Healthcare Assistants. Extensive consultation took place with Government Departments, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on this matter. A key principle of the policy is that individuals who bring family members to Ireland should be in a position to support them without reliance on State income supports. For this reason, financial thresholds remain part of the assessment process. Following the review, the Government decided that any future changes to these requirements should be linked to wage growth rather than reducing them below the income threshold used for the Working Family Payment. The review also introduced changes designed to make family reunification more accessible for General Employment Permit holders. In particular, the effective waiting period was reduced from 24 months to 12 months by reducing the amount of income evidence required from two years to one year. The review concluded that a further reduction in the waiting period could lead to a significant increase in applications and longer processing times. The policy continues to provide more favourable arrangements for Critical Skills Employment Permit holders. This reflects the State's objective of attracting workers whose skills are in short supply. Immediate family reunification is one of a number of measures that support this objective. While there are currently no plans to align the family reunification arrangements for General Employment Permit holders with those available to Critical Skills Employment Permit holders, the policy will continue to be kept under review to ensure that it remains fair, effective and responsive to changing circumstances. For information, the policy review report is available at: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/160c592a/Final_Report_on_the_Review_of_the_Non-EEA_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf. The Family Reunification Policy is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Family-Reunification-Policy-12-June-2026.pdf. I can further advise that current processing times and visa decisions at Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be viewed at: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to the Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently operational in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, thereby supporting improved processing efficiency. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing teams is intended to streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 2492. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the country of birth of each prisoner in the Irish Prison Service, by violent crime and nonviolent crime offences. [62739/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by the Irish Prison Service that while it records self-reported nationality, it does not routinely record country of birth. For the Deputy’s information, the Irish Prison Service has provided the attached table containing the self-reported nationalities of persons in custody as of 31 July 2026, categorised according to whether the offence for their most significant sentence length is an offence that falls into an Irish Crime Classification System grouping that includes violent offences.
