question: 2544. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the performance indicators used to assess whether the establishment of Cuan has improved access to accommodation, advocacy, protection and specialist supports for victims and survivors; the performance against each indicator to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63418/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2544, 2548, 2554, 2571, 2572, 2574, 2576, 2584, 2586, 2588, 2591 and 2616 together. Cuan is responsible for the coordination, monitoring, and reporting of Zero Tolerance – the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. The Agency reports on progress to my Department and also to a High-Level Oversight Board, chaired by the Secretaries-General of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Department of an Taoiseach, a Senior Officials Group, and the Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs. The provision of regular, timely, and accurate reporting on implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy supports robust and accountable cross-Governmental coordination, maintains implementation momentum, and facilitates the timely identification and resolution of delivery challenges by Cabinet and Heads of Department. My Department puts in place annual performance delivery agreements with Cuan, which are published on Gov.ie. The agreements define targets by which the performance of Cuan is measured and the mechanisms for monitoring and appraising performance. Cuan’s annual reports provide comprehensive details on delivery and achievements of the agency and can be accessed at Gov.ie/Cuan. In July, I announced publication of the 2025 Cuan Annual Report, detailing the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan which marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made, and I would like to direct the Deputies to this publication for a more in-depth look at the statistics and information they requested. It can be read here: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf In June 2025, I launched the third and final implementation plan covering the remaining period of the Zero Tolerance Strategy - 2025 and 2026. The plan sets out 95 actions across the Strategy’s four pillars of Protection, Prevention, Prosecution, and Policy Coordination, with 22 implementation partners responsible for leading on implementation across Government. Implementation partners report biannually to Cuan on actions and performance indicators through a bespoke online monitoring platform. These updates are analysed and collated to prepare regular progress reports on implementation for publication. The most recent progress reports on implementation are again available for review on Gov.ie. I announced publication of the Annual Progress Report for 2025 at the DSGBV Forum in March 2026 which was attended by stakeholders and services working to combat domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. This is another important mechanism which holds the Government to account on progress in meeting our objectives. While delivery of the Strategy’s objectives requires sustained effort over time, and significant work remains to ensure all victims and survivors are protected, supported, and able to access justice, this Progress Report demonstrates the measurable progress achieved in 2025 against key performance indicators. As we move into the final phase of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, our focus will be on consolidating progress, strengthening implementation efforts, and supporting the transition to the next phase, including the development of a Fourth National Strategy.

question: 2545. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the specialist domestic violence services funded or overseen by Cuan that are available on a 24-hour, seven-day-a-week basis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63417/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2532, 2545, 2546, 2551, 2573, 2577, 2581, 2585, 2587, 2590, 2592, 2596 and 2619 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. In July of this year, I published the 2025 Annual Report of Cuan, which details the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan, and marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made in combating domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and support victims and survivors. assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf The report highlights progress achieved through the four pillars of prevention, protection, prosecution, and policy coordination, supporting Ireland’s commitment under the Istanbul Convention and advancing implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy through coordinated national action. Cuan invested €58.4 million in 78 specialist services nationwide, ensuring that victims and survivors continued to have access to high quality, accessible and specialist supports. In total, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan-funded domestic violence services last year, of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. In 2025, Cuan allocated €3.2 million to facilitate a targeted funding call to support the expansion of services and innovation across a range of domestic and sexual violence services and perpetrator programmes. The funding call targeted key areas, including: expansion of counselling services for adolescent victim-survivors, improved access to domestic and sexual violence services for marginalised groups, increased capacity to address increasing service volumes across national helplines, training for staff and board members working in DSGBV organisations on a range of topics from governance to trauma-informed complex care, and increased access to perpetrator programmes. The funding provided by Cuan is expected to provide additional and improved training for more than 1,100 frontline professionals in 67 DSGBV services. An additional 5,484 victim-survivors will benefit from increased availability of services and appointments, and an additional 167 individuals will engage with perpetrator programmes. Prior to 2024 funding was split across a number of Departments and total figures are not available. For victims of domestic or sexual violence support services from State agencies and the voluntary sector are available to help. Anyone in any immediate danger should contact An Garda Síochána on 999/112. AlwaysHere.ie is a website that is run by Cuan, and lists all the DSGBV support services that are available both locally and nationally. Along with many other in-person services, there are a number of helplines that offer support to victim-survivors 24 hours a day and at weekends. The Women’s Aid 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a free, non-judgmental, and confidential service that offers support to women subjected to domestic abuse including coercive control. This includes emotional, physical, sexual, or economic abuse by a current or former partner. The National Freephone Helpline provides support in 240 languages. If English is not someone's first language, they can be helped in their own language through the free and confidential telephone interpretation service. The 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a gateway to local independent refuges and support services across the country. Anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or other forms of sexual violence can call the National Rape Crisis Helpline 1800 778888, a free and confidential listening and support service run by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre. Skilled crisis counsellors offer non-judgmental support to callers 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both Women’s Aid and DRCC receive funding from Cuan, the full details of which can be found in Cuan’s Annual Report 2025.

question: 2547. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total funding allocated to Cuan in each year since its establishment; the amount expended in each year; the amount provided directly to frontline services for victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63413/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2547, 2578, 2583 and 2593 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to confront the scourge of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Cuan, established in 2024, is the statutory agency responsible for the coordination and implementation of the Government’s response to DSGBV. The total budget for Cuan was €59.05 million in 2024, €66.9 million in 2025, and €79.2 million in 2026. Cuan’s overall budget each year includes spend on salaries for Cuan staff and business overheads, as well as funding for DSGBV services, and prevention measures including education and awareness raising campaigns. Cuan funds 78 DSGBV organisations nationally, including 20 domestic violence refuges. Cuan has provided the following levels of funding to organisations for the provision of DSGBV services, including refuges and support services: • €52.3 million in 2024; • €58.4 million in 2025; • the provisional allocation for 2026 is €69m. Prior to 2024, funding for DSGBV services was administered across a number of Government Departments and agencies, and consolidated funding figures for the sector are therefore not available. The establishment of Cuan has provided a more coordinated and strategic approach to funding and service development, ensuring that resources are directed towards identified needs and aligned with the objectives of the Zero Tolerance Strategy.

question: 2549. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the counties that currently have no dedicated domestic violence refuge accommodation; the plans for the provision of appropriate accommodation in each such county; the expected delivery date in each case, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63411/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2531, 2549, 2550, 2568, 2579, 2580, 2582, 2594, 2595, 2617 and 2618 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Refuge units and safe homes provide a vital place of safety for families in crisis. The Government is determined to continue to establish units across the country to ensure that those supports are available when they are most needed. At the start of the zero-tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. By the end of 2026, the target is to increase this to 94 safe homes,193 refuge units, with an additional 50 units under construction. All refuges scheduled to open in 2026 are on track, including 12 units in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown expected to be operational in Q4 2026. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. Furthermore, Cuan continues to explore additional opportunities for developing domestic violence accommodation, especially in areas where such facilities are currently lacking, while also considering interim refuges and alternative accommodation for those fleeing domestic violence. Work is also ongoing by Cuan to create a robust, scalable funding model, implement National Service Standards and develop a National Services Development Plan (NSDP). By working with partners across the sector, Cuan is building capacity, accelerating delivery of accommodation and ensuring that frontline professionals and support staff are trained to respond effectively. The are nine counties currently without a domestic violence refuge, they are; Carlow, Cavan, Laois, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan, Offaly, Roscommon and Sligo. However, five of these counties have Safe Homes, which is another form of safe domestic violence accommodation. Work is underway to develop safe accommodation capacity in the remaining four counties; beginning with Leitrim and Laois, with Laois identified as a priority area for refuge development. Cuan is also working to support the provision of domestic violence accommodation in Cavan and Monaghan. question: 2550. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of additional domestic violence refuge and emergency accommodation spaces that have become operational since the establishment of Cuan; the number available when Cuan commenced and currently; the number under development; the expected opening date of each planned facility, broken down by county, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63410/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2531, 2549, 2550, 2568, 2579, 2580, 2582, 2594, 2595, 2617 and 2618 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Work is also ongoing by Cuan to create a robust, scalable funding model, implement National Service Standards and develop a National Services Development Plan (NSDP). question: 2551. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the additional services for victims and survivors of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence that have become operational since the establishment of Cuan, distinguishing these from services that have been announced, planned or funded but are not yet operational; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63409/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2532, 2545, 2546, 2551, 2573, 2577, 2581, 2585, 2587, 2590, 2592, 2596 and 2619 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. In July of this year, I published the 2025 Annual Report of Cuan, which details the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan, and marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made in combating domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and support victims and survivors. assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf The report highlights progress achieved through the four pillars of prevention, protection, prosecution, and policy coordination, supporting Ireland’s commitment under the Istanbul Convention and advancing implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy through coordinated national action. Cuan invested €58.4 million in 78 specialist services nationwide, ensuring that victims and survivors continued to have access to high quality, accessible and specialist supports. In total, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan-funded domestic violence services last year, of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. In 2025, Cuan allocated €3.2 million to facilitate a targeted funding call to support the expansion of services and innovation across a range of domestic and sexual violence services and perpetrator programmes. The funding call targeted key areas, including: expansion of counselling services for adolescent victim-survivors, improved access to domestic and sexual violence services for marginalised groups, increased capacity to address increasing service volumes across national helplines, training for staff and board members working in DSGBV organisations on a range of topics from governance to trauma-informed complex care, and increased access to perpetrator programmes. The funding provided by Cuan is expected to provide additional and improved training for more than 1,100 frontline professionals in 67 DSGBV services. An additional 5,484 victim-survivors will benefit from increased availability of services and appointments, and an additional 167 individuals will engage with perpetrator programmes. Prior to 2024 funding was split across a number of Departments and total figures are not available. For victims of domestic or sexual violence support services from State agencies and the voluntary sector are available to help. Anyone in any immediate danger should contact An Garda Síochána on 999/112. AlwaysHere.ie is a website that is run by Cuan, and lists all the DSGBV support services that are available both locally and nationally. Along with many other in-person services, there are a number of helplines that offer support to victim-survivors 24 hours a day and at weekends. The Women’s Aid 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a free, non-judgmental, and confidential service that offers support to women subjected to domestic abuse including coercive control. This includes emotional, physical, sexual, or economic abuse by a current or former partner. The National Freephone Helpline provides support in 240 languages. If English is not someone's first language, they can be helped in their own language through the free and confidential telephone interpretation service. The 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a gateway to local independent refuges and support services across the country. Anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or other forms of sexual violence can call the National Rape Crisis Helpline 1800 778888, a free and confidential listening and support service run by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre. Skilled crisis counsellors offer non-judgmental support to callers 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both Women’s Aid and DRCC receive funding from Cuan, the full details of which can be found in Cuan’s Annual Report 2025.

question: 2552. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the estimated cost in 2027 if 270 recruit prison officers were recruited into Irish Prison Services; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63407/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by the Irish Prison Service that the estimated full year cost of employing 270 new Recruit Prison Officers, as per the most recent pay scales of 1st June 2026, is approximately €17.5 million, inclusive of Employers PRSI. These pay costs reflect salary and other allowances such as the Operational Allowance (8% of annual salary). They also reflect other premium payments and the allocation of up to 360 additional hours, as provided for in the Proposal for Organisational Change. Employers PRSI of 11.4%, as with the 1 October increase from 11.25% on total earnings, is factored into the overall pay cost of the 270 posts. As is the case with the recruitment of new staff members to an organisation, in addition to the above salary costings, there are a number of ancillary non-pay costs associated with the recruitment of a single Recruit Prison Officer, such as training, accommodation and uniform. The total current cost for such non-pay costs per Recruit Prison Officer is approximately €7,500. Salary Cert

question: 2554. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measurable performance indicators being used to determine whether the establishment of Cuan has resulted in victims receiving faster access to protection, accommodation, advocacy and other specialist supports. [63384/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2544, 2548, 2554, 2571, 2572, 2574, 2576, 2584, 2586, 2588, 2591 and 2616 together. Cuan is responsible for the coordination, monitoring, and reporting of Zero Tolerance – the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. The Agency reports on progress to my Department and also to a High-Level Oversight Board, chaired by the Secretaries-General of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Department of an Taoiseach, a Senior Officials Group, and the Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs. The provision of regular, timely, and accurate reporting on implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy supports robust and accountable cross-Governmental coordination, maintains implementation momentum, and facilitates the timely identification and resolution of delivery challenges by Cabinet and Heads of Department. My Department puts in place annual performance delivery agreements with Cuan, which are published on Gov.ie. The agreements define targets by which the performance of Cuan is measured and the mechanisms for monitoring and appraising performance. Cuan’s annual reports provide comprehensive details on delivery and achievements of the agency and can be accessed at Gov.ie/Cuan. In July, I announced publication of the 2025 Cuan Annual Report, detailing the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan which marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made, and I would like to direct the Deputies to this publication for a more in-depth look at the statistics and information they requested. It can be read here: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf In June 2025, I launched the third and final implementation plan covering the remaining period of the Zero Tolerance Strategy - 2025 and 2026. The plan sets out 95 actions across the Strategy’s four pillars of Protection, Prevention, Prosecution, and Policy Coordination, with 22 implementation partners responsible for leading on implementation across Government. Implementation partners report biannually to Cuan on actions and performance indicators through a bespoke online monitoring platform. These updates are analysed and collated to prepare regular progress reports on implementation for publication. The most recent progress reports on implementation are again available for review on Gov.ie. I announced publication of the Annual Progress Report for 2025 at the DSGBV Forum in March 2026 which was attended by stakeholders and services working to combat domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. This is another important mechanism which holds the Government to account on progress in meeting our objectives. While delivery of the Strategy’s objectives requires sustained effort over time, and significant work remains to ensure all victims and survivors are protected, supported, and able to access justice, this Progress Report demonstrates the measurable progress achieved in 2025 against key performance indicators. As we move into the final phase of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, our focus will be on consolidating progress, strengthening implementation efforts, and supporting the transition to the next phase, including the development of a Fourth National Strategy.

question: 2555. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of victims and survivors in Dublin West have accessed Cuan-funded domestic violence services in each year since its establishment; the way in which this compares with the equivalent figures before Cuan was established. [63383/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2555 and 2556 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to confront the scourge of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Refuge development in Dublin is being advanced as part of a coordinated, Dublin-wide programme rather than on an area-by-area basis. Services and emergency accommodation across Dublin city and county are accessible to those in need, irrespective of their place of residence. There is a range of DSGBV services currently operating across Dublin. Aoibhneas, based in north Dublin, provides 24-hour emergency accommodation through its refuge, which comprises 10 self-contained studio units. While located in north Dublin, its services are available to anyone requiring support. Aoibhneas is also progressing the development of a new 13-unit domestic violence refuge in Balbriggan, Co. Dublin. A stakeholder group has been established to support this project, and Cuan continues to engage with Aoibhneas, the Department of Housing, the Housing Agency and Fingal County Council in relation to its delivery. Construction on the site is expected to commence before before the end of the year Sonas Domestic Violence Charity supports people experiencing domestic abuse by providing and operating a range of services including emergency refuge accommodation. Their refuge in Dublin 15 provides eight refuge units for women and children. In October 2025, a new nine-unit refuge operated by Sonas opened in Dublin 4 with funding from Cuan, providing additional emergency accommodation for families experiencing domestic violence. A further nine-unit refuge in Dublin 22 opened in June 2026, also supported by Cuan funding. Cuan continues to work with Sonas to support the development of a new purpose built 12-unit refuge in Dun Laoghaire-Rathdown. Saoirse Domestic Violence Services supports people experiencing domestic abuse by providing and operating a range of services including emergency refuge accommodation. Their six-unit refuge facility in Dublin 24, provides safe and supported accommodation for those fleeing domestic violence. In addition to refuge accommodation, domestic violence service providers across Dublin provide safe home accommodation, offering an alternative form of safe and supported accommodation to victims-survivors and their families. The expansion of refuge capacity in Dublin forms part of the broader national effort to strengthen DSGBV services and ensure increased availability and accessibility of safe accommodation. At the start of the zero-tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. By the end of 2026, the target is to increase this to 94 safe homes,193 refuge units, with an additional 50 units under construction. All refuges scheduled to open in 2026 are on track. Cuan has advised that the attached table outlines safe accommodation units by county as of Q3 2026. Cuan has further advised that it is in the early stages of developing data sets for more robust figures on how many users each service has assisted, but these are not broken down by constituency. Monitoring on service activity and outcome for 2024 and 2025 has now been completed, providing for the first time, a national picture of service activity and impact across all DSGBV funded services 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan funded Domestic Violence services in 2025, and of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. DV Accomodation by County

question: 2559. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the plans in place to address significant overcrowding and capacity pressures across the prison system; whether consideration is being given to the construction of a new prison or other significant expansion of prison capacity; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63376/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2559 and 2560 together. I am acutely aware of the capacity constraints in our prisons and the resulting challenges faced by those who work and live in our prisons. Government has allocated funding for significant building in the prison estate. On conclusion of the NDP Review in July 2025, I secured a record capital investment of €528 million from 2026 to 2030, of which €495 million is being invested in building projects to further increase capacity. Since 2024, 292 spaces have been constructed across the prison estate, with 126 built in 2024, 106 in 2025 and 60 so far in 2026. A further 10 spaces will come on stream this year, and 102 in 2027. On 25 August, I signed the contract for a new extension at the Dóchas Centre that will increase the prison’s capacity by approximately 30%. The Rowan House Yard Extension project involves the construction of a two-storey extension to the existing block and will provide accommodation for 52 women, increasing capacity to over 225. The project is a key part of an overall extensive prison building programme which is expected to deliver over 1,500 new spaces between 2024 and 2031. On 23 July, I signed the contract for the construction of a new accommodation block at Cloverhill Prison which will increase capacity in the prison from 433 to over 700 spaces, and represents the largest single building project undertaken by the Irish Prison Service in several years. Construction has also commenced at Castlerea Prison to deliver a further 202 spaces by 2028. This building programme will include a large extension to the existing Cork Prison, a new block in Wheatfield, and an additional block extension at Midlands prison. This is in addition to spaces created at Mountjoy, the Dóchas Centre and Limerick Men’s Prison. The record capital allocation will also allow for work to start on the planning and development of a new prison on the Thornton site in North County Dublin. A master plan for the site is expected to be developed this year. Measures to support non-custodial sanctions are also important. Section 21 of the Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 has been passed by both Houses and will amend the Criminal Justice (Community Service) Act 1983 to support and encourage greater use of community service orders (CSOs). Budget 2026 also provides for a 13% increase in funding for the Probation Service. This additional funding will be used to increase the use of supervised community sanctions in the criminal courts, expand restorative justice services, and expand supervised temporary release schemes nationally. In response to capacity challenges in Irish prisons, a cross-sectoral Prison Overcrowding Response Group (PORG) was established in July 2023, composed of officials from my Department and representatives from relevant agencies. The Group considers evidence-informed measures with the potential to address capacity issues in the prison estate. Actions agreed by the PORG include developing new responses to deliver structured temporary release for suitable prisoners, actions to encourage greater use of community service, and advancing legislative changes to support delivery of community-based sanctions more generally. The PORG continues to meet and work to implement these actions is ongoing. The Future Prison Capacity Working Group was established in the second half of July 2024 to further consider future prison capacity needs and to make recommendations on the numbers and types of prison capacity needed out to 2035. I brought the Report of this Working Group to Cabinet and it was published on 4 July 2025. The report assesses the necessary upgrades to existing prison infrastructure and provides preliminary cost estimates for both capital investment and operational expenditure that delivers adequate capacity, while also ensuring a modern and fit-for-purpose prison estate that is humane, safe and secure. In line with government design principles, the Group considered how the design of prisons can contribute to rehabilitation, reducing recidivism and ultimately safer communities. The report was a key input into the NDP review negotiations. In addition, the Prison Overcrowding Risk Assessment Taskforce was established in 2024 by the Irish Prison Service Director General following a recommendation from the State Claims Agency (SCA). The SCA chaired the Taskforce and provided technical support, convening a series of focused workshops to identify risks, map existing controls, and determine additional short, medium and long-term measures needed to further mitigate prison overcrowding. This final risk assessment was forwarded to my Department and the Irish Prison Service in November 2025. The risk assessment sets out key recommendations across a range of thematic areas.

question: 2561. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on any planned reviews of the National Vetting Bureau Acts, specifically regarding the feasibility of digital vetting portability and transferable profiles for volunteers. [63367/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. question: 2564. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he has examined obligations for sellers of homes regarding the possible presence of asbestos; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62659/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2564 and 2565 together. The conveyancing of a property is a matter between a purchaser, vendor, and their respective legal representatives. I am advised that the conveyancing system allows purchasers of second hand houses to enquire as to the nature, quality and condition of a property prior to purchase. Detailed written queries and replies about the property (‘Requisitions on Title’) are exchanged between the vendor’s solicitor and the purchaser’s solicitor before the sale is completed, and the vendor may be bound by their replies to those questions. Obtaining appropriate professional and legal advice, including a structural survey, continues to form part of the due diligence that a person should undertake when considering the purchase of a property. While obtaining a structural survey is not a legal requirement for the purchaser, it is prudent practice and in the best interest of the purchaser. The purchaser should satisfy him/herself as to the condition of the property. By obtaining a structural survey, the purchaser can set out their specific requirements for the future use of the property to a preferred surveyor, who in turn has a contractual duty of care to identify any specified defects in the property. A Step-by-Step Guide to Buying a Home was published as part of the Interdepartmental Group on Conveyancing and Probate – led by the Department of the Taoiseach: https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/81591993/Your_Step_by_Step_Guide_to_Buying_a_Home.pdf Guidance is also available from the Law Society: www.lawsociety.ie/public/legal-guides/property/buying-a-home/ While all legislation is kept under review, there are no specific plans to amend conveyancing legislation. Legislation under the aegis of other Departments provides for building, environmental and energy standards.

question: 2566. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the commitment given at the outset of the Rapid Build programme that modular units would be offered to the relevant local authority for social housing after three years of use; and how that commitment is being applied to the Ballinure Way, Mahon, Cork city, and Charleville, County Cork, sites specifically. [60615/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Future use of the Rapid Build units, following the end of the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD), has always been an integral element of the Rapid Build project in order to provide value to the State and local communities. This includes the two sites referred to by the Deputy at Mahon and Charleville, Co Cork. While the units are highly durable with a 60-year lifespan, the sites were also developed with future use in mind, with all necessary infrastructure to support long term residency. A planning exemption remains in place for the current use of these units by those fleeing the war in Ukraine under the current Temporary Protection Directive. As the Directive has been extended on several occasions since the Rapid Build programme commenced, with the latest extension now agreed until March 2028, the planning exemption remains aligned with this. While this exemption is in place, these units cannot be utilised for any other purpose. However, to determine the long-term strategy for the sites post-TPD, a multi-stakeholder process commenced in March 2025, chaired by officials from my department and including representation from the Office of Public Works (OPW) and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH). In tandem with the consideration of the feasibility of potential future uses, this work involves exploring planning regularisation at each site. Work is also underway to determine the appropriate planning application process for each of the sites. To date, there has been no final decision made on long term future use, as discussions are ongoing with the need to explore all potential options within the local areas. However, these options include Social Housing and lower cost affordable housing such as Cost Rental.

question: 2567. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any flexibility that can be applied for the requirement to have an active third country visa under the process for Afghan citizens (details supplied) applying under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62857/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2131, 2132, 2133, 2137, 2145, 2146, 2147, 2148, 2149, 2152, 2156, 2157, 2346, 2347 and 2567 together. As the Deputy may be aware, the 2026 Humanitarian Admissions Programme, which operates under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme (IRPP) within my Department, commenced on 1 July 2026. For 2026, The Open Community has been appointed to administer the Humanitarian Admissions Programme, supporting the admission of 50 individuals through a community sponsorship (CS) framework. The deadline for submission of expressions of interest under the 2026 Programme has now elapsed. As the process of examining the applications received under the Programme is ongoing, the Deputy will appreciate that I am not in a position to comment on individual applications or pre-empt the decision making process. The Deputy will be aware that the EU Migration and Asylum Pact came into effect from 12 June 2026. The Pact contains a number of provisions around humanitarian admissions including a definition of ‘humanitarian admissions’, provisions around eligibility and the admissions procedure as well as requirements to be fulfilled in advance of admission under humanitarian admissions programmes. The Humanitarian Admissions Programme for 2026 was designed having regard to these requirements. In addition, when setting out the arrangements for the 2026 Programme, my officials were informed by issues including the presence of an Irish diplomatic presence in potential countries of first asylum, discussions with colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade around visa eligibility requirements in particular countries and the feasibility of facilitating travel to Ireland. As a result of these considerations, and given the shortened time period for completion of the 2026 Programme, applications from those persons in Pakistan and Türkiye will be considered for admission under the Programme this year. The Pact also sets out particular requirements in the area of collection of biometric data for all persons over the age of six years. These provisions will be applied to all such persons whose applications will be progressed under the 2026 Humanitarian Admissions Programme. Discussions are ongoing with relevant partners around arrangements for the collection of such data under this Programme.

question: 2568. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of additional domestic violence refuge and emergency accommodation spaces have become fully operational since Cuan was established; to provide a county-by-county breakdown showing the number of spaces available when Cuan commenced; the number available today; the number currently under development; and the expected opening date of each planned facility. [63507/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2531, 2549, 2550, 2568, 2579, 2580, 2582, 2594, 2595, 2617 and 2618 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Refuge units and safe homes provide a vital place of safety for families in crisis. The Government is determined to continue to establish units across the country to ensure that those supports are available when they are most needed. At the start of the zero-tolerance strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 DV refuge units in place. By the end of 2026, the target is to increase this to 94 safe homes,193 refuge units, with an additional 50 units under construction. All refuges scheduled to open in 2026 are on track, including 12 units in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown expected to be operational in Q4 2026. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. Furthermore, Cuan continues to explore additional opportunities for developing domestic violence accommodation, especially in areas where such facilities are currently lacking, while also considering interim refuges and alternative accommodation for those fleeing domestic violence. Work is also ongoing by Cuan to create a robust, scalable funding model, implement National Service Standards and develop a National Services Development Plan (NSDP). By working with partners across the sector, Cuan is building capacity, accelerating delivery of accommodation and ensuring that frontline professionals and support staff are trained to respond effectively. The are nine counties currently without a domestic violence refuge, they are; Carlow, Cavan, Laois, Leitrim, Longford, Monaghan, Offaly, Roscommon and Sligo. However, five of these counties have Safe Homes, which is another form of safe domestic violence accommodation. Work is underway to develop safe accommodation capacity in the remaining four counties; beginning with Leitrim and Laois, with Laois identified as a priority area for refuge development. Cuan is also working to support the provision of domestic violence accommodation in Cavan and Monaghan. Cuan is working with Safe Ireland to deliver six Safe Homes (3 in Monaghan and 3 in Cavan), and an interim refuge in Monaghan. It is anticipated that these will be operational by Q4 2026. question: 2569. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to urgently address issues raised (details supplied) in relation to garda Vetting turnaround times (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63506/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2281, 2339, 2343, 2344, 2412, 2490, 2561 and 2569 together. The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement. Responsibility for policy in relation to the Early Years sector, including safeguarding disclosure arrangements, rests with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality. In relation to vetting, that Department, together with Tusla, engages directly with the Garda National Vetting Bureau in An Garda Síochána on operational matters affecting the sector. While the delivery of vetting services is an operational matter or An Garda Síochána, in addition to the work to update the Garda vetting system, my Department engages on an ongoing basis with other Departments and stakeholders in relation to any relevant policy issues that may be raised or identified, as they arise.

question: 2570. Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a full and current update on the proposed new Dublin Family Courts complex at Hammond Lane, Smithfield (details supplied). [63503/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2529, 2570 and 2597 together. The construction of a purpose-built family law courts complex at Hammond Lane is a key priority for the Courts Service and a key Justice sector project in the National Development Plan. The new Dublin Family Courts Complex will be a modern purpose-built 19 courtroom facility where family law cases can be held in a dignified, secure and non-threatening environment with a range of support services to hand. It has been designed and will be built with the specific needs of Family Law court users in mind and will benefit families who interact with the courts at some of the most challenging junctures in their lives. The provision of a safe and secure environment for all court users is a key objective for the facility. A variety of measures will be implemented to achieve this including separate circulation routes for staff, judges, members of the public and persons in custody, clear and simple layouts providing clear sightlines, a variety of waiting spaces located throughout the building, private interview rooms where Courts Service staff can meet with members of the public in private, security screening areas, a custody suite, CCTV and access control. The provision of an on site security service is also proposed. Specifically in relation to domestic violence, the design of the facility provides for dedicated domestic violence accommodation, where providers of domestic violence support services will be able to meet clients/victims of domestic violence in a safe and secure private environment. It is proposed that the dedicated domestic violence accommodation will include office space, meeting rooms, bathroom facilities, video conferencing facilities, waiting areas and tea/coffee making facilities. Good progress is being made in delivering this much needed facility. Key achievements to date include: • Approval in principle to proceed with the project was granted by my Department in July 2023, following submission of a preliminary business case by the Courts Service as sponsoring agency. • Detailed plans/layouts for the building were developed by the OPW and approved by the Courts Service. The plans provide for a 6 storey over basement building providing approximately 18,250 sq m of purpose built accommodation. • Planning permission was granted by the Commissioners of Public Works in April 2024. • Technical and legal advisors were appointed by the National Development Finance Agency (NDFA) on behalf of the Courts Service in 2024. • The procurement process was initiated in July 2024. The project is being procured by the NDFA on behalf of the Courts Service in conjunction with the OPW, using the Competitive Dialogue procurement procedure pursuant to EU and national procurement law. • In November 2024 candidates were pre-qualified to participate in the tender competition for the project. • Following preparation of the tender documents the project was formally handed over to the NDFA for procurement in accordance with the project governance arrangements in August 2025. On 28 August 2025, the NDFA issued the tender documentation to the shortlisted candidates. • The competitive dialogue phase of the procurement process completed in Q1 2026. The closing date for receipt of tenders was 25th March. Subject to the successful completion of the procurement process, it is envisaged that construction will commence in 2027 with the building becoming operational during 2029. The Contract Notice for the project published in July 2024 shows an estimated capex cost of circa €150 million ex VAT. The actual costs will be informed by the procurement process.

question: 2571. Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration where Cuan targets have not been achieved, the reason for the delay; and the person or body responsible for delivery and the revised completion date. [63501/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2544, 2548, 2554, 2571, 2572, 2574, 2576, 2584, 2586, 2588, 2591 and 2616 together. Cuan is responsible for the coordination, monitoring, and reporting of Zero Tolerance – the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. The Agency reports on progress to my Department and also to a High-Level Oversight Board, chaired by the Secretaries-General of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Department of an Taoiseach, a Senior Officials Group, and the Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs. The provision of regular, timely, and accurate reporting on implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy supports robust and accountable cross-Governmental coordination, maintains implementation momentum, and facilitates the timely identification and resolution of delivery challenges by Cabinet and Heads of Department. My Department puts in place annual performance delivery agreements with Cuan, which are published on Gov.ie. The agreements define targets by which the performance of Cuan is measured and the mechanisms for monitoring and appraising performance. Cuan’s annual reports provide comprehensive details on delivery and achievements of the agency and can be accessed at Gov.ie/Cuan. In July, I announced publication of the 2025 Cuan Annual Report, detailing the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan which marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made, and I would like to direct the Deputies to this publication for a more in-depth look at the statistics and information they requested. It can be read here: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf In June 2025, I launched the third and final implementation plan covering the remaining period of the Zero Tolerance Strategy - 2025 and 2026. The plan sets out 95 actions across the Strategy’s four pillars of Protection, Prevention, Prosecution, and Policy Coordination, with 22 implementation partners responsible for leading on implementation across Government. Implementation partners report biannually to Cuan on actions and performance indicators through a bespoke online monitoring platform. These updates are analysed and collated to prepare regular progress reports on implementation for publication. The most recent progress reports on implementation are again available for review on Gov.ie. I announced publication of the Annual Progress Report for 2025 at the DSGBV Forum in March 2026 which was attended by stakeholders and services working to combat domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. This is another important mechanism which holds the Government to account on progress in meeting our objectives. While delivery of the Strategy’s objectives requires sustained effort over time, and significant work remains to ensure all victims and survivors are protected, supported, and able to access justice, this Progress Report demonstrates the measurable progress achieved in 2025 against key performance indicators. As we move into the final phase of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, our focus will be on consolidating progress, strengthening implementation efforts, and supporting the transition to the next phase, including the development of a Fourth National Strategy.

question: 2573. Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a comparison showing what services and capacity existed immediately before Cuan was established; and the additional services and capacity exist today as a direct result of Cuan's work. [63499/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2532, 2545, 2546, 2551, 2573, 2577, 2581, 2585, 2587, 2590, 2592, 2596 and 2619 together. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle all forms of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. In July of this year, I published the 2025 Annual Report of Cuan, which details the comprehensive steps taken during the agency's first full year operating under its 2025–2027 Corporate Plan, and marked the accomplishment of several high-impact, measurable initiatives. The milestones documented within the review reflect the scope and depth of progress made in combating domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and support victims and survivors. assets.gov.ie/static/documents/18b3e20a/Cuan_Annual_Report_2025.pdf The report highlights progress achieved through the four pillars of prevention, protection, prosecution, and policy coordination, supporting Ireland’s commitment under the Istanbul Convention and advancing implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy through coordinated national action. Cuan invested €58.4 million in 78 specialist services nationwide, ensuring that victims and survivors continued to have access to high quality, accessible and specialist supports. In total, 23,239 individuals were supported across Cuan-funded domestic violence services last year, of these: • 19,706 individuals received community-based supports outside accommodation settings. • 1,655 households were accommodated in domestic violence refuge and Safe Homes with an average stay of 6 weeks. There were 1,693 households accommodated in 2024 with an average stay of 7 weeks. • 3,284 children were supported by DV services, 3,015 were supported in DV accommodation. In 2025, Cuan allocated €3.2 million to facilitate a targeted funding call to support the expansion of services and innovation across a range of domestic and sexual violence services and perpetrator programmes. The funding call targeted key areas, including: expansion of counselling services for adolescent victim-survivors, improved access to domestic and sexual violence services for marginalised groups, increased capacity to address increasing service volumes across national helplines, training for staff and board members working in DSGBV organisations on a range of topics from governance to trauma-informed complex care, and increased access to perpetrator programmes. The funding provided by Cuan is expected to provide additional and improved training for more than 1,100 frontline professionals in 67 DSGBV services. An additional 5,484 victim-survivors will benefit from increased availability of services and appointments, and an additional 167 individuals will engage with perpetrator programmes. Prior to 2024 funding was split across a number of Departments and total figures are not available. For victims of domestic or sexual violence support services from State agencies and the voluntary sector are available to help. Anyone in any immediate danger should contact An Garda Síochána on 999/112. AlwaysHere.ie is a website that is run by Cuan, and lists all the DSGBV support services that are available both locally and nationally. Along with many other in-person services, there are a number of helplines that offer support to victim-survivors 24 hours a day and at weekends. The Women’s Aid 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a free, non-judgmental, and confidential service that offers support to women subjected to domestic abuse including coercive control. This includes emotional, physical, sexual, or economic abuse by a current or former partner. The National Freephone Helpline provides support in 240 languages. If English is not someone's first language, they can be helped in their own language through the free and confidential telephone interpretation service. The 24-hour National Freephone Helpline is a gateway to local independent refuges and support services across the country. Anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or other forms of sexual violence can call the National Rape Crisis Helpline 1800 778888, a free and confidential listening and support service run by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre. Skilled crisis counsellors offer non-judgmental support to callers 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Both Women’s Aid and DRCC receive funding from Cuan, the full details of which can be found in Cuan’s Annual Report 2025.
