question: 2634. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposals there are to roll out new CCTV schemes in Cavan and Monaghan in view of the value of these schemes in strengthening local crime prevention and community safety. [63966/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Community safety is a top priority for my Department and everyone has the right to be safe and to feel safe in their communities. CCTV in public places has a role in giving people a greater sense of security. It can also be effective in deterring criminal activity and antisocial behaviour and assists with the investigation of crime. The consideration and operation of CCTV by local authorities is a matter for the local authority concerned. As Minister, I have no role in relation to local authorities and updates on the rollout of individual community CCTV schemes should be sought from the relevant local authority. Local authorities work closely with An Garda Síochána in relation to CCTV schemes. The Garda National Community Engagement Bureau offer support and assistance in relation to all applications and processes. Each application is evaluated on the principles of necessity, proportionality and legality to ensure the CCTV application meets necessary human rights and privacy standards. All applications must be presented to the CCTV Advisory Committee and the need for each camera justified. The Deputy may wish to note that the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 provides for a new regime for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes, allowing for a member of Garda personnel or a Local Authority to apply in writing to the Commissioner of An Garda Síochána for an authorisation of CCTV. Pending the commencement of part 5 of the Act and the introduction of new arrangements, no new applications are being accepted. Prior to commencement, an amendment to section 7 of the Act that provides for transitional arrangements for existing CCTV applications, was also required. That amendment was included in the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Act 2026 which was signed into law by the President on 16 July 2026. The Commencement and Ministerial Orders are currently with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel (OPC) for drafting and I expect that the new CCTV provisions set out in Part 5 will be commenced at the end of the month. It should also be noted that under the Act there is a requirement for the Garda Commissioner to develop a Code of Practice for CCTV which will set out the procedures to be followed. As part of developing this new Code of Practice, An Garda Síochána consulted with the bodies listed in Part 8 of the Act and conducted a public consultation for any views or observations on the draft Code of Practice. The completion of the draft Code of Practice is an operational matter for the Garda Commissioner and I am unable to provide any timelines associated with the completion of this work by An Garda Síochána.

question: 2635. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposals to intensify cross-Border collaboration to deal with criminality with particular reference to the increasing prevalence of illegal drugs throughout the Island. [63965/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am pleased to inform the Deputy that there continues to be excellent ongoing cross-border engagement and co-operation with counterparts in Northern Ireland to tackle cross-border crime. I am in regular contact with my counterparts in the Ministry for Justice in Northern Ireland and I met with Minister Long in May for a meeting under the auspices of the Inter-Governmental Agreement on Co-operation on Criminal Justice Matters (IGA), in Armagh. At the meeting, Minister Long and I formally finalised the 2023-2025 IGA work plan and agreed a new plan to run from January 2026 to January 2028. The new work plan provides for continued cooperation across a range of criminal justice, public protection, forensic science, victim support and youth justice issues. This political level engagement is supported by close co-operation between my officials and officials in the Northern Ireland Department of Justice on a range of issues, between An Garda Síochána and the Police Service of Northern Ireland, and other agencies with their counterparts. Significant engagement also took place at Ministerial, senior official and operational level at the Cross Border Police Conference on Organised and Serious Crime in Co. Cavan in March of this year. This annual event, reinforces the aim of my Department to enhance understanding and cooperation between law enforcement agencies on both sides of the border, particularly in relation to cross border organised criminality and related issues. The objectives of the Conference include sharing experiences, identifying effective approaches and recommending actions to the Joint Agency Task Force aimed at enhancing cross-border working relationships to enhance our collective ability to tackle organised crime. As the Deputy will appreciate, the specific matters discussed at the Conference are sensitive and operational in nature, however I can advise the Deputy that robust and fruitful discussions around tackling cross border criminality took place. The 19th Cross Border Joint Agency Task Force report also highlights the ongoing commitment of law enforcement agencies on both sides of the border, which has been effective in disrupting their activities. The Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau leads in tackling all forms of drug trafficking and the supply of illicit drugs in Ireland. An Garda Síochána continues to implement an enhanced national anti-drugs strategy through Operation Tara. The focus of this operation is to disrupt, dismantle and prosecute drug trafficking networks, at all levels - international, national and local. The long-standing excellent cooperation between An Garda Síochána and their counterparts in Northern Ireland has been key to tackling cross border crime and ensuring security on the Island. I know that the Garda authorities will continue to work effectively with their counterparts in tackling crime and promoting safety for all communities on this Island.

question: 2636. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the proposals to establish new youth diversion projects in Cavan and Monaghan. [63964/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of Youth Diversion Projects (YDP) throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service. Cavan 365 and Monaghan Neighbourhood Youth Project (MNYP) are the YDPs in Cavan and Monaghan respectively, both operating in partnership with Foróige as the Community Based Organisation. The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone of the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people. This Department has, in recent years, significantly increased funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has almost doubled from 2020 to 2026, and the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million. With these funds, YDPs employ dedicated Youth Justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country. More than 570 full-time equivalent youth justice workers have been recruited in recent years.

question: 2638. Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of visa applications received from Palestinian nationals who have secured places in Irish higher education institutions for the current and upcoming academic years; the number approved, refused and pending; whether any measures are in place to expedite applications from students offered places in Irish colleges and universities; and if he will consider flexibility in documentation requirements where applicants are unable to obtain records due to the conflict in Gaza and the Occupied Palestinian Territories. [63947/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2185, 2186, 2241, 2284, 2289, 2290, 2291, 2305, 2309, 2405, 2431 and 2638 together. I can advise the Deputy that I am acutely aware of the grave humanitarian crisis in Gaza, and my Department continues to work closely with our colleagues in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to ensure a coordinated national response to this situation. This includes working with Irish citizens and their families who may require visa assistance. In common with the position applying to all non-EU nationals, the entry of Palestinian nationals is facilitated through the existing legal immigration pathways available. Palestinian nationals are visa-required and must hold a valid Irish visa before seeking to enter Ireland. Palestinian nationals may apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland for a variety of reasons, including employment, education, or joining a family member in the State. Details of these legal pathways can be found on the Department's Immigration Service website: www.irishimmigration.ie/. It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation. Visa applications from Palestinian nationals are examined by the Embassy of Ireland in Tel Aviv, which processes certain visa applications under delegated sanction on behalf of my Department. Officials in my Department's Visa Division are in regular contact with the Embassy regarding visa applications from residents of Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. Both Departments work together to ensure that visa applications from Palestinian nationals who meet the criteria for the granting of a visa are, wherever possible, processed as swiftly as possible. All visa applicants are advised that responsibility rests with them to provide as much information in support of their applications as they consider necessary. Guidelines in this regard are available on our website. Applicants who carefully follow these guidelines have a greater prospect of receiving a positive decision at first instance. The reasons for a refusal are outlined in the decision letter issued to the applicant. My Department does not collate statistics on the reasons for visa refusals. The table below details all study visa applications, including applications for English language courses, received from Palestinian nationals. My Department does not collate information on the intended commencement date of a student's course. The figures cover the period from 1 January to 31 August 2026. Short Stay (C) Study Received 6 Long Stay (D) Study Received 134 Short Stay (C) Study Granted 5 Long Stay (D) Study Granted 41 Short Stay (C) Study Refused <5 Long Stay (D) Study Refused 108 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. * A decision made in 2026 may relate to an application received in a previous year. * It is the policy of my Department not to release numbers where there are fewer than 5 in respect of any nationality, as there is a possibility that a person may be identifiable by releasing such information. * The Department does not collate information on the sponsorship details of applicants.

question: 2639. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the mechanisms in place to accommodate Irish citizens who do not have a passport in terms of travel to the UK by ferry following the decision to amend travel requirements (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64022/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2629, 2630, 2639, 2640, 2643 and 2646 together. Ireland and the United Kingdom have a shared responsibility and a shared interest in protecting the Common Travel Area (CTA). The CTA facilitates Irish and British citizens to move and reside freely across Ireland and the UK while maintaining access for citizens to a range of reciprocal rights and privileges central to everyday life. The CTA arrangements apply only to Irish and British citizens. All other nationalities remain subject to the immigration requirements in each jurisdiction. While there is excellent cooperation on CTA matters, the immigration rules that apply in the UK and Ireland are a matter for each jurisdiction. Each carrier must comply with the requirements of the jurisdictions in which they operate. It is a standard border management function to impose carrier liability fines on carriers who permit a non-national to travel with their airline or ferry without the necessary documentation i.e. no documents, false document, no visa or improper use of genuine documents. There is no requirement for Irish or UK citizens to produce passports when travelling within the CTA. However, airline and ferry carriers may require their passengers to have a passport in their possession before allowing them to board the craft. This is not an immigration requirement.

question: 2641. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reasons for the current delays in individuals applying for GNIB cards. [64053/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2439, 2440, 2441, 2442, 2443, 2444 and 2641 together. The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience exceptionally high demand for first-time registration appointments and immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended waiting times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is utilising every available avenue to facilitate as many applicants as quickly as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers in processing both first-time registration appointments and online renewals, with significant additional staff assigned to this work. This is having an impact, and waiting times are reducing. I expect them to reduce further over the coming months. I am happy to inform the Deputy that the time taken for a Stamp 4 renewal application to be reached for processing after submission has been significantly reduced in recent weeks, from over 17 weeks to fewer than 11 weeks. Work is continuing to further reduce this timeframe. The processing times for individual nationalities are not recorded by my Department. Immigration renewal applications are processed chronologically based on permission stamp type rather than nationality. The Registration Office provides a live processing date for each stamp category, which is updated every Monday and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing. Customers may submit their renewal application up to 12 weeks prior to the expiry of their permission to allow sufficient time for the application to be reached and processed before their current permission expires. The standard 12-week provision remains in place, as does the notice to employers regarding any concerns individuals may have about their eligibility to work while their application is being processed. Further information is available at: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/.

question: 2644. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardai assigned to roads policing units in July 2026, by garda division; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [64104/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. Information on the number of Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing are also published nationally, by Garda division. In addition uniform Garda members are to be deployed on high visibility roads policing operations, of 30 minutes duration, in each tour of duty. Technology also continues to play a significant role in supporting roads policing enforcement.

question: 2645. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of scrambler bikes seized by Gardai under the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026 known as 'Grace's Law'; and the number returned on payment of a fine. [64105/26]

Development and implementation of road traffic legislation and policy falls within the remit of my colleague, the Minister for Transport, and the vital role of enforcing road traffic laws is carried out by An Garda Síochána. To support An Garda Síochána, we now have an enhanced legislative framework following the signing into law of the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026, known as Grace's Law. Gardaí also have additional, and significant, legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of scramblers, quad bikes, e-scooters and other such vehicles under the Road Traffic Act 1961, the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, the Criminal Law Act 1997 and the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023. question: 2647. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the decision on the future use of 654 rapid-build housing units (details supplied); following the conclusion of their current use, to confirm if the units will be transferred to local authority housing stock, made available for allocation to households on local authority social housing waiting lists, or for other forms of housing provision; whether his Department assessed the suitability of these units for long-term social housing use; when the Government will make a final decision on the future ownership, management and allocation of these units; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61752/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Future use of these units following the end of the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) has always been an integral element of the rapid build project in order to provide value to the State and local communities. While the units are highly durable with a 60-year lifespan, the sites were built with future use in mind with all necessary infrastructure to support long term residency and are finished to enhance the local area. Under the Rapid Build Programme, the Office of Public Works (OPW) developed an exemplar single-storey modular design and specification to ensure Building Regulation compliance. The design is also aligned with the Department of Housing’s equivalent space standards to allow the units to be potentially utilised for social housing at a future date. Further to the first iteration, OPW leveraged this learning to also provide a modular two-storey housing option as a proof of concept. Twelve such units were built into the design at Backweston, Lucan, Co. Dublin. While the planning exemption remains in place for the current use of these units by people fleeing the war in Ukraine granted Temporary Protection, under the current Temporary Directive set to expire in March 2028, these units cannot be utilised for any other purpose. To determine the long-term strategy for the sites post-TPD, a multi-stakeholder process commenced in March 2025, chaired by officials from my department and including representation from the OPW and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH). In tandem with the consideration of the feasibility of potential future uses, this work involves exploring planning regularisation at each site. Work is also underway to determine the appropriate planning application process for each of the sites. To date, there has been no final decision made on long term future use, as discussions are ongoing with the need to explore all potential options within the local areas. However, these options include Social Housing and lower cost affordable housing such as Cost Rental. While current rapid build residents will not be required to vacate this accommodation until March 2028, they will be free to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process opens. To meet the conditions of the scheme, they must surrender their unit and leave their state provided accommodation in line with those in commercial accommodation. To date, full occupancy has been maintained, and we will continue to do so with eligible families to avoid having vacant units as developments and plans for their long-term future use have been finalised.

question: 2648. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the rapid-build modular housing sites at Ballinure Way, Mahon, Cork city, and at Charleville, County Cork, are to be transferred to Cork City Council and Cork County Council respectively for social housing use; and the timeline for any such transfer. [60611/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2182, 2183, 2184 and 2648 together. The rapid build programme has delivered 654 homes at 11 sites nationwide which are providing temporary accommodation for just over 2,600 people fleeing the war in Ukraine. Together, the two sites in Co Cork, referred to by the Deputy, comprise a total of 130 units designed for families of four, with 64 units at Ballinure Way in Mahon and 66 units at Charleville. These rapid build sites have a combined maximum occupancy of 520 people and there are currently no vacant units. A licence agreement is signed by each adult occupant allowing them to remain in their allocated unit while the Temporary Protection Directive (TPD) is in force. Residents must adhere to the conditions of the agreement and fulfil satisfactory annual unit inspections undertaken by the Approved Housing Body, Tuath Housing, who manage all rapid builds across the 11 sites. At present, the licence agreements are dated to 4th March 2027. Now that the TPD has been extended to 4th March 2028, these licenses can be extended on expiry of the current license period. Contributions are payable at a rate of 16% of income plus a flat fee of €40 per household per week towards utility costs. The same contribution is payable at all rapid build sites and there has been no change in the contribution percentage or utility amount since the sites were initially occupied. These contributions are offset against the management costs of the sites. The rapid build sites fall outside of the scope of the commercial accommodation wind down and, subject to meeting license conditions, current rapid build residents will not be required to vacate this accommodation until the end of the TPD. Rapid build residents will be able to apply for the new Temporary Protection Transitional Scheme when the application process becomes available. In order to meet the conditions of the scheme, however, they must first surrender their unit and leave state-provided accommodation. This same requirement also applies to those in commercial accommodation.

question: 3005. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the basis on which Tusla can be satisfied that a family reunification has been successful where it does not subsequently monitor, contact or follow up with the child or family following reunification. [62474/26]
answer: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality I propose to take Questions Nos. 3005, 3006, 3007, 3008 and 3009 together. Tusla is responsible for the safety, protection, and welfare of minors. The international protection status of migrant children is the responsibility of the Department of Justice through the International Protection Office. Tusla have advised that they have in place a robust procedure for ensuring that the young person is appropriately reunited including the following key steps: The social worker requests and gathers all available documentation from the parents, relatives or significant person, that provide evidence of their relationship to the child. This includes, but is not limited to birth certs, marriage certificates, baptismal certs, passports, identity documents, school documents, and in some cases, documents detailing a family history. A meeting is arranged to set out for the parents the process of decision making in relation to the request for the child to be placed/reunited into their care. If necessary, an interpreter is provided. They must be advised of the following: • Their right to have representation present for their interview. • The fact that local area checks will be undertaken. • Information on the decision-making process. Once the required assessments and procedures have been completed and reunification has been approved, the following arrangements apply: Where the reunification takes place in Ireland, a Tusla official physically accompanies a child to the point of handover. Tusla have advised that a home visit is undertaken to establish any additional support that the family may require. A copy of the family support plan is also provided to local area social work. On occasion where the reunification takes place internationally, a Tusla official may accompany a child, or Tusla may work with the International Association of Social Work to accompany the child. The local social work area to which the child has moved is also advised that if they require any additional information or need to take transfer of the file that this can be requested from the Principal Social Worker. Once Tusla is satisfied that the arrangement has the consent of the parents or legal guardians and that the child can be cared for in a safe and appropriate environment, the arrangement becomes a private family arrangement, and the case is closed by Tusla social work department.

question: 3011. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way in which Tusla exercises strategic oversight of separated children seeking international protection where key outcome information is held solely on individual case files and not collated centrally. [62467/26]
answer: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality I propose to take Questions Nos. 3010, 3011, 3012, 3013 and 3014 together. Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, has statutory responsibility under the Child Care Act 1991 for providing accommodation to Separated Children Seeking International Protection (SCSIP) who are referred by the International Protection Office. The responsibility for the operation of the international protection system rests with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Tusla advise that they hold a centrally accessible database for recording service data, which has been in place since 2024. This system will continue to be developed to meet service needs. The Deputy has been previously supplied with information available on the number of minors seeking international protection in care/accommodated for each year 2024, 2025, and 2026. Individuals who are service users have individual case files. In accordance with data protection requirements and safeguarding obligations, Tusla will not disclose information from individual case files that is personal in nature or that could lead to identification of an individual child or young person. Tusla SCSIP service also operates an oversight system in which social work and social care practitioners are line managed by Team Leaders and Principal Social Work Staff. In turn Area Managers for Residential Services and for Operational Services oversee their respective teams. All individual case files are reviewed through this oversight system. Once family reunification of a child occurs, the case is closed to the SCSIP service, and the local area is notified of the family reunification. Any child protection or welfare concerns identified post reunification are notified and managed by the local network area where the child and family reside. Tusla can account for individual’s final recorded outcome at the point where they age out of care, are discharged from care, are reunified or where they cease aftercare. This information is recorded on individuals’ personal files.

question: 4061. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the actions he will take to address concerns related to the approval of visa applications made by Palestinian students (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [61520/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science I propose to take Questions Nos. 4061, 4070 and 4072 together. I am conscious of the extremely challenging humanitarian situation in Palestine and, in particular, the devastating impact the conflict has had on students, educational opportunities and the higher education system, including the destruction of institutions in Gaza and the broader challenges facing higher education across Palestine. I remain committed to ensuring that the importance of educational opportunities for Palestinian students is understood across Government. However, the granting of visas is a matter for the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, and this Department has no role in the visa application process. Visa applications are assessed by the relevant authorities on a case-by-case basis and on their individual merits, in accordance with Irish immigration law and the applicable legislative and policy framework.

question: 4094. Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether his Department has considered any specific arrangements for beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine who entered the State as unaccompanied minors and are in Tusla care, but are unable to meet the residency requirements for student supports due to the length of time they have been resident in the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [63393/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science I propose to take Questions Nos. 4094 and 4095 together. Supports for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection in further and higher education will continue to be in place for Academic Year 2026/27. These supports vary depending on whether the student is a new entrant or an existing registered student in tertiary education, as well as the duration of their Beneficiary of Temporary Protection (BoTP) status. While there are no Department-specific arrangements for this cohort beyond the wider supports framework, a range of supports may also be available through individual higher and further education institutions and other relevant public services. Details on the supports available for BoTPs students for the Academic Year 2026/27 are available at the following link www.gov.ie/en/department-of-further-and-higher-education-research-innovation-and-science/publications/supports-to-beneficiaries-of-temporary-protection-botp-for-academic-year-20262027/ . Students in this cohort are encouraged to engage with the Access Office of the higher or further education institution they are attend, or intend to attend, as institutions may have additional supports and services available to assist them. Further information on supports is also available at [ ] hea.ie/funding-governance-performance/funding/student-finance/ . Given that the students concerned are unaccompanied minors in the care of Tusla, the Deputy may also wish to engage with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality for further information on any additional supports that may be available to these students through that Department.

question: 4103. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his views on the need for clear guidance for higher education institutions regarding applying EU fee status to students living here under temporary protection following withdrawal of the temporary tuition fee support scheme for Ukrainian students starting courses in 2026/2027 (details supplied); and his plans to support such students who were admitted through the CAO and assessed as an EU student prior to the change in position. [63861/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science As part of the State's emergency response to the war in Ukraine, the Government introduced a range of temporary supports for people arriving in Ireland under the EU Temporary Protection Directive. These measures included education supports for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BoTP) who were entering further and higher education. Subsequently, in line with the wider approach across Government to transition from emergency responses to more sustainable long-term arrangements, it was necessary to review these supports and bring them more closely into line with those available to Irish citizens and other eligible students. This approach reflects the need to place supports on a sustainable footing while continuing to provide access to education through the mainstream student support framework. Accordingly, in May 2025 the Government advised both prospective students and the higher education sector that the Temporary Tuition Fee Support Scheme, the BoTP Stipend, and the PLC Bursary would close to any applicant commencing a new course in the 2026/27 academic year. This advance notice was provided to allow students and education providers sufficient time to plan for the changes. As a result, persons from Ukraine commencing a new higher education course in the 2026/27 academic year are subject to student support eligibility criteria that apply under the relevant support schemes, primarily the free fees initiative and the student grant scheme. Information is available at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-further-and-higher-education-research-innovation-and-science/publications/supports-to-beneficiaries-of-temporary-protection-botp-for-academic-year-20262027/ . It should also be noted that higher education institutions are autonomous bodies and are responsible for determining their own policies and procedures in relation to tuition fee classifications. This includes the criteria that students must meet to qualify for an institution's own EU rate of tuition fees or whether an institutions non-EU fee rate applies. The assessment of an individual student's fee status and the determination of the applicable fee category and fee rate are matters for the institution concerned. The Department remains committed to supporting equitable access to education and continues to engage with the sector to ensure that students from Ukraine are informed of the supports available to them through the mainstream student support system.

question: 4163. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he intends to introduce minimum notice periods for changes to SICAP or IPAS related funding streams to ensure adequate workforce planning and programme delivery; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [62849/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP), is our country’s primary social inclusion intervention programme overseen by my Department. This is a national programme that is delivered in both rural and urban areas by Local Development Companies (LDCs) to help those in the greatest need. It was vital that I secured an additional €1.5m for SICAP in Budget 2026, bringing the annual funding for SICAP to over €50m and continuing the positive funding trend in recent years, in line with commitments in the Programme for Government. In regard to SICAP's work with New Arrivals, additional New Arrivals supports were introduced in 2022, in response to the arrival of Ukrainians to communities across Ireland and this was later extended to provide supports to International Protection Applicants. Since 2022, approximately €46m in additional funding has been allocated for delivery of supports to New Arrivals through SICAP. While SICAP is a multi-annual programme, year to year funding allocations are subject to agreement as part of the annual budgetary estimate process. This is also the case with the additional New Arrivals funding, which is not a multi-annual commitment. This distinction is communicated to SICAP Programme Implementers with each of the allocations every year. The additional funding allocated to SICAP in respect of New Arrivals is for delivery of SICAP services only to individuals and groups that fall under SICAP’s target groups, which already include refugees and international protection applicants, among others. Primary responsibility for the policy-related aspects of IPAS and associated funding streams rests with the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. I am keenly aware of the challenges the budgetary timelines can present to Programme Implementers in terms of workforce planning, and my officials are fully committed to notifying Programme Implementers of their core SICAP allocations and any additional funding streams as soon as is possible.
